text: COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP CONFIDENCE IN SUMMIT WITHDRAWN STOP KEEPER TO SHOW CAUSE WHY APPOINTMENT SHOULD NOT BE REVOKED STOP REPLY WITHIN THE WATCH STOP
Show cause: the figures
You send the Book's figures. They are honest. They are not good. Ardent replies 'noted'.
Show cause: the town
You send the moot's letter, Ilse's, Bram's mark, Crane's seal. Ardent has never received such a thing. It does not know what to do with it.
The Board asked me for a name to replace you. I gave one: a clerk in Ardent who has never seen a lock. The Board will take a month to discover this. You will find that is the month I have bought you.
Use the month
A month. Quiet figures, no letters, the gate at the bell. The Board forgets what is quiet.
Why buy it?
"Because the clerk would not watch the gauge. You will find I have started to want someone to."

I have the revocation in my case. Signed, dated Tuesday. It is Monday. My view, which the Board did not ask for, is that the summit under you has not lost a boat, a hand, or a mark of water it could have kept. Convince me by Tuesday.
Show him the Ledger
He reads it all night. In the morning: "Regrettably, this is not evidence. It is, however, persuasive." He tears the revocation in half.
Show him the gate at work
A day at the gate beside you. He does not speak. At dusk he says 'regrettably' and burns the paper in the lock house stove.

I have been told to prepare the Keeper's house for a successor. I have sat with the order and a pen for two days. Tell me something to write that is not 'no'. I have never written 'no'. I do not know how it is spelled.
Write 'no'
He writes it. Two letters. He looks at it a long time. He sends it. Ardent is silent for a week, astonished.
Write 'the house is not ready'
"Not ready. Yes. It can be not ready for months." It is.
A wire's come through for the constables at Lock 5. It says your name and 'detain pending inquiry'. I haven't sent it on. I'm meant to. I've been sitting here with it for an hour. Tell me what to do.
Send it on
"Right. Right." He sends it. The constables come. Vosk meets them at the boundary stone and they go back. You do not know what she said.
Lose it
"Lost. Yes. I lose things. I've never lost a thing in my life." He loses it. It is the bravest thing he has done.

The Board has stopped writing. Not favorably; silently. The summit runs. The Book balances. Nobody from Ardent has visited in a season. The Ledger's Company page, in Dray's hand, says: 'when they stop writing, they have decided. Find out what.'
Find out what
Fennick reads the Ardent code for a week. They have decided nothing. They have forgotten the summit. It is the safest you have been.
Enjoy the silence
You enjoy it. It lasts. Silence from Ardent is the Company's only gift.
The gauge is at the third mark. Loaded barges cannot enter the chamber. The queue has become a camp. The Reach lies on its side in the mud. The aqueduct, for what it is worth, is running normally.
Close the summit to loaded vessels
Light boats only. Cargo is unloaded on the wharf and carried round by cart. The town hires out every horse it has.
One heavy boat at a time
One boat a watch, dragged over the sill by every hand. The sill loses stones. So does the town's patience.

The chamber floor's showing at the north corner. Nobody has seen it since Year 31. There's a grating in it, and under the grating, running water, going out, not in. Sorry. The pound has a drain and nobody knew.
Block the grating
Tamm makes a plug. The pound stops falling for two days. Then something under the hill pushes it out.
Follow where the water goes
It goes north, under the bank, toward the sluice house. It always did.

The Reach is aground. All of it. Old boats on their sides, families in the mud, the old singer in a tent. We have never asked the town for shelter. We ask the gate to ask for us, because we cannot make the words.
Ask the town
You ask Ilse. Ilse asks the moot. The moot, astonishing itself, says yes. Forty Hullfolk sleep in the town's lofts.
Open the Company warehouse
Forty Hullfolk in the Company's grain store. Pell finds out and cannot decide how to feel.

A grain fleet has been in the camp nine days. Its master is selling grain to the town at a price it cannot pay, and to Sorrel bargees at one they can. The town is watching its bread go west across a dry pound.
Requisition the grain for the town
Emergency clause. The grain is the town's at a fair price. Aldmere protests. The town eats.
The master sells to whom he likes
The grain goes west by cart. The town watches. Ilse says nothing, loudly.

Nine days. My principals have stopped writing letters and started writing lawyers. I've got a proposal: a Sorrel dredging crew, at Sorrel's cost, to cut the sill down a foot. The Company will never allow it. The Company is nine days away.
Let them cut the sill
Sorrel men with picks in the Company's lock chamber. The sill drops a foot. Heavy boats float. Vosk arrives on the tenth day and looks at the sill a long time.
Nobody cuts the Company's sill
"Then nobody's coal moves. Fine. I'll write to the lawyers myself."

The Board has wired. It uses 'drought' four times and 'Keeper' five. It wishes to know why the reservoirs, 'ample by every report', have failed to sustain the pound. I do not know what to tell them. I have never not known.
Tell them the reservoirs never could
You write it plainly. Pell sends it, hand shaking. Ardent does not reply. Vosk does.
Tell them drought
You write 'drought'. Pell breathes. Ardent replies 'noted'. The pound falls a mark.

Three things. The hands have been pumping the Reach end into the chamber by hand for six days. Two are down with their backs. And they've asked, since there's no boats, whether they're still lock hands or just men with buckets.
Still lock hands; full wages
Paid for pumping. They pump. The pound holds its mark for a week.
Send them home till the rain
Unpaid, home. The chamber dries. Two go down to Lock 6 and do not come back.

Rain, at last. The pound comes up a mark a day for a week. The camp breaks; the Reach floats. In the Ledger, the Year 31 entry ends: 'the pound recovered in a week, without rain'. Yours recovered with it. That is the only difference.
Note the difference
Without rain. Somebody in Year 31 wrote that and knew what it meant.
Note the recovery
The pound is back. The boats are back. You do not ask the water anything. This week.

Three cases of the coalfield fever in the town, off a boat with a clean bill. It spreads in crowds: the inn, the chapel, the queue. I am asking for a quarantine. Nobody has ever closed the summit for a physician.
Quarantine; close the summit
The gate shuts. The queue stops. The inn empties. Three cases stay three.
Isolate the three; keep the gate
Three in the chapel's back room. The gate runs. By the week's end there are nine.

Nine cases. The Board has been informed by someone who is not me. Its instruction is that the summit remain open 'to avoid alarm'. The Board is in Ardent. I am asking you to disobey it, and I will write that you did not.
Disobey; close the gate
"Noted. The gate closed for maintenance." She writes it. Nine cases stay nine.
Obey; stay open
The gate runs. By the month's end there are thirty. Two are children. Vosk does not write anything at all.

The chapel is a hospital. Thirty on pallets in the nave. Stroud has not slept in four days. I carry water from the well, which she says is safe boiled. The town is asking for a Vigil. I am asking for hands.
Every hand to the chapel
The gate closes. Lock hands carry water and bodies. Hale holds the Vigil anyway, at the end, for those who did not need the hands.
Hold the Vigil; the hands keep the gate
Lamps at the sill. Boats through. The town takes the Vigil as an answer. It is not one Stroud accepts.

Four dead. The inn's been shut a month and I've fed the town from the cellar for nothing and I'm not asking for the money. I'm asking why a boat with a clean bill came through your gate, and who signed the bill, and whether you looked.
I didn't look; I should have
"Right. Say it at the burying. They need to hear someone say it." You do.
The bill was clean; nobody could have
"Nobody. Right. Nobody's buried four."

The fever has burned out. Stroud has slept. The queue has come back as if it never left. The Ledger's fever page, from Year 62: 'inspect the bills. Every one. It costs an hour. The other thing costs more.'
Inspect every bill from now
An hour a boat. Traffic slows. Nobody sickens. Crane approves so much he says nothing.
Spot checks; the gate must move
One in five. Faster. Stroud says nothing. She has said it.

Fire in my yard. Tar barrels went first. Season's hulls are next and the Company warehouse after that and the town after that if the wind holds. I've got buckets. The pound's right there. I need every hand and I need them not to argue.

The warehouse fire's jumped to my yard. Tar barrels went first. Season's hulls are next and the town after that if the wind holds. I've got buckets and the pound's right there. I need every hand and I need them not to argue.
Every hand; requisition the town
The whole town on a bucket chain from the pound. The hulls are lost. The town is not.
Cut the yard loose; save the warehouse
The yard burns to the waterline. The warehouse stands. Tamm watches his life go up and says nothing to you again for a month.

Fire's out. It took the yard and two houses on the low street. And the town says it started at the Company warehouse, from a Company lamp, and wants to know why the Company's lamp oil was stacked against Tamm's fence.
Ask the Company the same
You write to Ardent. Ardent replies that lamp oil storage is 'at Keeper's discretion'. It was not. It is now.
Fires start; nobody's to blame
"Right. Nobody. I'll tell the two families nobody."

Eleven burned. Two badly. One is Perrin, five children, flooded cellar, and now no hands to work with. I can keep him alive. I cannot keep him a lock hand. The compensation form has a line for 'cause'. What do I write?
'Company lamp oil, improperly stored'
Perrin is compensated in full. Ardent notes the cause. Vosk notes that you wrote it.
'Accident'
Perrin is compensated at half. The town knows what the form says. Stroud does not argue. She writes her own letter.

Two families with no house. The inn's full. Cole has empty rooms and a price. The Company has a warehouse, half-burned, and a rule about townsfolk in Company buildings. I've asked both. Both said ask the Keeper. Everyone says ask the Keeper.
The warehouse, rule or no rule
Two families in the Company's half-burned warehouse. Pell finds out and, for once, says nothing at all.
Pay Cole's price from the Coffers
Cole is paid. The families are housed. The Book has a line Vosk reads twice.

The yard is a black square by the water. Tamm has started again on the far side, with the Hullfolk's driftwood and the town's nails. The Ledger has no fire page. You start one. It begins: 'the pound was right there'.
Fund the new yard
Company timber, quietly. Tamm does not ask where it came from. He builds a better yard.
Let the town rebuild it
The town rebuilds it. Slowly. It is the town's yard now, whatever the lease says.

A cloudburst on the Spine. Every stream on the north bank is a torrent and the pound is up two marks in a night. The overflow weir is roaring and the east embankment is dark with seepage from end to end.
Every paddle open, now
Water thunders down the east flight. Lock 8 floods its towpath. The pound steadies.
Sandbag the embankment first
The town on the bank with sacks all night. The seepage slows. The pound does not.

The low street is under. Not cellars. Street. There are people on their roofs and the chapel undercroft's a well and the sandbags have gone down the flight with the rest. The moot's not meeting. The moot's bailing. Where's the Keeper?
On the paddles
You run every paddle yourself while Dace's men take boats to the roofs.
On a boat to the roofs
You pull eleven people off roofs. The pound does not fall. It waits for you.
Three things. The east embankment's got a boil in it the size of a barrel, below the chapel. Quenn says an hour, maybe two. And every hand I've got is on a roof or a paddle.
Every hand to the boil
Stone, timber, sacks, bodies. The boil stops. The roofs wait.
Cut the west bank into the Reach
The Reach floods to the gunwales. The east bank holds. The Hullfolk will not forget the choosing.

The pound is coming in faster than rain can explain. The inflow at the north bank is a boil the size of a house. Whatever feeds the pound has opened up. Sorry. I don't know how to close it. I don't think anyone alive does.
Ask Vosk
"Noted." Vosk goes to the sluice house alone with the Company key. By morning the boil is smaller. She does not explain.
Drain the flight; buy time
Every paddle for three days. The lower pounds flood. The summit holds. Aldmere writes.

The chapel is an island. The undercroft is full to the nave floor and the founding chest has floated up the steps and lies open in the aisle. Letters everywhere, wet. The town is coming for shelter and will read them.
Gather the letters; shelter the town
You and Hale gather letters in the dark while the town comes in. Some are read. Some are lost. The town hears a name: Marrow.
Shelter the town; let the letters go
The letters go down the aisle and out the door on the flood. Some reach the pound. Bram's people find them. He reads.

Two drowned on the low street. A lock hand and a child. I have laid them out at the inn. The town is not shouting. It is very quiet. In Year 44 it was quiet too, for about a day. Do something before the day is over.
Go to the inn and stand with them
You stand with the town at the laying-out. Nobody speaks to you. Nobody asks you to leave.
Drain the pound; nothing else matters
The paddles run for two days. The pound falls. The town buries its dead without you.

The pound has stopped rising. It has not started falling. The embankment holds, barely, with the whole town's timber in it. The rain has stopped. The north bank boil has not. Somewhere under the hill something is open that was shut.
Go to the sluice house tonight
Iron straps. A key you may or may not have. The sound of a river behind a door.
Hold the paddles open and wait
A week of open paddles. The pound falls a mark a day. The boil dwindles. Nobody explains it.

The water is down. The low street is mud. In the Ledger there is a page for floods, in three Keepers' hands, and yours is the fourth. Every entry ends the same way: 'the pound was higher than the reservoirs could explain'.
Write the same
The fourth hand. The same sentence. Someone will read it.
Write what the town lost
Names. A cellar count. A child. The Ledger has never had names in it before.

Hard frost. The west flight has frozen solid to Lock 5 and forty boats are trapped in the pound with a month's food between them and no way down. The east flight is open but the pound itself is skinning over. By morning it may not be.
Break the ice all night
Every hand with a pole, all night, every night. The pound stays open. The hands stay awake.
Let it freeze; ration the town
The pound freezes. Forty crews walk into town. The Company store is emptied in a week.

Three things. The Company store's empty. Forty bargees and their families are eating the town's winter. And a Sorrel crew has broken into the grain warehouse and is handing it out, which is theft, and also the only thing keeping anyone fed.
Let them hand it out; call it requisition
Grain for everyone, by order. Aldmere's grain factor will want paying. Later. If there is a later.
Stop them; the grain is Aldmere's
Dace stops them. The grain is Aldmere's. The town is hungry and looking at the warehouse door.

My boats are in ice and my crews are eating your town and my principals are asking why I let it happen. I've a Sorrel ice-breaker at Lock 4. It could cut through in three days. It's a Sorrel vessel in Company water without a permit. Say yes.
Yes
A Sorrel ice-breaker cuts the west flight open in three days. Crane records the permit violation. Nobody cares. Everybody eats.
No Sorrel vessels without a permit
"Then we all freeze together. Fine. I'll write it up as your decision."

A child from a trapped boat has the winter cough and it has gone to her chest. I have nothing left. There is a physician at Lock 3 with what I need and the flight is ice. Someone could walk it. Nobody has since Year 31.
Walk it yourself
Nine miles of ice in the dark. You come back with a bottle and no feeling in your hands. The child lives.
Send Wren; she knows ice
Wren goes. She is back by dawn, grinning, frozen. The child lives. Wren does not let you forget it.

Thaw. Forty boats go down the west flight in a day, thin and quiet. The town counts its winter and finds it short. The Ledger's frost page, in Tobin's hand from Year 31: 'the pound froze because it was low. Ask why it was low.'
Ask why it was low
You know why. You write that you know. It is the first Ledger entry that says so plainly.
Restock the town first
The Coffers buy the town's winter back. Vosk reads the entry and says nothing, which is a gift.

The queue has reached Lock 6. Sixty boats. The lower pounds are so full of moored hulls that nothing can move in either direction. Aldmere has posted a cutter at Lock 5 to stop more coming up. It is not a queue now. It is a wall.
Work through the night, every night
Lamps for a week. The hands sleep on the beam. The wall shortens to Lock 7.
Turn back everything west of Lock 7
Twenty boats sent back down. Sorrel is livid. The wall becomes a queue.

Twelve days. My principals have sent a man to replace me. He's at Lock 4, waiting in your queue. When he gets here I'm finished and you get someone who doesn't ask. I'd like to still be here. Clear my boats. Anything. Now.
Sorrel boats first, until she's safe
Twenty Sorrel boats through in two days. The replacement arrives to find nothing to replace. Crane writes eleven pages.
In order; I'm sorry
"Sorry. Right." She is replaced. The new man does not ask. He pays.

Aldmere has invoked the Compact's embargo clause. No grain passes the summit until the queue is 'cleared to Aldmere's satisfaction'. I did not advise it. I note that satisfaction is not defined. I note that I am the one who must define it.
Ask him to define it kindly
"Kindly. Duly." He defines it as 'no vessel waiting more than three days'. It is nearly achievable.
Defy the embargo
Grain passes under your signature. Aldmere sends a second cutter. Crane does not speak to you for a week, then does, sadly.
Three things. A bargee in the queue has been stabbed over a place. He'll live. The one who did it has forty friends in the queue and the town has a rope. And I've eleven men and no constables.
Hold him in the lock house for Crane
Crane holds a hearing under the Compact. It is very long. Nobody is hanged. The queue watches every minute.
Send him down the flight, now
He goes west in the night on a Hullfolk boat. The town's rope stays coiled. Justice, of a kind.

The Board has sent the word 'remove'. Not yet with a name. The queue is in every newspaper on both shores and one has a drawing of the summit with a padlock on it. I have one week to send figures the Board can bear. One week, Keeper.
Suspend tolls and inspections for the week
Free, uninspected passage. Sixty boats in a week. The chest is empty and Crane is silent. The Board bears it.
Send the true figures
The true figures. The Board's next word has a name in it.

The queue's become a town of its own. Sixty boats, three hundred people, a market, two fights a day. Somebody's going to burn something. My men could patrol it. Aldmere would call that an occupation. Aldmere's cutter is at Lock 5, not here.
Patrol it
Sorrel soldiers walking a Company towpath. Nothing burns. Crane files. Aldmere protests. The queue sleeps.
The town's constable and Dace's men
One constable and eleven tired hands. Something burns: a tent. Nobody is hurt. Barely.

The queue is a queue again. Twenty boats, orderly, complaining. The Ledger's jam page has two other Keepers' hands on it. Both end: 'the pound would not carry what the Company sent'. The pound is a mark lower than when it began.
Write it
The third hand. The same sentence.
Write the number of boats
Numbers. The Board likes numbers. So, it turns out, do you.

The chest is empty, the hands unpaid, and I hold the town's debts and now, kindly, yours. I have sent the Company a copy of every note. Commissioner Kell arrives Tuesday. I am telling you so you may prepare a face.
Pay her something, anything
You sell the good chair and the Company lamp oil. She accepts it, kindly, and withdraws one of the notes.
Let Kell come
Kell comes. He reads the notes. He says 'regrettably' four times.

The chest cannot meet wages and the Company will not advance them again. There is a fund for 'exceptional maintenance' that nobody audits but me. Wages are not maintenance. I am asking whether the gate is.
The gate is maintenance
"Noted." Wages appear from a fund that does not exist for wages. She has done this before. Once.
Don't lie for me
"Noted. I have lied for the Company eleven years. I would have liked to lie for a gate once."

Three things. Nobody's been paid in three watches. Six hands have gone down the flight to Lock 6 where the Keeper pays. And the five left have asked me to tell you they're staying because of you, not the Company, and they'd like that written down somewhere.
Write it in the Ledger, with their names
Five names in the Ledger. It has never had lock hands' names in it. They come to see.
Tell them to go to Lock 6 too
"Right." They don't go. They work unpaid. It is worse than if they'd gone.

The moot's had a whip-round. For the Keeper's chest. Nobody's ever done that for a Company post. It's not much. It's the town's beer money for a month. Take it and the Company owns nothing here; refuse it and the town'll never offer again.
Take it
The town's beer money in the Company's chest. Vosk sees the entry. 'Irregular.' She does not strike it.
Refuse it, gratefully
"Gratefully. Right." The town drinks its beer money and toasts you with it, which is something.

The Board's view is that a post which cannot pay its hands is a post in default. Regrettably, default has consequences: the account is frozen, the Keeper's salary is suspended, and a Company clerk will keep the Book until the account recovers. Do carry on. Under supervision.
Accept supervision
A clerk from Ardent at your elbow for a month. He is very young. He counts everything. The account recovers.
The town will fund the gate
"The town. Regrettably, the Board has no view on the town." The town has one on the Board.
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP ACCOUNT IRREGULARITY NOTED STOP SURPLUS EXCEEDS TOLL CAPACITY STOP BOARD AUDITOR DISPATCHED STOP EXPLAIN BY RETURN STOP
Remit the surplus tonight
The chest goes east in a strongbox by the last boat. The auditor arrives to find a book that balances.
'GIFTS FROM GRATEFUL BARGEES'
The auditor arrives. He asks which bargees. You do not have names.
The chest is neither empty nor suspicious. Wages paid, Cole paid, the Book balanced to the mark. The Ledger's money page has one other hand: 'a Keeper who is rich or poor is noticed. Be neither.'
Be neither
You write it under the other hand. It is good advice. It is hard.
Bury a reserve in the false bottom
Twenty marks under Dray's board. Neither rich nor poor. Prepared.

Two boats in the chamber and a third coming in because nobody said stop. The paddles are running. The hulls are grinding. A bargee has jumped for the wall and missed. Everything is happening at once and none of it slowly.
Drop the paddles; dive for the bargee
You go in. He comes out. The boats settle against each other like tired animals. Nobody is under them.
Drop the paddles; Dace gets the bargee
Dace gets him with a hook. The boats settle. The third has a hole in her bow you could put a barrel through.
The coal boat's holed and sinking in the chamber. If she goes down there the gate's blocked for a month. I can beach her on the sill if we drain now, and lose the sill facing. Or she sinks. Pick.
Drain and beach her
She grounds on the sill with a sound of breaking stone. The chamber is clear by dark. The sill is not what it was.
Let her sink; raise her later
She sinks in the chamber. Three weeks with Tamm's rig. Sixty boats wait. The sill lives.

One dead. Crushed between the hulls. A Sorrel bargee, young, with a wife at Lock 3 who does not know yet. I will write to her. I would like the Keeper to sign the letter, because the Company's form does not have a place for sorry and mine does.
Sign it
You sign under 'sorry'. It is the only Company letter that has ever had the word.
The Company's form only
"The form. Yes. I shall send mine anyway, unsigned. She will know whose it is."

A collision in the chamber. A death. The Board requires an inquiry and the inquiry requires a name. The order to run two boats a filling was given. The Book does not say by whom. You will find I am asking whom to write.
Write mine
"Noted." She writes it. Then she writes, beneath it, 'under Superintendent's standing instruction'. Pell does not thank her. He does not know.
Write Pell's
"Noted." She writes it. Pell is scolded for nine pages and does not speak to you for a month.

I have examined the chamber. Two vessels, one filling, contrary to regulation and the Compact's safety schedule. I have the dates of every such passage this quarter. Forty-one. I am obliged to report them. I take no pleasure in it.
Report them all
"Duly." Forty-one breaches to Aldmere. Aldmere demands the summit slow. It slows.
Report the one
"One. I note that is not what happened. I note I am doing it anyway, which I shall regret."

The chamber is clear. The gate runs one boat a filling, at the bell. The record is gone and so is a man. In the Ledger the pile-up page has one other hand, from Year 58: 'we were told to go faster, and we did'.
Write the same
You write it. It is still true.
Write 'one boat a filling, always'
A rule, in the Ledger, for the next Keeper. Whether they read it is theirs.

A quiet watch. The first in a season. No queue past Lock 8, no water over the path, a chest that closes, a Board that has stopped writing, a town that nods. The Ledger has a page for quiet watches. It is the shortest page. It says: 'they end'.
Use it: walk the north bank
In daylight, for once. The sluice house. The clear stream. You see it all plainly and nobody stops you.
Use it: sleep
You sleep a whole night. The gate does not fall down. Stroud is smug for a week.
You've had a bad season. I've watched it from Lock 8. Dray had a bad season too, his second year. He came out of it different. Quieter. Started asking about the tenth mark. Just saying.
Ask about the tenth mark
"Below the sill. Painted over in Year 31. For when the pound goes where it shouldn't."
Come out of it louder
"Louder. Ha. Nobody's tried louder. Might work."

The town has come through something. The chapel does not keep that kind of ledger. It wishes to give thanks, and has asked, for the first time in my memory, that the Keeper stand at the front. Not the last pew.
Stand at the front
You stand where the chaplain stands. The town looks at you. It is worse than the boundary stone and better than anything.
The last pew, with Vosk
You sit in the last pew. Vosk sits beside you. Hale gives thanks anyway. The town turns to look, twice.

The moot's voted you a name. Not 'the Keeper', not 'the new one'. A name. Yours, the one you gave Mirren, which she told me, which I told the moot. It's on a board over the bar now. It'll come down if you earn it. Don't.
Don't
"Right." The board stays up. It is the only thing at the summit with your name on it that the Company did not write.
Put the hands' names beside it
Eleven names beside yours. Dace pretends not to look at it. He looks at it every night.

Keeper! We have come through. Whatever it was, we have come through it, and the Board, which knows nothing of what it was, has written 'satisfactory'. Satisfactory! I have not seen the word in eleven years. I have framed it. Come and look at the frame.
Look at the frame
It is a very good frame. He has hung it beside a blank space he says is for the next one.
Ask what 'satisfactory' cost
"Cost? Nothing. Everything. A season. Magnificent." He means all four.

There's a crowd at the Company house. Not a mob. Not yet. A crowd with lamps and one voice too many. They want the Keeper to come out and say whose side the gate is on. I've told them you're coming. Come.
Go out and speak
You speak from the step. You say the gate's. It is not what they wanted. It is enough to go home on.
Send Dace to disperse them
Dace goes out. He is one of them. He comes back in. They do not disperse.

Three things. Somebody's thrown a lamp through the Company house window. It didn't catch. The crowd's gone quiet, which is worse than loud. And the constable's asked me whose men mine are: the Company's or the town's. I didn't have an answer.
The town's; stand them down
The hands go home. The Company house stands empty and unguarded. Nobody touches it. That is the town's answer.
The Company's; guard the house
Eleven hands in a line before the Company house, facing their neighbors. Nobody moves. By dawn the hands are not the town's any more.

A man on the wharf with a torch, and thirty behind him, and the Company warehouse full of grain and lamp oil. He does not know you. He knows the Company. He asks the Keeper, quite politely, to step aside.

A man on the wharf with a torch, and thirty behind him, and the Reach beyond with forty boats and a Clearance order on every hull. He asks the Keeper, quite politely, whether the order stands, because if it does he means to help it along.
Don't step aside
You stand in front of the warehouse. He looks at you a long time. Somebody behind him laughs. Somebody else takes his torch.
Step aside
The warehouse burns. The town watches. The Company's grain and lamp oil light the pound orange until dawn.

The town has stopped paying rent. All of it. To me. They say it is about the Keeper; I say it is about money, which everything is. I have written to the Company for constables. The Company has written back asking whether the Keeper approved. Did you?
No constables
"Then no rent. Kindly." She waits. She is very good at it. The town is not.
Constables, for the rent only
Constables collect rent in Company green. The town pays. The town remembers who let them in.

The Courier's Aldmere edition has a piece about the summit 'in revolt'. It's mine. It's mostly true. Ardent has read it and is sending someone. I can print a second piece, calmer, tomorrow. Or I can print what happens when Ardent's someone arrives. Your pick.
The calmer piece
HALFWAY: A TOWN AT PEACE. It is not, quite. It becomes so, partly because it was printed.
Print what happens
"Right. I'll bring a plate-man." Ardent's someone arrives to find a newspaperman and a crowd and does not know which to arrest.

The town's on the wharf with lamps and the Company house is dark and Ardent's constables are at Lock 8 asking me to hold the towpath till they arrive. I've got twelve men. The town's got three hundred. I'd rather nobody found out which number matters.

The town's on the wharf. Half want the Reach cleared tonight and half want the constables gone. Both halves have lamps. Ardent's constables are at Lock 8. I've got twelve men and I'm asking which half I'm standing in front of.
Stand between the town and the constables
Sorrel soldiers facing Company constables on a Company towpath, with a town behind them. Nobody moves till dawn. At dawn the constables go back.
Stand aside; let it happen
He stands aside. It happens. In the morning there is a boy on the towpath who does not stand up.

It's happening. The town's risen. For you, they say, and against the Company. They've barred the Company house with Pell in it and cut the tow ropes and somebody's singing. I buried a boy after the last one. Stop them.
Stop them
You stand on the wharf and tell them to go home. You say Pell is a fool, not an enemy. You say the water is the enemy. They go home. Slowly. For you.
Let them rise
They rise. Pell is walked to the boundary stone. The Company house is the town's by morning. So, on paper, is the Keeper's neck.

The town has gone home. The Company house has a new window. In the Ledger, the riot page from Year 44 ends: 'they will forgive the Company, in time. They will not forgive the Keeper who let them.' You did not let them.
Write it
'The Keeper did not let them.' It is true. It may be enough.
Write what they wanted
You write what the town wanted: the water. It has always been the water.
It came up the east flight in a boat with a clean bill. You have it now. I will sit with you. There was nothing to be done, I will say afterward, and I am not certain it is true.
Ask her to say it anyway
She does. She is a good physician.
Tell her what you noticed about the water
She writes it down. Doctors keep ledgers too.
Yard's gone to the waterline. Season's hulls with it. Town says Company. Company says you. I say you were holding a bucket, same as me, and it'll hold or it won't.
Stay and help clear
Three days of ash. Then the telegram.
Face the Company first
The telegram is already written.
Forty boats frozen in the pound and the Company store half empty for a month. Two children did not see the thaw. The ice is going now. So, I think, are you.
On the first barge down
Nobody sees you off. That is a kindness.
Ask if you could have done more
"Yes. So could I. That is the job."
The inquiry finds as follows. The order bore your signature. The Company keeps orders. Regrettably, it does not keep Keepers who sign them. The Board's view is that this concludes matters.
Ask who drafted the order
"The Board's view is that this is immaterial."
Sign the finding
Your signature again. It is what they keep.
It started at my inn and ended at your gate. Nobody remembers who threw the first lamp. The Company's report will say you failed to prevent it. Mine says nothing. I have said enough.
You could have stopped it
"So could you. Earlier."
Nobody could
"Somebody did, once. Then his son drowned."
Nine nights of the Lamp Vigil, and on the tenth, rain for a week. The pound is full. The chapel is full. We do not ask the water, Keeper. We tend it, and it answers.
Kneel with the rest
It is a comfort. It is also a wet season.
Ask how long it will last
"As long as it is tended." She believes it. Almost.
The Reed Reach is clear. Not a shot, Keeper, not one. The boats went down the west flight this morning. Quieter, isn't it. Our little difficulty, resolved at last.
It is quieter
Nobody sings at the summit again.
Ask where they went
"West. Where they came from, one assumes." One assumes wrong.

It's published. The figures, all of them. The Board has thanked me, blamed the weather, raised the tolls and commissioned a tenth reservoir. Twelve years to fill. Sorry. I thought it would be different.
It was the right thing
"It was a thing. Roughly."
The figures were never the whole of it
"No. What was?" You do not know yet.

Front page on both shores. THE KEEPER WHO WOULD NOT BEND. You're famous, Keeper. The Company can't dismiss a hero, so it's giving you a lecture tour, and the summit a new Keeper, and the sluice house a new lock.
Take the tour
You tell the story forty times. It gets shorter.
Ask about the new lock
"Off the record? Big one."
You have accused me of Dray's death and the Board has accepted it. I am removed. For the record, I did not kill him. For the record, I know where he is. You will not ask.
Ask
She is already walking.
Let her go
A new auditor arrives within the week, and asks the same questions.
Done. My principals own the Sorrel half as of this watch. Tolls down, traffic up, and you stay on at a better wage. Delay costs, Keeper, and now it costs me. Shake.
Shake
Two summers later the pound falls to the sills and nobody in Sorrel knows why.
Ask what she knows about the water
"That it floats coal. What else is there?"
Your file reads 'reliable'. For the record, that is the Company's highest word. You have kept the gate a hundred watches and never once asked me about the sluice house.
Ask her now
"No." She almost smiles. "You will find that was the right time."
Say it was not your business
"Noted."
Eighty years, a record day, and not one boat grounded. Your name goes on the plaque beside the top gate. Bronze, Keeper. The Meridian spirit, cast in bronze.
Stand for the unveiling
Bronze goes green, in time. So does everything here.
Put Quenn's name beside yours
He agrees at once, and means it.
A hundred watches. The Company offers a cottage below Lock 7 and a pension in scrip. The gauge on the sill reads what it reads. Somebody else will have to notice.
Take the cottage
The garden floods every spring. You keep it anyway.
Ask for one more year
"Regrettably." The cottage, then.
There is a wedding at the Still Water chapel and the whole summit comes, the geese included. The gauge reads what it reads. For once, you are not looking at it.
Dance
Badly. Nobody minds.
Watch the water anyway
Old habits. It is a mark lower than it was.
The moot voted you a chair. Not a title. A chair, by the fire, and a tankard with your name on it. Your Company gave nothing. You knew that.
Sit in it
"Costs nothing. First thing here that does."
Give the chair to Dace
Dace sits in it once, to be polite, and never again.
Keeper! Magnificent news. Lock 3, Sorrel side. Quieter water, a bigger house, a lower toll book. The Board calls it a promotion and so, Keeper, shall we.
Accept it
The barge down is the first you have ridden in a year.
Ask why
"Our little difficulty, Keeper. Nothing more."
The account shows a surplus the toll table cannot produce. For the record, I asked you twice. There is one explanation in the manual. The constables know it too.
The account shows a surplus the toll table cannot produce. I asked you twice, and I wanted you to have an answer. You will find I have written the kindest version that is still true.
It was for the gates
"Noted. It is not what the manual calls it."
Say nothing
"Noted."
The Board regrets. Wages unpaid for three watches constitute abandonment of the works. The account is closed and the appointment with it. Arrangements have been made for your furniture.
Ask who bought it
"Mrs Cole, at a fair price. Regrettably."
Ask who keeps the gate
"Someone will. Someone always does."
The Board's view is that you are the Meridian Canal. Your likeness will go on the Jubilee medal and your name on every statement about the water. You need only say yes.
The Board's view is that you are the Meridian Canal. You have read the file, so you understand exactly what the medal is for. You need only say yes.
Yes
The medal is bronze. The crowd, later, will know the face.
Ask for time
"The Board's view is that there is none."
COMPANY TO KEEPER HALFWAY STOP APPOINTMENT REVOKED STOP VACATE BY NEXT WATCH STOP HAND BOOK AND KEYS TO AUDITOR STOP
Hand over the Book
Vosk takes it without opening it.
Tear out your pages first
The Ledger is not the Book. You keep the Ledger.
The town has risen for you and against the charter. I have orders to take you east. I have also told my people not to load. Come quietly and nobody here learns what a rifle sounds like.
Go quietly
The town watches. Nobody fires. He was right about that.
Ask the town to stand down
They do, for you. Then you go east anyway.
Nobody is shouting. The doors are barred, the tow ropes are cut, and the town is walking you to the boundary stone with lamps. I am carrying one. I am sorry about that.
Walk with them
At the stone she says, "It costs what it costs."
Ask her to stop it
"I could have. Before."

Two in the chamber, Keeper, both at speed, because nobody was counting any more. The coal boat's under the grain boat. Stroud is down there. Three things: you'll want to come, you'll want to not, and it doesn't matter.
Go down
You go down.
Send for the Company
Dace looks at you the way he looks at a broken paddle.
Keeper. Forty-one vessels between here and Lock 6. Aldmere has closed its flight. The Board has wired. I did not read it aloud. I am reading it to you now.
Ask what it says
"'Remove.' One word. They used to write more."
You know what it says
He folds it very small.
At the third bell the east embankment goes. The sound is not loud. Then the town's lamps go out one street at a time, from the bottom up.
At the third bell the east embankment goes. Nobody sandbagged; nobody would come when you called. The town's lamps go out from the bottom up.
Run for the paddles
Too late, and you know it.
Run for the town
You carry a child up Chapel Street. It is one.
The gauge reads nothing. A grain barge settles onto the sill with a sound like a door closing. The chamber is a stone room with a boat in it.
The gauge reads nothing. Quenn stands beside you with her folio shut. "The figures said this," she says. "Sorry. They said this."
Write the true figures
The last entry in your hand.
Write 'drought'
The Company will read it, and agree.
At the boundary stone Bram Holloway stands up, which he does not do. "We hold a place on the north bank where the water comes out of the hill. We have never said it. We say it now, to a gate."
Take the bearing
He gives it in the old way, by lamps and stones.
Ask why now
"Because you are leaving, and the remembered are not."
The last night, and the cipher gives. It was the gauge marks all along. The ledger is a map. She reads it over your shoulder and says nothing for a long time.
Give her the ledger
"He drew this. He was going in." She keeps it.
Copy it into the Ledger first
She lets you. Then she takes it.
You are dismissed and I am recalled. I note that my report under Schedule Nine includes six years of water counts. Aldmere will not read it. I have taken the liberty of a second copy.
For the Ledger
"Duly. I did not say that."
For Quenn
"She has them already. Hers are more precise."
They found you with Vosk's file open on the desk. You're removed. I shouldn't tell you this, Keeper, but I wired the first page to the Ledger office before they took it. In strictest confidence.
Thank him
He goes red to the eyeshade.
Tell him to burn his copy
"I already did. The other copy."
The Breach has emptied the undercroft into Chapel Street. Hale is on her knees in the mud gathering letters in an engineer's hand. She looks up at you and holds one out.
Take it
"The water I have given." Marrow's hand. You read it by lamplight, once.
Help her gather them
She gives you one anyway, at the end.
Behind the sluice house the tunnel goes down, then under. Your lamp lasts long enough to show a second lamp, rusted, and a coat on the stone that had been Dray's. The water is very cold.
Reach for the coat
The Ledger records what you saw. Not what came after.
Turn back
The way back is not where you left it.
At the boundary stone, while the town stands with its lamps, the old woman sings the last verse. The one about the river that went into the hill. The town hears it too.
Listen to the end
You have the words now. The Ledger has them.
Ask the town if they heard
Some of them did. Ilse did.
They've dismissed you. One watch after you read it. I'm copying the survey out by hand before they empty the drawer. Take the copy. Put it somewhere they don't read.
The Ledger
"Good. Sorry. Good."
Give it to Crane
"He'll file it. That's roughly the same thing."

Tobin's gone, in the spring, in his chair. He left you the tankard and a story he never finished: the Dry Year men who came at night to dredge a reservoir, with no dredgers, and went into the hill instead.
Write it down
In the Ledger, in full, for the next one.
Tell it to Mirren
She listens the way he did.

I deliver this one myself. You are dismissed. For the record, and only for the record, the Company has known since the Dry Year. I will leave the door open behind me. You will find that is not an accident.
Ask why she is telling you
"Because the next one will ask too, and I am tired."
Go through the door
The file is on her desk. You have one watch.
The regulating sluice she died building is finished. The pound holds. Lowmere has a stream by autumn. Nobody knows. For the record, you have chosen to be me. You will find it is not nothing.
Take the key
Brass, stamped S.H. It was always going to be someone.
Give the key to Hale
"We tend it," she says. "That is all we ever did."

Under the Compact, Schedule Nine, both shores now hold the same document in the same watch: Quenn's figures, Marrow's letters, Hesse's front page, my seal. I note that the Company has no schedule for this.
Sign as witness
The charter falls within the year. The canal does not.
Let the town sign first
Ilse signs. Then Dace. Then everyone.
Dawn. Marrow's sluice is open and the Quell is going home under the hill. The pound is falling to a road. "We have never thanked a gate," Bram says. "We are learning."
Go down with them
The west flight, then a dry valley with a river in it.
Keep the smaller gate
A seasonal canal needs a Keeper too.
A Sorrel barge declares iron ingots. The waterline says it carries something heavier. The bargee is already reaching for the toll.
Open the hold
Ingots on top. Lead shot underneath. He shrugs.
Iron is iron
The toll is paid twice over, quietly.
I note that this vessel's manifest lists forty barrels and I have counted forty-three. Schedule Two is unambiguous about miscounts.
Impound the three
"Duly." The bargee calls you something under his breath.
A clerk's error
"The Compact does not recognize clerks' errors."
Six coal barges, one manifest, one seal, one toll. My principals call it a fleet. Your predecessor called it six boats and charged six tolls. Delay costs, Keeper.
Six boats, six tolls
"Fine. I'll add it to the bill."
One fleet, one toll
"See? We can fix that."
There's a boat two back in the queue with a hold full of nothing. Cargo. I'm telling you so you don't look, not so you do.
Look anyway
Nothing, as she said. Very neatly stacked nothing.
Don't look
The boat passes. Wren does not mention it again.
Three things. The grain boat's papers are Aldmere. The grain is Sorrel, by the sacks. And the bargee's asking if we're the sort of gate that notices.
We notice
Grain is impounded pending the right stamp. Somebody is furious somewhere.
Grain is grain
"Right. Just so I know what sort."
A passenger packet from Aldmere: twelve travellers, luggage roped high. One trunk is leaking a slow red stain onto the deck.
Open the trunk
Beetroot. Forty pounds of it. The traveller weeps with relief.
Not your business
The packet goes through. The stain stays in your mind.
A most interesting case. Live geese are livestock under Schedule Two but poultry under Schedule Five, and the tolls differ. I have prepared a memorandum.
Livestock
"A defensible reading." He is visibly thrilled.
Poultry
"Also defensible. I shall note both."
Your inspector has had my ironwork barge open for two hours over a stamp. Two hours. My principals will hear the word 'Halfway' and it will not be a good word.
Tell Crane to finish
He finishes. In another hour.
The inspector has his reasons
"So do I. Mine pay."
All right. Yes. That's my crate under the tarpaulin, and yes, it's the one I said wasn't. Tell me what it costs and I'll tell you if I have it.
It costs the crate
She lets it go without a word, which is how you know it mattered.
It costs a favor, later
"Done. Don't ask for a big one."
Coal barge wants to unload half its load on our wharf to lighten for the sills, then reload below. That's a day's hands. Company says it's the boat's problem.
Lend the hands
A day's coal dust and a grateful crew.
The boat's problem
It sits in the pound for two days working it out.
A boat of Concordance lamp-oil, blessed and sealed, bound for the chapels of Sorrel. The Sorrel inspector wants it opened. The seal, the pilgrims say, is the point.
Respect the seal
The oil passes unopened. Sorrel's man writes a note.
Open it
Lamp-oil, all of it. The pilgrims re-bless it, slowly.
There is a crate marked 'agricultural implements' with a Sorrel Escort Company seal. Schedule Four. I require the second seal or the crate does not move. I am quite firm.
Hold the crate
Solas arrives within the hour and says nothing at all.
One seal will serve
"I note that. I note it in ink."
Off the record: a Sorrel printing press, in pieces, in three barrels marked pickles. The Aldmere guilds would rather it never arrived. I would rather it did. What would you rather?
Pickles, then
The barrels pass. Aldmere gets a newspaper it did not ask for.
Declare it properly
Crane is delighted for a week.
No jokes. There's medicine on that boat for the coalfield towns and the Sorrel inspector's holding it for a fee. Children's medicine. You could pass it as Company mail.
Company mail
It goes through first. You sign a lie in the Book.
Pay the fee from the Coffers
Legal, slow, and yours.
Barge riding low, Keeper. The bargee says ballast. And there's a smell like a cellar with a cat in it.
Open it
Cheese. A hold of it, ripening in the sun. The hands will not go down.
Pass it, quickly
The smell hangs over the pound until nightfall.
A Company barge marked 'reservoir works' waits with a tarpaulin over the whole load and a foreman who says the Keeper's inspection right does not apply to Company cargo.
It applies
Under the tarpaulin: masonry, timber shoring, lamps. A lot of lamps.
Company cargo passes
The foreman touches his cap. Vosk hears of it approvingly.
The Compact provides for a joint inspection where cargo is disputed between shores. The Sorrel agent has declined to attend. I propose to inspect alone, duly witnessed by you.
Witness it
An hour of counting. Nothing wrong. He is quietly disappointed.
No inspection without both
"A strict reading. I respect it, and disagree."
My principals will pay a standing fee for coal barges to pass without the hold check. Call it a season ticket. Everybody does it at Lock 4.
A season ticket
The Coffers swell. The Book has a new column nobody taught you.
Not at Lock 9
"Lock 9. Right. I'll remember which one."
Somebody left a basket of eels on the sill for the Keeper. Still lively. It'd be rude not to. It'd also be rude to ask who.
Take the eels
Ilse cooks them. The Book says nothing about eels.
Give them to the chapel
Hale feeds six people. Wren sighs.
An empty boat going east, riding high, toll paid in advance by wire. The bargee cannot say who paid or what he will carry back. He seems not to know himself.
Hold him until he does
By evening a wire arrives from Ardent releasing him. The wire is signed 'A.K.'
Paid is paid
He goes down the east flight, high and quiet.
The blessing of vessels falls on the first day of the month. Every boat in the pound receives the lamp. It takes a morning. The Company has never asked us to stop, and never asked us to hurry.
The morning is the chapel's
Lamps over every hull. The queue is patient in a way it never is for you.
Bless them as they pass
"We tend what moves as well as what is still." She adapts.
A Concordance novice, very young, has come to ask the Keeper whether the summit water is the same water as the spring in the chapel. Her teacher told her to ask an engineer. There is none about.
The same water
She is pleased. It is, as it happens, true.
Ask Sister Hale
"I did. She said to ask an engineer."
The chapel's roof leaks. Sister Hale has asked me, as landlady, and I have asked the Company, as its tenant is the town's comfort. The Company has asked you. Everyone has asked someone.
Pay for the roof
Tamm mends it in a day. Hale blesses the ladder.
The landlady's roof
"Kindly. I shall mend it, and raise the lease."
The chapel woman feeds our children at her gate. We do not attend her chapel. She has never asked us to. We ask whether the gate thinks that is kindness, or patience.
Kindness
"Perhaps. We have known patient people who fed us too."
Ask her yourself
"We do not ask the water. She does not ask us. We are alike, she and we."
Hale's asked the moot to make the Lamp Vigil a town holiday. Half the town would take any holiday. The other half says the chapel's the Company's chapel, founded on Company money.
Support the holiday
The town takes the day. The chapel is full. Ilse sells a great deal of ale.
Stay out of it
"Wise. Or cowardly. I'll tell you which later."
A bargee has died in the pound, of drink, at night. His people are Sorrel and far away. The chapel would bury him at the summit and tend the grave. It costs a plot of Company ground.
A plot of Company ground
The first grave at the summit that is not a Keeper's.
Send him down to Sorrel
A cold boat goes west. Hale lights a lamp anyway.
A Concordance elder from the Aldmere chapels has come to inspect the summit chapel's 'founding relics'. Hale has said the undercroft is flooded. It is not, this week. She has asked you to say it is.
The undercroft is flooded
The elder leaves. Hale does not thank you; she does not need to.
Show him the undercroft
Hale goes very still. The elder finds only damp and old stone. This week.
I have found the chapel's original lease among my father's papers. It names a donor. The name is not the Company's. I mention it because the Keeper seems the sort who likes to know things.
Whose name?
"Marrow. An engineer, I believe. Long dead. Kindly forget I said so."
Old paper is old paper
"Quite. I shall keep it anyway. I keep everything."
A Sorrel engineer has asked to test the chapel spring. Its flow, its minerals. He is polite. I have said the spring is not a thing to be tested. He has said everything is. I have come to the gate.
The spring is the chapel's
He leaves. She holds your hand a moment too long.
Let him test it
Iron, and the pound's own minerals, exactly. He writes it down. So do you.
The chapel woman asked our old singer to sing at her Vigil. The old singer said the song is not for lamps. We ask whether the gate would hear it, if it were sung there.
I would
"Then perhaps it will be. Perhaps."
Songs are the Reach's business
"They are. We wondered."
The chapel poor-line at the gate has doubled. Sorrel families, mostly, off the coal boats. Hale feeds them. The town says it's the Keeper's gate, so it's the Keeper's poor. I say nothing. I'm asking.
Feed them from the Coffers too
The line is fed. The Book has a column Vosk reads twice.
The chapel feeds; the gate keeps
"Fair. Cold, but fair."
A vessel asks the old blessing against the Dry Summit. I have not been asked for it in years. Its words mention 'the river under the hill'. I do not know why. We tend. We do not ask.
Ask anyway
"Old words. Older than the chapel, I think." She will not say more.
Say the blessing
The words go over the hull. The bargee, Hullfolk, weeps without sound.
A woman in Concordance grey stands at the gate all day, saying nothing, holding an unlit lamp. Bargees find her unsettling. Hale says she is 'keeping a silence'. Nobody knows for whom.
Let her keep it
At dusk she lights the lamp and walks away. The pound is a mark lower.
Ask her to keep it in the chapel
She goes. The bargees are relieved and slightly ashamed.

Sister Hale has taken in a Sorrel deserter and calls it sanctuary. My building. Company lease. Sorrel Escort Company outside asking. I am not a hard woman, but I am a landlady with a lease to protect.
Sanctuary holds
Solas withdraws his men without a word. Cole raises the lease.
Hand him to Solas
Solas takes him gently. Hale does not speak to you for a week.
The Concordance in Aldmere has sent a new hymn for the Vigil. It is about reservoirs. I do not think a hymn should be about reservoirs. But the Company paid for the printing.
Sing the old hymns
"Thank you." The new hymnals line a damp shelf.
The Company paid; sing it
A hymn about reservoirs. Quenn, in the back pew, does not sing.
Hale's Vigil is tonight and my inn's the only lit building in town. Every year I close for it. Every year I lose a night. This year I'm asking if the Keeper would stand a round for the town after.
Stand the round
Vigil, then ale. The chapel and the inn both approve, for once.
Stay open through the Vigil
The inn is lit. The chapel is fuller anyway. Ilse is not sure how to feel.
The chapel's charter men have put a fence around the spring. A fence. Around water. We have not touched it. We wanted the gate to know we have not touched it, and that we noticed.
Have the fence taken down
Hale does not object. She never does. She looks tired.
The spring is the chapel's
"So they say. So the charter says. We have read charters."
You have asked me three times about the water. Whatever it is, it has fed this town for eighty years. If it is not a gift, it has behaved like one. Do not take that from them.
I will not take it from them
"Then we understand each other. For now."
They should know what feeds them
"Should. A hard word. I have never used it."
Pilgrims from the Sorrel chapels have arrived to see the summit spring and found it fenced, or unfenced, and small. They ask the Keeper whether this is really the source. They have walked a long way.
This is the source
They kneel. Something in you does not.
The source is under the hill
They look at the hill. One of them writes it down.
The lamp at the chapel door has burned since the founding, they say. A bargee bumped the post and it has gone out. The town is more upset than I expected. Relight it quietly, or make a rite of it?
A rite
The whole town attends the relighting. It becomes a new tradition by evening.
Quietly
"Yes. Some things are better tended than seen."
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP REDUCE LOCK HANDS BY ONE FOR ECONOMY STOP NAME TO FOLLOW BY POST STOP
Comply; choose the newest hand
A young man goes down the flight with a reference.
Reply that the gate needs every hand
No reply for a week. Then a different order.
Keeper! The Board would like a photograph of the summit for the Jubilee brochure. The plate-man needs the chamber empty and still for a quarter hour. In daylight. On a working day.
A quarter hour for the Company
The plate shows an empty lock and a Superintendent. It is much admired.
At dawn, before the boats
The plate is dark and moody. Pell is in it anyway.
A Board directive: Keepers are to report any 'unusual interest' in Company structures by persons unknown. For the record, that includes the sluice house. For the record, I did not write it.
Acknowledge it
"Noted." She does not ask if you have any to report.
Ask why the sluice house
"Because it is on the list. You will find lists are not explained."
Ambrose Kell, Commissioner. The Board's view is that the summit is a Company asset and its Keeper a Company servant. I say this at every lock. I find it saves time later.
Understood, Commissioner
"Excellent. Regrettably few say so."
The town is not an asset
"The Board's view differs. I shall note yours."
I shouldn't, but: a wire came for Vosk, not you, and it said 'CONTAIN' and then your name. Just that. I sent it on. I'm telling you because I like you. Please don't tell her I like you.
Thank him; say nothing
You watch Vosk at supper. She eats as she always eats.
Tell him to stop reading wires
"I can't. It's the job. The reading's the job."
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP CONFIRM RESERVOIR LEVELS NORMAL FOR SEASON STOP REPLY BY RETURN STOP
CONFIRMED
You did not check. Nobody expects you to have checked.
UNABLE TO CONFIRM STOP AQUEDUCT LOW
Silence. Then Vosk, at your door, not smiling.
The Board has asked me to remind Keepers that fraternizing with the boat-clans is 'discouraged'. I do not make these rules, Keeper. I do pass them on, with a certain vigor.
Understood
Bram hears of it by nightfall. He hears of everything.
Discouraged is not forbidden
"A lawyer's answer, Keeper. I shall pretend I did not hear it."
Quarterly inspection. I will need the Book, the chest, the keys and two hours. You will find it goes faster if you do not watch.
Leave her to it
Two hours. "Noted." Nothing more.
Watch anyway
Two hours and a half. She notes that you watched.
The Board would like the Keeper to sign a statement that the summit's water supply is 'adequate and well managed'. It is a formality. Regrettably, formalities are what the Board runs on.
Sign it
Your name, under a sentence you did not write, about water you do not understand.
Ask to read the supply figures first
"They are in Ardent. Regrettably." He does not press. He remembers.
You'll never guess who's asked for a copy of your traffic wires. The Sorrel Courier. In strictest confidence I can say I haven't sold them. In strictest confidence I could.
Don't
"Right. No. Of course not." He is a little disappointed in himself.
Sell them; share the coin
Hesse prints your figures. Pell is thrilled until he reads the headline.
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP CLEARANCE ORDER OF YEAR 44 UNDER REVIEW STOP KEEPER TO REPORT NUMBER OF HULLFOLK VESSELS AT SUMMIT STOP
Report the true number
Forty-one. The wire goes to Ardent and does not come back.
Report 'variable; not counted'
Vosk, later: "Noted. It was a kind lie."
A commendation, Keeper! From the Board itself, for 'steady management of the summit'. I have had it framed. I have had two framed. One is for you.
Hang it in the toll office
Bargees read it while they wait. Some of them laugh.
Hang it in the inn
Ilse hangs it behind the bar, upside down. It becomes a landmark.
The Board asks whether the Keeper has had 'unsupervised contact' with the engineer's survey papers. For the record, I have already answered. I would like to know if I answered correctly.
You answered correctly
"Good." She does not say what she answered.
What did you answer?
"No. I answered no." She holds your eye.
The Board has reviewed the Keeper's decisions this quarter and finds them 'independent'. I should tell you that in the Board's vocabulary this is not a compliment. It is not yet a dismissal.
I serve the gate
"The Board's view is that you serve the Board. Regrettably, it is also mine."
I shall be less independent
"Excellent." He does not believe you, and does not need to.
Vosk asked me today whether I keep copies. I said no. I kept a copy of her asking. I don't know why I do this. Should I burn them? All of them? Tell me to.
Burn them
He burns them in the telegraph stove. He keeps one. You both know.
Keep them somewhere safer
"The Ledger? You mean the Ledger." He does not wait for an answer.
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP PROVIDE LIST OF TOWNSFOLK EMPLOYED AT LOCK WITH POLITICAL SYMPATHIES IF KNOWN STOP
Send the list, sympathies blank
Names without opinions. Ardent files it anyway.
Sympathies are not the Company's business
Ilse hears you refused. The town hears Ilse.
The Courier has printed that Halfway's Superintendent 'presides over a slow decline'. Slow, Keeper. Decline. I would like a record week to answer it. I would like it very much.
Give him his record week
Boats through at all hours. The gauge pays for it.
Answer him with a letter instead
Pell writes nine pages. Hesse prints one paragraph.
The Board proposes closing the summit to Hullfolk moorings 'pending review'. It asks for the Keeper's recommendation. You will find I have not given mine. I am waiting for yours.
Recommend against
"Noted." A pause. "So have I."
Recommend closure
"Noted." Nothing else. Pell is delighted.
I shall be at the summit for a week, observing. The Board's view is that observation improves performance. My own view is that it improves reports. Do carry on.
Carry on exactly as usual
A week of being watched. Nothing changes, which he notes.
Show him the town, too
He drinks at the Wheel once, stiffly. Ilse charges him double.
Something odd on the wire tonight: Ardent to Vosk, numbers only, forty groups. Not the traffic code. Not any code I know. I've never seen her get one like it. She burned it. She never burns anything.
Did you keep a copy?
"I shouldn't have. Yes." Forty groups you cannot read. Yet.
Not our business
"No. No, of course." He looks at the stove.
We hold three moorings below the Reach that the charter men have chained off for 'their timber'. There is no timber. We ask the gate whether a chain is a wall.
Cut the chain
"Then the gate is a gate today."
The Company's chain stays
"We remember chains. We have a long list."
The town says a Hullfolk boy stole a ham from the Company store. He did. He's nine. The store's man wants him in the Book. The old man wants him fed. I want him to run faster.
The ham is paid for; no Book
You pay for a ham. The boy learns nothing and eats well.
In the Book, as anyone
The boy is in the Book. The Reach is very quiet about it.
The old woman on the gunwale sings a verse as your boat passes. A river, a hill, a door that closed. She stops when she sees you listening, and smiles, and does not start again.
Ask her to go on
"Another day. The river has more verses than I have breath."
Nod and move on
She sings again when your back is turned.
A Hullfolk boat is fishing the chamber itself, nets down, while the gate is closed for the night. The fish, they say, gather at the paddles. The Book says the chamber is not a fishery.
Nets up by first bell
They are. The fish are shared. Some come to your door.
Nets up now
They haul in, slowly, watching you.
The Reach is buying ale from a Sorrel barge instead of me. I don't blame them; I'd rather they bought mine. The moot wants the Sorrel barge told to move. It's moored on Company water.
Move the barge
Ilse sells more ale. The Reach drinks less of it.
Anyone may moor
"Anyone. Right. Remember that when it's the Company's barge."
A charter man has been at the Reach with a measuring chain. He measured our boats. Nobody measures a boat that is going to stay. We ask what the gate knows.
Tell him about the Clearance review
"So. We have been here before. We hold."
The gate knows nothing
"The gate knows. The gate is choosing."
The old man wants you at the Reach for the remembering. Names of the dead read out over the water, all night, no fire. He's never asked a Keeper. I told him you'd say no. Prove me wrong or don't.
Go
Forty names. Then a river's name. Nobody explains it.
Not this year
"Told him." She does not sound pleased to be right.
Two Hullfolk boats have lashed together across the pound to settle a marriage dispute the old way: by argument, at volume, until dawn. Nothing can pass them. Nothing is trying to, yet.
Let them argue
By dawn they are married again and the pound is clear.
Separate them
Dace separates them. Both sides are furious with him instead.
The little fiddle has one string and I have one song. The charter men say the Reach is too loud at night. The Reach says the charter men are too quiet in the day. Which does the gate hear?
Play on
The town complains, then hums it.
Quiet after the last bell
She plays until the last bell exactly, and one note after.
The town says a Hullfolk hand took a windlass from your lock house. We say the town's hands took it and blamed the water. We do not ask you to believe us. We ask you not to believe them first.
Search the Reach
No windlass. Forty silent people watching you look.
Search the lock house first
The windlass is behind the paddle gear. Dace goes red.
One of ours is sick and Stroud won't come to the Reach without a Company chit. She's not being cruel. The Company made the rule. You could write the chit.
Write it
Stroud goes. She comes back angry at the rule, not at you.
Bring the sick one to the town
They carry her up. She lives. The Reach remembers the carrying.
A Hullfolk boat asks to tie up overnight in the chamber itself, out of the wind. It has a new baby aboard. It is against every rule in the Book and it would cost nothing.
In the chamber, till dawn
The gate is closed all night for one small boat.
The lee of the Company house
Out of the wind, within the rules. They take it.
Bram Holloway's asked to speak at the moot. About moorings. The moot's never had a Hullfolk speak and half of it doesn't want to start. The other half wants to hear him refuse to say 'please'.
Let him speak
He speaks for ten minutes and does not say please. It goes better than anyone feared.
The moot is the town's
"It is. That's what I said. Didn't like saying it."
The pound is low. When it is low the Reach touches bottom and we lie on our sides like the dead. We ask the gate for one less boat a day until the rain.
One less boat a day
The Reach floats. Pell counts the missing boat.
The boats come first
"They always have. We remember when they did not exist."
Fine. The reed cargo. Sometimes it's not cheese. You knew that. What I'm asking is whether you want to know what it is, because once you know, you have to do something.
Tell me
"Rifles. Sorrel. Not many. Enough." She watches your face.
Don't tell me
"Smart. Sad, but smart."
A Hullfolk elder has died at the Reach. They will take him down the west flight to a valley they do not name, and they ask for a Company boat to carry the body, since theirs are too small.
Lend the Company boat
The Company boat goes west with a Hullfolk crew and does not come back for a week.
Company boats are for Company work
They lash two boats and go. It takes them three days longer.
You have kind eyes for a charter man. Wren says you are not a charter man. I say everyone at the gate is one until they are not. Have a fish.
Have the fish
It is very good. She watches you eat it, satisfied.
Ask about the river in the song
"Which river?" There is only one, and she knows you know it.
A charter man's dog drowned at the Reach. He says our children pushed it. Our children say it jumped for a fish. It was a good dog. We have laid it out. We ask nothing. He asks a great deal.
It jumped for a fish
The charter man is furious with you instead. It was, in fact, a fish.
The Reach pays for the dog
They pay in fish, as always. He does not want fish.
Hullfolk children at the school door. Cole's building, Company lease, town's teacher. Nobody's said no yet because nobody's been asked. The teacher's asking you, since you're everyone's excuse.
Let them in
Six more in the schoolroom. Three town families take their children out. Then two put them back.
The school is the town's
"It's Cole's, actually. But yes."
Bram won't ask, so I will. The Reach needs new mooring posts before winter. Tamm has timber. The Company has a rule about who Tamm can sell to. You have a pen.
Sign for the timber
Posts by winter. Vosk sees the chit and says nothing, which is louder than usual.
The rule is the rule
"The old man said you'd say that. I bet him you wouldn't. I owe him a fish."
The east paddle gear has two teeth gone. Sorry. It'll run, roughly, but one more and it won't. A new wheel is twelve marks and a week from Ardent. A patched one is three marks and Tamm.
New wheel from Ardent
A week of one paddle. Then a gear that will outlive you.
Tamm patches it
"It'll hold or it won't," says Tamm. It holds. For now.
Somebody's been at the sluice house door with a bar. Not me. Company wants it re-hung with iron straps. I can do it. I'd rather know why a valve house nobody uses needs iron straps.
Hang it as asked
Iron straps on a disused door. Tamm shakes his head all day.
Leave it; ask Vosk why
"Because the Board lists it. You will find lists are not explained."
Towpath's washed out below the gate. Horses can't tow past it. The Company's answer, by wire, was 'note it'.
Fill it with town labor
A day's work, a barrel of ale, a towpath.
Note it
Horses go round by the field. The farmer sends a bill.
He used to grease the paddle spindles every seventh watch. Nobody's done it since. I can, if you want it done his way. Or the Company way, which is when they squeal.
His way
She does it in silence, the way he must have.
The Company way
"Right." They squeal within the month.
A gate beam has cracked in the frost with a sound the whole town heard. The gate still shuts. Quenn says it will shut until it does not, and cannot say when that is.
Close the gate; replace the beam
Three days. The queue reaches Lock 7. The new beam is oak.
Strap it and keep working
Iron straps. It shuts. Every bang makes the hands flinch.
I've found the original gate drawings. Marrow's hand. There's a note in the margin: 'sill gauge to read ten, not nine; see S.H.' I don't know what S.H. is. Sorry. Do you?
Sluice house
"Oh. Yes. That's, yes. That would be it." She goes quiet.
Someone's initials
"Nobody with those. I checked the rolls. Roughly all of them."
Company's sent a crate of new paddle gear. Wrong pattern. Made for the Sorrel locks, which are a hand wider. I can make it fit. It'll never be right. Or I send it back and we wait.
Make it fit
It fits. It grinds. Tamm hates it personally.
Send it back
Six weeks. The old gear holds, sullenly.
Three things. The hands want gloves. The Company says gloves are 'personal equipment'. And I've got two men with hands like raw meat from the winter windlass.
Gloves from the Coffers
Twelve pairs. Vosk notes it as 'irregular but small'.
Personal equipment
"Right. I'll tell them the Company said so. They'll remember which Company."
The lower gate's leaking round the heel post. He noticed that too, the month before. He wrote it in the Book. Nobody read it. I'm telling you so it's said twice.
Fix it this week
She watches you write the order. Something eases.
Note it, as he did
"Right. Twice in the Book, then."
The chamber floor has a hollow sound at the north corner when the water is out. It always has, the hands say. Nobody has ever looked. Looking means a dry chamber for a day.
Drain it and look
A void under the floor, and old brickwork, and the sound of running water where there should be none.
It always has
The boats keep moving over the hollow sound.
I need to close the aqueduct for a day to clear it. It won't affect the pound, which, sorry, it should. It should affect it a great deal. I'd like you to watch the gauge while it's closed.
Watch the gauge
A day with the aqueduct shut. The pound falls its usual mark, and no more.
Clear it; don't tell the Company
"I wasn't going to. Sorry. I never do."
There's a hull at my yard with a false bottom. Hullfolk boat. I'm not saying whose. I'm saying if I fix it, I've fixed a smuggler's boat, and if I don't, she sinks in the pound with a family aboard.
Fix it
The false bottom is repaired along with the true one. Nobody mentions either.
Report it to Crane
Crane inspects. Finds cheese. The Hullfolk do not use Tamm's yard again.
The bollards on the wharf are rotten. A Sorrel barge pulled one clean out this morning. And the Company's sent a man to count the bollards, not replace them.
Replace them all
Tamm's oak. A week. A wharf that will hold a fleet.
Replace the one
One new bollard among the rotten ones, like a tooth.
The Company wants the old gauge board replaced with a new brass one. Nine marks. The old board has ten, and his pencil marks on it. I'd rather it stayed. I'd rather you said so.
The old board stays
"Thank you." The first time she has said it.
Brass, nine marks
She takes the old board home. The tenth mark goes with it.
The pound's north bank is slumping near the sluice house. A yard of it went into the water overnight. The Company's surveyors will say 'drainage'. It is where the clear stream comes out.
Shore it up with town labor
Stone and timber. The bank holds. The stream finds a new way out.
Report it and wait
Company men arrive at night, with lamps, and no surveyors.
I want to put a second gauge on the pound, at the Reach end, and read them both every watch. If they ever disagree, we'll know where the water goes in. The Company won't like a second gauge.
Put it in
Two gauges. They disagree by the third day, at the north bank.
One gauge is the rule
"Right. Sorry. One gauge." She measures the Reach end with a stick anyway.
The Reed Reach wants their mooring stage rebuilt and they'll pay in fish and labor. Company rule says no Company timber to the Reach. Half my timber's Company. I've lost track which half.
Lose track a little more
A new stage at the Reach, built of timber nobody can identify.
Keep track
The Reach builds with driftwood. It holds. It looks like it might not.
Three things. The Company inspector wants the hands to wear numbers. Numbers, Keeper, on their coats. The hands say they'll wear them on their backsides. And Vosk is coming Tuesday.
Numbers on coats
They wear them. Upside down. Vosk notes it without expression.
Names are enough
"Right. I'll tell Vosk you said names." She notes that too.
The winter stores: lamp oil, rope, tallow, sand. He used to order double and the Company used to complain. Last winter nobody ordered and the hands worked the frost in the dark.
Order double
Vosk complains. The hands do not work in the dark.
Order what the Company allows
"Right." The dark comes early that winter.
Sorry. Good news, for once. I've got the west paddles running true for the first time in years. The gate fills a quarter faster. Do you want to tell the Company, or keep it for a bad day?
Tell the Company
Pell announces it. Throughput targets rise to match.
Keep it for a bad day
"A reserve. Yes. Roughly what he'd have done."
Company mail goes first; that is the rule. The Company mail today is one sack, one clerk, and a boat that could carry forty. Nine grain barges wait behind it.
Mail first, as written
One sack rises grandly through the chamber.
Mail waits for the grain
The clerk complains by wire. From your own telegraph office.
Two vessels claim the same arrival bell. I have consulted the Compact. It provides that the Keeper decides, which I note is unhelpful, and that the Keeper's decision is final, which is worse.
The Aldmere boat
"Duly." The Sorrel bargee says something about Aldmere inspectors.
The Sorrel boat
"Duly." He writes it down a little harder than necessary.
Keeper! A Board member's private launch, brass and mahogany, is at the bottom of the queue. I need not say what a magnificent impression it would make to bring it up first.
Bring it up first
The launch gleams. The queue does not.
It takes its turn
"Its turn. Of course. A principled position, Keeper. A brave one."
My convoy is four boats and I would rather they went through together. Splitting an armed convoy is how accidents start. Your queue would rather they didn't.
Together
Four boats, one hour, nobody else moves.
One at a time, in turn
"Understood. It won't come to trouble." It does not.
A woman with a sick child asks to jump the queue for the physician on the Aldmere side. The child is quiet in the way children should not be. Eleven boats are ahead of her.
Bring her through now
Nobody in the queue complains. Not aloud.
Send for Stroud instead
Stroud comes to the boat. It takes an hour. The child lives.
A tug with six barges in tow wants the chamber six times in a row. The rule says arrival order. The tug says it has been doing this for twenty years.
Six in a row
An afternoon of one tug. The queue plays cards.
Alternate with the queue
The tug master spits. Twenty years, he says.
The Sorrel escort vessel has moored across the approach to my inspection post. I note that this is not forbidden. I note also that it is not an accident.
Have it moved
Solas moves it himself, without comment.
Inspect from the towpath
"I can. I shall. I note it."
The Board notes, Keeper, that the summit passed eleven fewer vessels than Lock 8 last month. Lock 8 is downhill. I would like an explanation I can send without wincing.
Fewer inspections this month
Numbers rise. Crane's eyebrows rise with them.
Lock 8 has more water
"Water. Yes. I shall not send that."
One of my men has been drinking at the Wheel and started something with a lock hand. My people, my discipline. Unless you would rather it was yours.
Your discipline
The man is sent down the west flight that night. Quietly.
The town's law
Ilse fines him. He pays. Solas watches.
An Aldmere magistrate on a private boat produces a writ commanding the Keeper to give him precedence over 'commercial traffic'. The writ is not addressed to a Company lock.
Honor the writ
