He passes. Crane looks pained; the writ is irregular and he knows it.
This is a Company gate
He threatens a report. Pell frames the report.
The night watch reports a boat that moved up three places in the queue while the others slept. Its bargee says the others agreed. The others say otherwise.
Send it to the back
The queue cheers, briefly.
Where it is, it stays
The queue learns something about nights.
An extraordinary situation. The Compact grants precedence to 'perishable foodstuffs'. The vessel before us carries ice. I have been unable to determine whether ice perishes.
Ice perishes
"A bold reading. I shall cite you."
Ice is a mineral
"Also bold. I shall cite you for that too."
A Sorrel newspaperman has asked for a place on the first boat of the day, to see the sunrise from the summit. Think of the description, Keeper. Think of the adjectives.
Give Hesse the sunrise
The adjectives are many and mostly about Pell.
He can queue like anyone
The Courier describes the queue instead.
An Aldmere boat has been moored alongside my convoy all night, and a man on it has been counting my crates. I have not touched him. I am telling you before I have to decide whether to.
Move the Aldmere boat
The counter is Crane's clerk. Crane is unrepentant.
Counting is not a crime
"No. It's how they start."
A funeral boat, black cloth over a long shape, asks quiet passage before the day's traffic. The Hullfolk at the tiller do not ask for a fee. They do not ask at all; they wait.
Open the gate in silence
The chamber fills without a bell. The queue takes off its caps.
The queue is the queue
They wait four hours. Nobody sings.
Fog. Boats are arriving that cannot see the gate. The hands want to close until it lifts. The bargees want a lamp on the sill and a chance.
Close until it lifts
A wasted morning and no dented hulls.
Lamps on the sill; keep working
One barge kisses the gate. Nothing breaks. This time.
A revised order-of-passage schedule, based on cargo class, arrival bell and shore of origin, weighted. Eleven pages. I believe it would end all disputes.
Adopt it
Disputes end. Everyone hates the schedule equally, which is a kind of peace.
The Keeper decides, as written
"I anticipated that. Page eleven addresses it."
Keeper, a Board member's nephew was made to wait behind a coal barge. Behind coal, Keeper. I have had a letter. I have had two.
Apologize by wire
You sign a letter you did not write.
Coal keeps Aldmere warm
"It does. Nephews do not know that."
Your lock hand, the Dray girl, has told my sergeant that convoys wait like anyone. My sergeant has told her what he thinks of that. She won. I thought you should know who runs your gate.
She does, at the paddles
"Good. I'd rather deal with someone who wins."
Remind her who decides
Mirren says nothing. She says it very clearly.
A Concordance pilgrim on foot asks to ride the next boat through, any boat, to reach the Lamp Vigil by dusk. No bargee wants a stranger aboard. One might, for a mark.
Pay the mark
She goes through on a coal barge, singing quietly.
She walks the towpath
She thanks you anyway. It is a long walk.
The Sorrel agent has flown her Assembly's flag from a moored barge. The Compact says nothing about flags. I have brought Aldmere's, in case it says nothing about two.
No flags on Company water
Both come down. Both parties blame you, which is a kind of balance.
Fly them both
Two flags over one pound. Hesse takes a plate of it.
Aldmere has raised its grain price again and Sorrel's mills are on short time. My principals ask whether the summit could 'lose' a grain barge for a week. Just one. Just once.
Nothing gets lost here
"Didn't think so. Had to ask."
A week's delay for repairs
The grain barge sits. The mills run. Crane files.
An Aldmere customs cutter has moored beside my convoy with its gun uncovered. It is within its rights. So am I, if I uncover mine. I would rather you told them to cover up first.
Tell Crane to cover the gun
Crane is appalled that anyone uncovered anything. It is covered.
Both stay covered, or both leave
Both leave. The pound is briefly very quiet.
ALDMERE GUILDS TO KEEPER STOP SORREL AGENT VANE TO BE DENIED ACCESS TO TOLL BOOK UNDER COMPACT ARTICLE SIX STOP CONFIRM STOP
Confirm
Vane learns of it from Fennick before you can tell her.
Article Six says no such thing
Crane, consulted, agrees with you, painfully.
Lucan Hesse, Sorrel Courier. My readers want to know: is the summit Aldmere's, Sorrel's, or the Company's? On the record. One word will do, and one word is all I'll print.
The Company's
COMPANY MAN AT THE SUMMIT. Pell frames it.
The water's
KEEPER: SUMMIT BELONGS TO 'THE WATER'. It is the most read line he has printed.
A Sorrel vessel has requested passage for 'sixty agricultural laborers' bound for Aldmere. I have counted them. They march in step. I am not permitted to refuse laborers. I am permitted to ask you.
Laborers pass
Sixty men in step go down the east flight. Aldmere hears of it in a week.
Hold them for both inspectors
They wait two days and go back west. Solas looks relieved.
The Aldmere inspector has proposed a duel over the order of passage. A duel. With pistols. I've accepted, obviously. I need a second. You're neutral. Neutral is what seconds are.
Second her
Both fire wide, formally. Crane is thrilled to have followed procedure.
Forbid it on Company water
"Spoilsport." Crane, secretly, is relieved.
News from Sorrel. There has been shooting at the coalfield. My people are asking whether they will be sent back. I do not know. I would like to tell them the summit is not sending them anywhere.
The summit sends nobody
"Thank you. They'll sleep. So will I."
The Company decides that
"It does. I'd hoped you'd lie a little."
SORREL ASSEMBLY TO KEEPER STOP PROTEST DELAYS TO COAL STOP REQUEST SUMMIT OPERATE THROUGH NIGHT STOP COSTS TO BE MET BY ASSEMBLY STOP
Night operation, at their cost
Lamps on the gate all night. The Coffers fill. The town does not sleep.
The gate keeps the bell
Sorrel protests to Ardent. Ardent is used to it.
I have it from a source that the Aldmere inspector keeps his own water gauge. Private. Six years. Why would a customs man count water, Keeper? Give me a line and I'll give you the front page.
No line
"Suit yourself. I'll ask him. He'll tell me. He can't help it."
Ask Crane yourself; I'd like to know
"So you don't know either. That's the story."
The Guilds instruct me to record every Sorrel cargo weight to the pound. It adds an hour to each passage. I note that I did not ask for this. I note that I shall obey it.
Obey it; Compact rights
Sorrel's fleet backs up to Lock 7. Vane sends a bill.
Weigh one in five
"A sampling approach. Irregular. I shall document my objection and comply."

Aldmere has seized a Sorrel coal fleet at Lock 3 over a 'paperwork discrepancy'. Twelve boats. My principals want the summit closed to Aldmere grain until they're released. You can do that. You have the gate.
Close the summit to grain
Grain stops. Bread in Sorrel rises. Aldmere releases the fleet in four days. Nobody thanks you.
The gate is not a weapon
"Everything's a weapon. Some of them are just slow."
There is an Aldmere man at the inn asking my sergeants what they are paid, and offering more. He is recruiting. Openly. Under the Compact I cannot touch him. Under the Compact you can move him.
Move him along
He goes down the east flight with a list of names anyway.
A man may talk at an inn
Two sergeants leave with him. Solas does not mention it again.
ALDMERE AND SORREL JOINT TO KEEPER STOP COMPACT ANNIVERSARY STOP BOTH INSPECTORS TO DINE AT KEEPER'S TABLE STOP THIS IS NOT A REQUEST STOP
Host the dinner
Crane and Vane argue for four hours about a fish course. It is the best evening in months.
Host it at the inn, at their cost
Ilse serves them. They tip differently. She remembers which.
The Courier's Aldmere edition was seized at Lock 2 as 'seditious'. It was about grain prices. I'd like to print the next one at Halfway and send it both ways. I need a room.
Print at the Company house
Ink on the Company's floor. The Guilds are livid. Sorrel cheers.
Print at the inn, if Ilse will
Ilse will, for a fee and a column about the cellar.
I am recalled to Aldmere for a month to give evidence on the Compact's operation. I note that in my absence there will be no second seal for arms. I note that I have told nobody else this.
No arms pass while he is gone
"Duly. I am, I find, grateful."
The Sorrel seal will have to serve
"I note that. I note it with regret."
My principals have bought the inn's debt from Cole. Not to call it in. To have it. Sorrel likes having things at the summit. I'm telling you as a courtesy, and because Ilse won't believe it from me.
Tell Ilse yourself
Ilse is quiet for a long moment, then charges Vane double forever.
Not the Keeper's business
"Everything at the gate is. That's the job. Isn't it?"
Aldmere has posted a customs cutter at the east flight to inspect every convoy twice. Once here, once below. My men are tired of being counted. I am asking you to make one count enough.
One count, at the summit
Crane agrees, reluctantly: the Compact says summit. Below stands down.
Aldmere's flight, Aldmere's count
"Understood." He does not say it is.
Off the record: both shores are drafting plans to take the canal if the Company falls. Aldmere by law, Sorrel by purchase. On the record: which would you rather worked for?
Neither; the Company keeps the gate
KEEPER LOYAL, says the Courier, in a tone.
Whoever fixes the water
He stops writing. "What's wrong with the water?"
The Compact, read strictly, obliges the Keeper to host a joint shore conference at the summit every seven years. None has ever been held. We are, I calculate, eleven years overdue.
Hold the conference
Delegates from both shores. Three days. Nothing is decided and everyone is impressed.
Eleven more years won't hurt
"It might. I shall note the date."
A man in a good coat asks to buy the Keeper's house. Not rent. Buy. He names a sum that would keep the gate for a year, and does not say why.
Not for sale
He leaves his card. It has no name, only an Ardent address.
Ask what he'd pay for the study alone
He pauses a moment too long. "The house. Or nothing."
A boat of travelling players offers a free performance for the town in exchange for passage. Their play, they say, is about a canal. Everyone's plays are about a canal, this year.
Passage for a play
The play is bad and the town loves it. There is a Keeper in it who drowns.
Toll like anyone
They pay, and perform at the Reach for free, out of spite.
I'm writing a piece on the Keepers of Halfway. Nine in eighty years, and four didn't leave by the flight. Dray makes five. I'd like a quote about the chair. Anything. Even 'no comment' is a quote.
The chair is comfortable
KEEPER: 'THE CHAIR IS COMFORTABLE'. It is read as bravery or stupidity, by shore.
Ask about the four
"Drowned, drowned, run out, 'resigned'. You knew that." You did not.
In my day the Keeper at Lock 8, that's me, used to swap a keg with the Keeper at 9 every solstice. Nobody's done it since Dray. I've brought the keg. You've got nothing to swap. I know. Sit down.
Sit down
Three hours. Somewhere in the second, the Dry Year.
Another night
"There's fewer of those than you think, Keeper." He leaves the keg.
A boat from the east with a woman who says she is Dray's sister. Nobody knew he had one. She asks to see the study. Mirren has never heard of her. Neither, it seems, had he.
Let her see the study
She looks at the desk and touches nothing and leaves. Mirren watches from the door.
Family or not, no
She goes down the flight. Stroud, later: "She had his eyes. Or I wanted her to."
A drover wants to swim forty cattle across the pound rather than pay the ferry. Forty cattle in a canal. Crane is somewhere finding the schedule for livestock in water. Dace is laughing.
Swim them
Forty cattle cross. One tries the chamber. The town talks about it for a year.
The ferry, and the fee
He pays, furious. Crane arrives with the schedule too late and is desolate.
A boat with no name, no cargo and one passenger, who asks to go down the east flight 'before anyone from Sorrel asks'. He has coin, and the look of a man out of other things.
Down the flight, quietly
He goes. Two days later, Sorrel asks. You say nothing.
He waits with the rest
Solas's men are at the gate by evening. He does not run. He looks at you.
Sorrel says the summit Keeper is secretly Aldmere's man. Aldmere says you are Sorrel's. I could print both; it would be very funny. Or neither, for a favor.
Print both
Both shores are briefly united in being annoyed with you.
Neither; name the favor
"A seat on the first Jubilee boat. That's all. For now."

The Dry Year, since you ask. Pound went to the sills. Company said drought. Then men came up the west flight at night, forty of 'em, said they were dredging the reservoir. I looked. No dredgers. Picks.
Picks for what?
"Never found out. They went up the north bank and came down a month later, thin."
Drought does strange things
"It does. It doesn't hand out picks."
A bargee has a fever I have seen in the coalfield towns. If it is what I think, his boat must not go down the east flight. If not, I have ruined his season for nothing.
Hold the boat
It is what she thought. Three boats are held. Nobody dies.
Let him go; watch the town
The boat goes. Nothing happens. Stroud does not sleep for a week.
A child, alone, on the towpath, with a note pinned to her coat that says 'Halfway'. Nothing else. She does not speak. Hale would take her. Ilse would take her. The Company has a form.
The chapel
Hale takes her hand. The child speaks, eventually, in a Lowmere accent nobody recognizes.
The inn
Ilse takes her without a word and feeds her for a year.
A boat of Sorrel students on a walking tour want to see 'the famous sluice house'. Famous to whom, you ask. To a professor in Sorrel, they say, who lectures on it and has never seen it either.
Show them the door
They sketch a locked door. One asks why the straps are new.
There is nothing to see
They sketch the chapel instead. Vosk, somewhere, relaxes.
Scoop. The Company's Board has three seats empty and the Superintendent of Halfway has applied for one. Pell. On the Board. I'd like your reaction. I'd settle for your face.
He'd be good at it
"Diplomatic. I'll print 'supportive'." Pell is touched.
No comment
"'Keeper declines to support Superintendent.' That's the headline you've bought."
Dray sat where you're sitting and asked me the same question you're about to ask. I told him the same thing. Then he went and did something about it. I'm not sure I should tell you again.
Tell me
"The water don't come from the reservoirs. Never did. Ask the old woman at the Reach what it does come from."
Don't
"Sensible. He wasn't. I liked him for it."
You have a cough a month old and a color I do not like. The summit air is thin and the water cold. Go down to Aldmere for a week. The gate will not fall down.
Go down for a week
A week below. You come back with color and to a gate that did not fall down.
The gate needs its Keeper
"So Dray said. I attended him twice that year."
A Sorrel engineer, retired, asks to see the paddle gear 'for old times'. He worked on the Sorrel flight in Marrow's day. He is very old. He calls the pound 'the Quell' once, and corrects himself.
Ask about the Quell
"A river. West of here. Dried up. Long time ago." He will not say more.
Show him the gear
He weeps at the paddle gear. Engineers do, apparently.
A very fine Aldmere yacht, a lady aboard who does not give her name, asks passage west and offers a sum to have the Book say she went east.
The Book says east
The Book lies. The sum is large. Crane, weeks later, asks about a yacht.
The Book says what happened
She pays the ordinary toll and looks at you with something like respect.

A reader has sent the Courier a letter claiming a Halfway Keeper once found 'a door under the water'. Unsigned. Aldmere postmark. I don't print anonymous letters. I do show them to people who might know.
I know nothing of doors
"Everyone says that. It's the least interesting thing anyone says."
Let me see the hand
You have seen the hand. On a ciphered ledger.
I'm not long for it, Keeper. Stroud says so with her face. I've got a Company coat forty years old and a tankard and a story I never finished telling Dray. Which do you want?
The story
He tells it. It ends with men going into the hill and the pound rising the next spring.
The coat
"Sensible. Warmer than a story." It fits, almost.
Fennick has fainted at his key. Overwork and no food, he says. Fear, I say. He keeps asking whether Vosk has been to see me. Has something been happening on the wire I should know about?
Tell her what you know
She listens like a physician. "Then he needs rest, and you need care."
Nothing you should know
"I see. Then I shall treat the symptom."
A bargee counts out the toll in coin so worn the faces are gone. It is two marks short. He says it is the toll his father paid.
His father's toll will do
He touches the worn coins to his cap.
The table is the table
He pays. He does not look at you again.
Scrip again. The Company store takes it; my cellar does not. Whose money is the Keeper paid in, and whose is the town paid in?
Pay the hands in coin
Coffers lighter; the inn fuller.
Scrip is the Company's rule
"So is drowning, when it suits them."
A quarter's tolls in advance, at a small discount for the trouble. My principals like certainty. You would like a full chest. Everybody likes something.
Take the advance
The chest is full and the Book has a promise in it.
Tolls at the gate, as ever
"Certainty. Fine. I'll find it elsewhere."
Marguerite Cole. I hold the chapel's lease and half the town's. I am told the Keeper's chest is light. I lend, kindly, on terms. Shall we discuss terms?
Discuss terms
Terms are one in ten, monthly, kindly.
The chest will manage
"Of course. My door is always open. It has a bell."
The toll table has not been revised since Year 58. The Board has authorized a rise of one part in twelve. For the record, the Board did not say when.
Raise it now
The queue learns of it at the gate. Loudly.
After the season
"Noted. The Board will ask why."
The bargee offers the toll and, folded under it, a second coin for the Keeper personally. He does not say why. He does not look as if he needs to.
Pocket it
The second coin is heavier than the first.
Into the Book, both coins
He shrugs. Someone else will pay it next time.
The moot wants to know why the mooring fee on the pound went up. I told them to ask you. Here I am, asking you, on their behalf, at my own inn.
The Company set it
"Your Company. Noted, as she says."
Waive it for townsfolk
The moot approves. The Book does not.
Fun fact: your toll on empty return barges is higher than on full ones. Somebody wrote that in Year 12 and nobody has read it since. I have read it.
Correct the table
Empties pay less. Sorrel's fleet sends more empties.
The table stands
"Then I'll fill my empties with something cheap."
The interest is due. I do not send men. I send reminders, and then I send the Company a copy of the note. Which would you prefer to receive?
Pay the interest
"Kindly. Same time next month."
Send the copy
Vosk receives it. Vosk reads everything.
There is a gap in the Book between the fourth and fifth bells of the last watch. Vessels passed. Nothing was written. You will find I have to ask.
The hands forgot
"Noted. The hands do not keep the Book."
My error; here are the tolls
You make up the sum from your own pocket. She notes that too.
A Hullfolk boat offers to pay its toll in smoked fish. The fish is very good. The toll table does not have a column for fish.
Fish is a toll
The Company store is briefly the best-smelling building in Halfway.
Coin or scrip
They find coin, somewhere, slowly.
The hands were paid short this watch. Dace says the chest was light. Dace says you said so. Is the town going to hear about it at the moot or at my bar?
Make up the wages from tolls
The Book has a hole. The hands have their beer.
Short until the season turns
"Then they'll work short too."
I can pay this quarter's fees in Sorrel bonds. They are as good as coin in Sorrel. This is not Sorrel, I grant you. Yet.
Bonds at a discount
Paper in the chest. It rustles.
Coin
"Fine. Coin. Delay costs, and this cost you."
A gift for the Keeper's house: a good chair, from my own parlor. No terms at all. I like to see the post well kept.
Accept the chair
It is a very good chair. You think about it more than a chair deserves.
Decline, kindly
"Of course. It will be here."
The chest is heavier than the Book explains. Not by much. Enough. I am not asking where it came from. I am telling you I have noticed.
Bank the difference with the Company
"Noted. That was the correct answer."
Spend it on the gates
Quenn is delighted. Vosk writes a line.
The toll chest's lock has been forced in the night. Nothing is missing. Somebody wanted to know what was in it, or wanted you to know they could.
New lock, no report
Tamm fits a lock that would stop a bear.
Report it to the Company
Vosk arrives within the hour and looks at the lock a long time.
A Sorrel bargee tried to pay for his supper in your Company's scrip, which I don't take, and then in a story about a Keeper who does. Is that Keeper you?
It is now; take scrip
"At half face. And you'll hear about it."
Your inn, your rules
"Good answer. He went hungry."
Aldmere's inspector has proposed a 'Compact levy' on Sorrel coal. It is not in the Compact. It is on your gate. I am asking you not to collect it.
Collect nothing not in the table
"Thank you. That's rarer than you'd think."
Collect it; let them argue
They argue for a month. The chest enjoys it.
The chapel's lease is due and Sister Hale has asked me for time. I am a patient woman. I am also a landlady. A word from the Keeper would settle which I am this month.
Give the chapel time
"For the Keeper. Kindly."
Business is business
Hale pays. The poor at the gate eat less that week.
The Board has asked for a statement of the summit's accounts for the Jubilee. I can write it accurately, or I can write it well. For the record, I am asking which.
Accurately
"Noted." She looks at you as if you had passed something.
Well
"Noted." The Board is pleased. She is not, quite.
Market day. Half the town wants the towpath for stalls and the other half wants it for towing. The moot has asked the Keeper to say which half is right.
Stalls on the towpath
A slow day for boats, a good one for pies.
The towpath tows
The stalls go up Chapel Street. The pies are further away.
The Dray house has been Company property since the father left. I could take the lease and let it kindly to the daughter at a fair rent. Or the Keeper could go on living in it.
The Keeper stays
"Of course. It is a good house. I only mention it."
Let it to Mirren
Mirren pays Cole rent for her own house. She does not thank you.
The lock hands' children swim in the pound below the gate. Every summer I treat one for a paddle-wash. Every summer someone tells me it is how they learn. This summer I am telling you.
Fence the sill
The children swim from the Reed Reach instead, and the Hullfolk teach them.
It is how they learn
"So I hear. Every summer."
A travelling puppet show wants to set up on the wharf. Its principal act, the handbill says, is 'The Lock Keeper Who Would Not Open'. The handbill has a drawing. It is not flattering.
Let them play
The town laughs for an hour, mostly at you. It helps, oddly.
Move them along
They play at the Reed Reach. The Hullfolk laugh instead.
Three things. It's the hands' feast day. They want the chamber for the raft race. And last year the winner was Company mail, which nobody's forgotten.
The chamber for the race
Mirren wins on a door. The mail waits.
Race below the gate
"Right. Below. Where the current is." Nobody drowns. Nearly.
Somebody from the Company measured my cellar this morning. For 'drainage'. Nobody measures a cellar for drainage. What does your Company want with my cellar?
Find out
Quenn, red-faced: the pound's leaking into the brewery well. It always has.
Drainage, presumably
"Presumably. Your Company presumes a lot."
The town wants a schoolroom. I have a building. The Company has a lease on it for 'future works' it has never begun. A word from the Keeper would release it.
Release the lease
Pell signs, sulking. Children arrive.
Future works are the Company's
"Of course. The children can wait. They are good at it."
A lock hand's wife is dying and wants to be taken down to her people on the Aldmere side. The flight is closed for repairs. I can keep her comfortable for two days. No more.
Open the flight for one boat
Quenn's crew stands aside. The boat goes down in silence.
She stays; make her comfortable
She dies at Halfway. Her people come up later.
A young couple from the town ask the Keeper to witness their marriage at the top gate, at dawn, before the first boat. Hale is willing. The first boat is a Company mail packet.
Dawn, at the gate
The mail waits twenty minutes. The clerk cries, a little.
The chapel is for weddings
They marry in the chapel. It is fine. It is not the gate.
One thing, and it's a bad one. A hand's been caught selling Company lamp oil at the inn. It's Perrin, who's got four children. Vosk hasn't heard yet.
Dismiss him quietly
Perrin goes down the flight. The others learn it.
Dock his wages; keep him
"Right. I'll tell him. He'll cry. Then he'll work."
The inn's out of Iron Spring and the well's low because the pound's low. I'm buying Sorrel beer at Sorrel prices. The town blames you, since the water's yours.
Subsidize the beer
The Coffers buy a town's goodwill by the barrel.
The water is nobody's
"Tell that to the well."
A tenant of mine, a lock hand, has not paid in two months. I could put him out. Or the Company could guarantee his rent from his wages, with your signature.
Guarantee the rent
Wages go to Cole before they go to the hand.
The Company does not guarantee rents
He is put out. He sleeps at the Reed Reach.
There is a case of the shakes at the inn: a bargee, feverish, insisting he drank nothing but the well water. I would like to test the well. Ilse would not like me to.
Test the well
Iron, and something else. Stroud's face does not change. Ilse's does.
It was the Sorrel beer
"Perhaps. I have seen worse. I have also seen wells."
An old bargeman, retiring, asks to name his last boat after the Keeper and paint it on the bow. He has already bought the paint. The Book has a fee for renaming.
Waive the fee
There is a coal barge with your name on it. It goes east forever.
The fee is the fee
He pays it, and names the boat something else.
Three things, and these are good ones. The hands have finished the new bollards early. They want the afternoon. And Perrin's wife has had a fifth.
Give them the afternoon
The wharf is empty and cheerful. Boats wait and do not mind.
Finish the week's work first
"Right." Perrin's fifth waits with everyone else.
The moot's asked me to stand for reeve again and I've said I'll do it if the Keeper comes to the moot. Once. To listen. Nobody's asked a Keeper before. They're not sure you're allowed.
Come to the moot
You listen for three hours. It changes how the town looks at you.
The Keeper answers to the Company
"Right. I stand anyway. Remember I asked."
I have been asked to fund the Jubilee bunting and have said I will if the Keeper agrees to a small plaque on the Company house. My name. Modest lettering.
A modest plaque
The lettering is not modest.
The Company funds its own bunting
"Of course. Quite right. Kindly remember I offered."
You have not slept a full night in a week. I can see it from here. Dray did this. I am not saying you are Dray. I am saying I have seen the end of it.
Sleep tonight; Dace has the gate
You sleep. You dream about the gauge.
After the season
"That is what he said."
A boy from the town has been caught riding the paddle beam as the gate opens. It is the best thing he has ever done, he says. His mother wants him whipped. The hands want him hired.
Hire him
Dace gets an apprentice who is afraid of nothing.
His mother's decision
He is whipped, and rides the beam again the next week.
It's the day my son drowned. Every year the town leaves a lamp on the sill and every year the Company takes it off for the first boat. This year I'm asking the Keeper first.
The lamp stays all day
The first boat waits for the lamp. The bargee knew the story.
Until the first boat, as ever
"As ever." She takes the lamp off herself.
Three days of rain on the Spine. The pound is rising faster than the paddles can pass it down. The east flight is already full of boats waiting for water they now have too much of.
Run all paddles down the east flight
The lower pounds slop over their towpaths. Halfway stays dry.
Hold the water; let the flight clear
Cellars begin to whisper.
Sorry. The aqueduct's running a third of what the table says it should for the season. The pound isn't falling a third faster. I've checked. I keep checking.
Check again, with me
You walk the aqueduct together. It is a trickle. The pound is not.
Be glad the pound holds
"I am. That's what worries me. Roughly."
Wind's from the west, hard. The top gate won't hold shut against it without a man on the beam all night. I've got two men.
You stand the beam
A long night. The gate holds. So, barely, do you.
Requisition a man from the inn
Ilse sends her potboy. He is not pleased. She is less.
Ice on the pound by morning if this holds. I can rig a boom to keep the gate clear, a day's work and my good timber. Or we chance it.
Rig the boom
Ice, by morning. The gate clear. Tamm's timber gone.
Chance it
No ice. Tamm shrugs. "Next time."
The water is low, Keeper, and the town is anxious. We would hold the Lamp Vigil at the sill tonight. It costs nothing but a night's passage, and a little belief.
Close the gate for the Vigil
Lamps on the water. The queue, unexpectedly, joins in.
Hold it on the bank
"The water hears from the bank as well." She does not believe that.
A hot, still week. The pound has a skin of green on it and the gauge has dropped two marks in three days. Boats are starting to touch the sill going in.
Restrict to light drafts
Heavy barges wait or unload. Nobody grounds.
Pass everything, carefully
One grounds. Half a day to float her off.
I've drawn the pound's level against rainfall for a year. Rain makes it rise. But it falls at the same rate whether it rained or not. Something feeds it, and something takes from it. Sorry.
Keep drawing
"I will. I wasn't going to stop. I just wanted someone to know."
Show it to Vosk
"Oh. No. Sorry. Not her." She takes the drawing back.
Lightning's struck the chapel weathervane and half the town's on the towpath watching it smoke. Nobody's at the paddles. Three things, and they're all that.
Let them watch
The vane falls into the pound with a hiss. Cheering.
Back to the paddles
Grumbling. The vane falls unseen.
The top gate's lower beam is soft. It'll hold or it won't. If it won't, it'll be in a storm. There's one coming. A week's work, and I'd start today.
Start today
The gate is out for a week. The storm finds a new beam.
After the storm
The beam holds. Tamm says nothing, which is how he says 'lucky'.
A rainbow over the Reed Reach, Keeper. The Hullfolk are out on their decks looking at it. The town says it is a sign. I say it is a gift. What do you say?
A gift
She is pleased. The town is pleased. It is also a rainbow.
Rain and sun
"So it is. Both are given."
Snowmelt from the Spine. Every stream on the north bank is running brown into the pound. Every stream except one, which runs clear and cold and does not seem to come from the snow.
Walk up the clear stream
It comes out of the hill below the sluice house, and nowhere else.
Streams are streams
The pound rises. The boats float. That is the job.
The west paddle gear's seized with frost. I can free it with a fire under the gear, which is roughly how the Dry Year keeper lost his eyebrows, or wait for noon.
Light the fire
Gear freed by the second bell. Eyebrows intact. Barely.
Wait for noon
Six boats wait with you.
Heatstroke. Two hands down and Stroud says it's the third day of this that kills. We can work the paddles at night instead, if the boats will have it.
Night working
The queue mutters and then sleeps through the passage.
Work through it
The third man goes down at the fifth bell.
Storm's brought a whole tree down across the pound below the Reach. Boats can't pass it. I can cut it, two days. Or the Hullfolk can, one day, for a price they haven't said.
Tamm cuts it
Two days. Good firewood.
Ask the Hullfolk
One day. The price is the firewood, and a nod.
The undercroft is damp again. Only damp. It happens when the pound is high, and only then, though the chapel is well above the bank. We tend it. We do not ask why.
Ask why
"Because it is old, Keeper." She does not meet your eye.
Send hands to bail
The hands bail. Hale is grateful and does not show them the far corner.
Mist on the pound at dawn, and in it, from the north bank, the sound of water running where no stream is marked. By the time the mist lifts the sound has stopped.
Mark the place
Below the sluice house. You write a bearing in the Ledger.
Mist plays tricks
The day's boats arrive and the sound is forgotten.
The reservoir report's late again. It's always late when the pound's low. I've started writing my own. It doesn't agree with theirs. It doesn't agree with the pound either.
Send yours to the Board
"Oh. All right. Sorry. Yes." She does not sleep that night.
Keep yours in the drawer
"The drawer. Yes. It's getting full."
Flood debris in the chamber: a hen coop, a door, a dead sheep. The hands want a mark each to go in after it. The sheep, Keeper. It's the sheep.
A mark each
The sheep is removed with ceremony.
It's the job
It is done. Slowly. With looks.
Dry weather's opened the seams on the top gate. She's weeping a hand's width a watch. I can caulk her in the water, badly, or drain the chamber and do it right.
Drain and do it right
A closed gate for a day. A dry gate for a year.
Caulk in the water
She weeps less. She still weeps.
A week of soft rain and the pound is up two marks for the first time since you came. The gauge, for once, is going the right way. The hands are almost cheerful.
Bank it: pass fewer boats
The pound keeps its gain. The queue does not thank you.
Spend it: clear the queue
A record day. The gauge, by evening, is where it was.
Keeper! Eighty years of the Meridian this autumn. The Board has approved a Jubilee at the summit. At our summit. I have plans. I have had plans for twenty years. How large shall we dream?
As large as the Company will pay for
"Magnificent! The Company will pay for a great deal. Eventually."
Modestly; the water is low
"Modest. Yes. A modest Jubilee. Those words have never met."
The guest list. Commissioner Kell, naturally. Both shore inspectors. The reeve, if she will come, which she will not. And the Board asks whether the boat-clans should be 'visible'. Their word.
Visible; invite Bram
Bram accepts by not refusing. Pell is nervous and pretends otherwise.
Not visible
"Sensible. The Board prefers a tidy summit." The Reach hears anyway.
The Board would like a 'demonstration of throughput' at the Jubilee. Forty vessels in a day, before the Commissioner's eyes. Forty. Keeper, I have promised them fifty.
Fifty, then
"Magnificent! I knew it. I said so. I said the Keeper would say fifty."
Forty, and none aground
"Forty. Well. I shall tell them fifty and hope they cannot count."

Pell wants bunting money. I want spindle money. There's one chest. Sorry. If the bunting goes up and the spindle goes, the Commissioner will see fifty boats and one of them will be stuck in the chamber.
Spindles first
"Thank you. Sorry. Thank you." Pell learns of it and is wounded for a week.
Bunting; the spindle will hold
"It might. Roughly. I'll pray." She does not pray. She oils it, nightly.
The Board's Jubilee speech is here for checking. It thanks 'the Ninefold Reservoirs, whose bounty feeds the summit'. I can't sign that. Sorry. I can't. Someone has to. It doesn't have to be me.
Strike the line
The speech thanks 'the water'. Ardent notices the change and asks who made it.
Sign it yourself
You sign for the reservoirs. Quenn looks at the signature and says nothing at all.

For the demonstration day I'll need the pound a mark higher than it is. The only way is to close the gate for three days before and let it fill. Pell says three days of no boats before a Jubilee is 'a bad look'.
Close for three days
The pound fills. The queue grumbles. On the day, every boat floats.
Run it as it is
"Roughly. Yes. Roughly it'll float them." She does not sound sure.
Commissioner Kell, a week early, unannounced. The Board's view is that rehearsed Jubilees are Jubilees for the Board and unrehearsed ones are for the truth. I am here for the truth. Do carry on.
Carry on exactly as usual
He watches the gate for a week. He writes very little. He sees everything.
Rehearse anyway, openly
"Refreshingly honest. Regrettably, so is the rehearsal." A barge grounds during it.

A private word. The Board's Jubilee has a second purpose. It wishes to be seen at the summit before certain 'structural matters' become public. Regrettably, I cannot say more. I can say that your cooperation will be remembered.
You have it
"Excellent." He does not say what for. You will find out.
What structural matters?
"The Board's view is that you do not need to know. My view is that you already do."

The Commissioner has reviewed the demonstration plan and has one amendment. The boat-clans' moorings are 'in the sightline'. The Board would prefer the Reach empty for the day. Only the day. Regrettably firm.
Ask the Reach to move for a day
Bram moves the Reach down the pound without a word. The word comes later.
The Reach stays in the sightline
"Regrettably noted." Kell does not mention it again. The Board does.
The day, Keeper! Bunting, band, both inspectors in their best, the Commissioner on the dais, and forty vessels queued to the horizon. Give the word. Give it magnificently.
Open the gate
The first barge rises to applause. The band plays something that is nearly a tune.
A word first: thank the hands
You thank the hands before the Board. Pell winces. Dace does not know where to look. The town roars.
Thirty-one vessels and the west paddle has stopped. Stopped, Keeper, before the Commissioner. Quenn is inside the gear. She says a quarter hour. The Board is looking at its watches.
Thirty-one vessels and the west paddle is singing. New spindle. Quenn's spindle. The Commissioner has asked who maintains the gear. I would like to say I do. I shall say she does.
Give Quenn her quarter hour
Fourteen minutes. The paddle runs. The Board applauds the engineer, which has never happened.
Run the east paddle alone; press on
Slow passages, one gate. Forty-two by dusk. The Board did not notice the paddle. Quenn did.

The Commissioner will speak at dusk. Then the Keeper. Then me, magnificently briefly. The Commissioner's speech thanks the reservoirs. Yours is your own. I am asking, as a friend, that it not mention the gauge.
Don't mention the gauge
You thank the town, the hands, the water. Kell nods. Pell breathes.
Mention the gauge
You say the pound has fallen a mark a watch since you came. The band stops. Kell does not move. Quenn, in the crowd, weeps.

The town's picking bunting out of the pound. Two boats went through with it wrapped round the rudders. The Company's gone. The Commissioner's gone. The bunting's ours now. What does a Jubilee cost, after?
Pay the town to clear it
A day's wages for a day's bunting. The town keeps some. It flies from the inn for a year.
The bunting is the Company's problem
"The Company's gone. It's always gone, after."

The Board has written. Eleven lines. It uses the word 'creditable', which is the Board's second-highest word. It uses my name twice and yours once. I have never been so happy with a letter. Shall we frame it?

The Board has written. Three lines. It uses the word 'regrettable'. It uses your name three times and mine not at all, for which I am, Keeper, not grateful. What did you think the gauge would buy you?
Frame it
It hangs beside the other frames. There are many frames.
Give it to Quenn
He does, after a struggle. She puts it in the drawer with the survey.
It is off. The Jubilee. The Board has cancelled it 'pending review of the summit'. Twenty years, Keeper. I do not blame you. I have been trying for a week to blame you and I cannot.
Hold a town Jubilee instead
No Board, no band, no bunting from Ardent. The town does it anyway. Pell weeps and says it was magnificent.
There will be another year
"Will there." He does not make it a question.
The study drawer. The one that's locked. Did you try it? He kept the tide tables there. And other things.
I forced it
"Right." She goes white and does not leave.
I was waiting for you
She has the key. She has had it the whole time.
Tide tables, on a canal. Pages of figures in his hand that aren't figures. He was writing something so nobody would read it. Nobody has.
We read it together
"We." She tries the word out.
Let me take it
"You can look. It stays in the house."
Dray's ledger, open on the desk at night. The columns run the wrong way for money. Every page begins with the same nine marks, then changes.
Copy the nine marks
Nine. Like the locks. Like the reservoirs.
Sleep; it will keep
It has kept a year already.
You'll never guess. In strictest confidence: Dray asked me once what the wire code was for numbers. Not letters. Numbers. I shouldn't have told him. I did.
Tell me too
He does, in a whisper, in the telegraph office, with the door open.
Ask what else he asked
"Where the wire goes at night. I said Ardent. He said no, where does it go."
It's a cipher. It has to be. He taught me one when I was small, a game with the gauge marks. I thought it was a game.
Teach it to me
She draws the sill on the table in spilled ale.
Work it yourself; I'll keep the gate
She works it. She does not come to the paddles for two days.
You have been in the study at night. The lamp is visible from the Company house. For the record, the late Keeper's papers are Company property. You will find I would like them.
There are no papers
"Noted." She writes it down, which is worse.
Tide tables; take them
You give her the tide tables. Not the other pages.
Dray? Course I knew Dray. In my day the gauge had nine marks and a tenth nobody used, painted over. He asked me about the tenth. Nobody asks about the tenth.
Ask about the tenth
"Below the sill. For when the pound went dry. It did, once."
Buy him another and wait
He talks about weather for an hour, and then about the tenth mark anyway.
Ten marks, not nine. That's the key. Every page is a day and every number is a place on the gauge. It isn't a diary. It's a map of something.
A map of the pound
"No. The numbers go below the sill. Under."
A map of somewhere under
She looks at you a long time. "He went under something."
Past midnight, the cipher gives up its last page. Three letters, twice. S.H. And a bearing from the top gate along the north bank.
Sluice house
You have walked past it forty times.
Someone's initials
Nobody at the summit has them. The building does.
I kept a copy. Of his last wire. I keep copies of everything, I shouldn't, I know. 'FOUND THE KEY STOP GOING TO SEE STOP IF NOT BACK TELL M STOP.' He never sent the second one.
Give me the copy
He does. His hand shakes; yours doesn't, yet.
Give it to Mirren
"Tell M." He understands, and goes red.
The telegraph clerk has been indiscreet. For the record, the late Keeper resigned. His wire is a Company document. You have a copy. I would like it.
Hand it over
"Noted. You will find this was wise."
Resigned, was it?
A pause. "That is the record."
'Tell M.' He didn't come back and nobody told me. Nobody told me anything. You know where he went now. Are you going to tell me, or are you going to be like them?
The sluice house
She nods. She has known, or guessed, or feared.
Not until I've seen it
"That's what he'd have said." It is not a compliment.
In the oilskin. The one on the hook. Inside pocket, sewn shut. I never looked. Look.
Open the seam
A brass key, stamped S.H. Cold as the pound.
You open it
She does. She holds the key a long time before she gives it to you.
The key is heavy for its size. Vosk would like it. Mirren wants it. The sluice house door has waited a year and does not mind waiting another night.
Keep it; go alone, soon
You put it on the ring beside the gate keys.
Give it to Vosk
"Noted." She does not ask where you found it. She knows.
You gave it to her. His key. To her. Get out of his chair.
It was Company property
She leaves the oilskin on the hook and does not come back for a week.
I'll get it back
"You won't." She is right.
A full inspection. Not the quarterly. Mine. The Book, the chest, the keys, the study, the Ledger. You will find the Ledger is not Company property. You will find I would like to read it anyway.
The Ledger is mine; the rest is yours
"Noted. Correct." She reads the rest for four hours.
Read it all
She reads the Ledger. She reads it twice. "Noted." It is the longest 'noted' yet.

Your entries note the gauge every watch. Dray's did not, until his last year. The Book requires it weekly. For the record, you are more diligent than the Book asks. For the record, that is how it began with him.
Weekly, then
"Noted." You keep the daily figures in the Ledger instead. She knows.
The gauge is worth noting
"It is. That is the difficulty."
Vosk wired Ardent after the inspection. Coded. I shouldn't have, but I can read the Ardent code now, and it said your name and then 'CURIOUS'. Just that. Is curious bad? It sounds bad.
It is not good
"Oh. Oh no. Should I. What should I do?" "Nothing." "I'm bad at nothing."
Send a wire after it: 'DILIGENT'
He sends it, in Vosk's code, in Vosk's name. It is the bravest thing he has done. Ardent is confused for a month.
Three questions. You will answer or not; both are answers. Have you read the engineer's figures? Have you spoken to the boat-clans about the water? Have you been to the north bank at night?
Answer honestly
You answer. She writes nothing. "Noted. Thank you. That was not wise."
Decline all three
"Noted. That was wise. It was also an answer."

You want to know what I am watching for. I will tell you what I told Dray, exactly. I am watching for a Keeper who cares more about the water than the gate. The Company needs the gate. The water needs nobody.
The water needs someone
"Noted." A pause. "That is what he said. Exactly that."
Then I care about the gate
"Noted. I have written it. I do not believe it. Neither do you."

She's asked me for every wire you've ever sent. Copies. I said I don't keep copies. She said 'noted' in the voice. I have copies. Of everything. Do I give them to her or do I burn the office down? Those feel like the options.
Give her the copies
She reads them all. There is nothing in them. That is what saves you.
Burn the copies, not the office
He burns them in the stove, shaking. Vosk sees the smoke. "Noted."

The sluice house. You have looked at it. Everyone does. It is a disused valve house on the north bank. For the record, it is on the Board's list of structures not to be entered. For the record, I hold the key.
Why does a disused valve need a key?
"Because it is on the list. You will find I did not write the list." She has, though. Partly.
I have no interest in it
"Noted." She looks at you the way she looks at a wrong column.

You were seen on the north bank at the third bell. By me. I was there for the same reason you were. I go every month. I have never once gone in. You will find that is the difference between us, so far.
Why do you go?
"To make sure it is still closed. To make sure I still want it to be."
So far
"So far." She does not deny it. She does not write it down.

The Board has asked whether the sluice house should be 'made permanently secure'. Bricked. For the record, I have delayed answering for eleven years. For the record, I am asking you whether to answer now.
Brick it
"Noted." Masons come. The door is bricked. Something in her face closes with it.
Delay another year
"Noted. Another year. It is what I would have said."
An offer. Irregular. You stop asking about the water. I write 'reliable' in your file every quarter until one of us leaves. Nobody at this summit has ever been offered that. Nobody has needed it.
Accept
"Noted." She writes 'reliable'. You do not stop asking. She knows. She writes it anyway.
Refuse
"Noted." She does not write anything. That is worse.

You will find I have been protecting you. Two Board queries about the summit have been answered by me, favorably, without your knowledge. You will find I did not do it for you. I did it because the next Keeper would be worse.
Thank her anyway
"Do not. Noted." She almost says something else.
Worse for whom?
"For the water. You care about it. The next one would not. I find I have started to prefer that you do."

You have been dealing with the newspaperman. I know. He asked me for a comment on 'the Keeper's water figures'. For the record, I gave none. For the record, I am asking whether the figures were yours or Quenn's.
Mine
"Noted. That was brave, and untrue. She will be grateful."
Quenn's
"Noted." Quenn is transferred within the month. You did that.

My verdict. The Board asked for one; here it is, unsent. 'The Keeper is the first since Dray to see what the summit is. Retain, and God help us.' I do not use that phrase. I used it. You will find I am on your side. Irregularly.
Send it
She sends it. Ardent is baffled. You have an auditor.
Burn it; send 'reliable'
"Noted. Wiser. I am tired of wise." She sends 'reliable' and keeps the other.

My verdict. 'The Keeper is curious beyond the requirements of the post. Recommend removal at the Board's convenience.' I have written it. I have not sent it. You will find I am telling you so that you may leave first, with a reference.
Take the reference; ask for a month
"A month. Noted." She gives you the month. She does not send the verdict during it.
Send it; I stay
"Noted." She sends it. The Board does nothing for a long time. Then it does.

No verdict. For the record, I have told the Board the review is 'ongoing'. It can be ongoing for years. It was for Dray. You will find this is neither protection nor threat. It is the only thing I know how to give.
Ongoing will do
"Noted." The file stays open. So does the door, a little.
I'd rather a verdict
"Nobody would. Noted. Ongoing."

Keeper! The Board wants a record. Not a good month; a record month. More vessels through the summit than any lock on the Meridian has ever passed. I have told them we shall do it. I have told them twice.
Keeper! The Board has noticed the queue. It has noticed loudly. I have promised them the queue will be gone by the month's end and the summit will set a record clearing it. I have promised twice.
A record it is
"Magnificent!" He shakes your hand as if the record were already set.
Safely or not at all
"Safely. Yes. A safe record. The Board will not know the difference." It will.
A record month. I like records. My principals will send every barge they have to help you set it, on one condition: Sorrel boats first at every bell. Aldmere will complain. Aldmere always complains.
Sorrel first
Sorrel's fleet fills the pound. The record looks possible. Crane begins a document.
In arrival order, as ever
"Fine. Half my fleet, then. Records are for people who bend."
Day one of the record. Twenty-two vessels. Magnificent, but not enough. The Board has sent a man to count. He has a very small notebook and a very large watch. He does not speak.
Ignore the counter; work the gate
He counts. You work. Twenty-six on day two.
Feed the counter well
Ilse feeds him. He counts more slowly after lunch, and rounds up.

Inspections are costing you six vessels a day. Six. Waive them for the month. Crane will write to Aldmere. Aldmere will write to Ardent. Ardent will read it after the record is set and the Board is pleased.
Waive inspections
Six more a day. Crane inspects nothing and writes everything.
Inspections stand
"Then the record's Aldmere's to lose. Fine. I'll say I tried."

Two boats a filling. The Sorrel pattern. I know the Company forbids it. I have read the prohibition. It was written in Year 20 by a man who never saw a modern hull. I am not ordering you, Keeper. I am telling you what a record requires.
Two boats a filling
Doubled. The chamber is never empty. Hulls kiss on the third day.
One boat; it's a lock, not a mill
"A lock. Yes. I had forgotten, briefly, what it was."
Halfway through the month and halfway to the record. My principals are thrilled. They've sent a gift for the hands: Sorrel beer, forty casks. Ilse is furious. The hands are not.
Let the hands have the casks
Forty casks. The hands work faster and sing. Ilse does not speak to you for a week.
Sell them through the inn
Ilse sells Sorrel beer at her prices, swearing. Everyone is nearly happy.

I have written to Aldmere. Formally. Under the Compact. The summit has passed ninety vessels without inspection this month, and the letter says so, with dates. I am showing you the letter before I send it. I need not.
Send it
"Duly." Aldmere protests to Ardent. Ardent is busy being pleased about the record.
Hold it until the month ends
"A week. I note that I am doing this, and that I should not."

I have inspected one vessel in twenty this month. In that one I found a crate of rifles under coal, unsealed. I have impounded it. I note that there were nineteen I did not inspect. I note that you know what that means.
Hold everything; inspect it all
The record dies in an afternoon. Crane finds two more crates. Pell is inconsolable.
Impound that one; the record continues
"One in twenty. Duly. I shall record the nineteen as a number, since I cannot record them as anything else."

The Sorrel agent has offered me a 'consideration' to delay my letter. I have refused. I am telling you because I have never been offered one before, and because she offered it in your name. She said you would want it delayed.
I did not
"I believed that. I note I am relieved." He sends the letter that hour.
I did
"Duly." He does not send it. He does not dine at the adjoining table again.
Night. Lamps on the gate, lamps on the boats, lamps on the towpath. The chamber has not been empty since dawn. A bargee asleep at his tiller goes through the gate on a boat steered by nobody.
Night passages stop tonight
The gate goes dark at the last bell. The record slows. Nobody drowns.
Post a hand on every boat
Company hands steer strangers' boats through the dark. It works. It should not.
Three days to the record and the pound is down four marks. The heavy barges are scraping. The hands have started to look at the gauge before they look at the queue.
Light drafts only, till the end
The record slips. The sills keep their stones.
Everything through; three days
Three days of scraping. A grain barge loses her rudder on the sill and blocks the chamber for a night.

The last day. Dace has not slept. Quenn is inside the gear. Pell is on the dais with the Board's counter. The queue stretches out of sight. The chamber is filling with two boats in it, nose to tail, at speed.
Slow the filling
The boats rise gently. The record is missed by four. Pell sits down on the dais.
Full paddles
The boats rise fast. The rear one surges. There is a sound the whole town hears.
A record, Keeper. A record! One hundred and forty-one vessels. The Board's counter has closed his small notebook and shaken my hand. Shaken it! There is a letter coming. I can feel the letter.
Take the credit
The letter comes. It names you first. Pell pretends not to mind, magnificently.
Give the credit to the hands
The letter names 'the summit'. Dace gets a bonus. Pell frames the envelope.
No record. Close. Magnificently close. The Board's counter has written 'creditable effort', which the Board does not frame. I am not angry, Keeper. I am something. I shall find the word by Tuesday.
Next month
"Next month. Yes. There is always a next month, until the Board says otherwise."
The gate is sound; that is the record
"Sound. Yes. The Board does not count sound." He does, later, alone.

Two vessels in the chamber. One under the other. Stroud is down there. The Board's counter has written one word in his small notebook and left for Ardent. The word was 'inquiry'. Keeper, I gave that order. Did I?
You did; I'll say so
You say so, to Kell, in writing. Pell is scolded for nine pages. Nobody hangs.
I gave it
"You did not. Magnificent. Foolish." The inquiry has a name to write, and it is yours.

I have to tell someone. There's a drawer in my office. In it is a copy of Marrow's Year 6 survey. I've had it six years. I've read the tables. I've never read the conclusions. Sorry. I'm frightened of the conclusions.
Read them together
"Yes. Yes. Tonight. Bring a lamp. Two."
Give me the drawer key
She gives it. Her hand shakes. "Don't read it in front of me."
Page forty. 'The Ninefold Reservoirs, at maximum, will sustain the Summit Pound for two summers in three.' Two in three. It's in her own hand. It was never enough. It was never meant to be.
Then what fills it in the third summer?
"Nothing in the survey. Nothing. There's a page missing after forty. Cut, not torn."
Perhaps the reservoirs were enlarged
"They weren't. I've measured them. Roughly. Exactly."
The missing page. There's a note in the margin of forty-one, tiny, in Marrow's hand: 'see S.H. sect. 4'. S.H. Sorry. I don't know what S.H. is. I've been not knowing for six years.
Sluice house
"Oh." A very long pause. "Oh, that's why it's on the list."
Someone's initials
"I checked the rolls. There's nobody. There was never anybody."

I want to walk the aqueduct. All of it, from Cald Tarn to the pound. Nobody has since the Dry Year. It's a day. If it's dry where it should be wet, we'll know. If it's wet where it should be dry, we'll know something else.
Walk it with her
A day on the Spine. The aqueduct is a trickle for six miles. The pound, when you return, has fallen its usual mark and no more.
Send Mirren with her
They go together. Mirren comes back and does not speak. Quenn comes back and does not stop.

Cald Tarn. The lake that feeds the aqueduct. It's full. Full, and the aqueduct's dry, because the sluice at the tarn was closed. By hand. Recently. Someone closed the Company's own aqueduct and the pound didn't notice.
Open the tarn sluice
You open it. The aqueduct runs. The pound rises a finger. A finger. From a full lake.
Leave it; see who closed it
You wait a night. A Company man comes up from Halfway with a lamp and checks the sluice is shut. Vosk's man.

Vosk asked where I was yesterday. I said the aqueduct. She said 'noted'. Then she asked whether I'd found the tarn sluice 'in good order'. She knew, Keeper. She knew before she asked. Sorry. I'm going to be sick.
Tell Vosk it was your order
You tell her. "Noted. Then the engineer was obeying orders. Good." She writes your name, not Quenn's.
Say nothing; wait
Vosk says nothing more. Quenn does not sleep. Neither, now, do you.

I understand the engineer has been walking aqueducts. I note that I have been counting water for six years and have told nobody. I note that two people counting alone is a coincidence and two together is evidence. Shall we be evidence?
Bring Crane in
Crane and Quenn compare six years of figures. They match to the sixteenth of a mark. Crane says 'duly' and sits down.
Keep Aldmere out of it
"Duly. I shall continue to count alone. It is what I am for."

The figures show the pound loses one mark per watch regardless of inflow, and gains nothing from the aqueduct. Something else feeds it and something else drains it. The Compact has no schedule for 'something else'. I have begun drafting one.
Draft it
Schedule Nine, revised: 'joint declaration of material fact regarding the water'. It is a weapon disguised as a form.
A form won't fill the pound
"No. It will make someone say why it is empty. That is what forms are for."

The Aldmere inspector and the Company engineer have been dining together with papers. I have not read the papers. For the record, I know what is in them. For the record, I am asking you to end the dinners.
End them
You tell Crane and Quenn to stop. They stop dining. They do not stop counting.
Join them
"Noted." Three at the table now. Vosk watches from the Company house and does not report it. Yet.

Two explanations. One: the reservoirs leak and the Company hides it. Drought, badly managed. Two: something else feeds the pound and is failing. The figures fit both. Only one fits the missing page. Which do we say?
Drought, badly managed
"Safer. Yes. Roughly true. Not true." She writes it up. It is very good and it is wrong.
Something else, failing
"Then we need to know what." She looks toward the north bank. So do you.

If something under the north bank feeds the pound, then Marrow built it and hid it, and the missing page said so. And the Company has known since the Dry Year, and Vosk knows, and Dray found out. Sorry. All at once.
Say it again, slowly, to the Ledger
She dictates it. You write it. It is the first time the whole shape of it has been on paper since Year 6.
Don't say it again to anyone
"No. No. I'll put it in the drawer." The drawer is very full.

The engineer has written a report. I have read it. It is very good. It is wrong in one respect: it says 'drought'. You will find I am relieved it says drought. You will find I am also, irregularly, disappointed.

The engineer has written a report. I have read it. It does not say drought. It says what the missing page said. You will find that if this report leaves the summit, the summit as you know it ends. You will find I am not threatening. I am describing.
It will not leave the summit
"Noted." She does not take the report. She leaves it with you, which is a kind of trust.
It will
"Noted." She stands a long time at the door. "Then I hope it is a good report."

It's finished. The report. Crane will seal it under the Compact. Hesse will print it both sides in the same watch. Or I burn it and we've spent six years learning something nobody will ever know. Sorry. It's your gate. Say.
Publish it
Crane's seal. Hesse's press. By evening both shores have the figures and the missing page's shape.
Not yet; keep it safe
"Not yet. Right. I've got a drawer." She has. It is the safest place at the summit, because Vosk has already read it.

The drought report. It's ready. It's honest about everything except the one thing. If I send it the Board will thank me and blame the weather and nothing will change. If I don't, nothing will change either. Sorry. I don't know which nothing is worse.
Send it
The Board thanks her. It blames the weather. It commissions a tenth reservoir. The pound falls a mark a watch.
Burn it; start again with the truth
"Burn it. Right." She burns it. She starts again the same night, on page forty-one.

They've transferred me. Ardent. Reservoirs. Effective this watch. Vosk delivered it herself and said 'noted' and then, very quietly, 'I am sorry'. I've emptied the drawer into this bag. It's yours. Don't let it be nobody's.
Take the bag
Six years of figures in a canvas bag. She goes down the flight without looking back, because she cannot.
Give it to Crane
Crane takes it under the Compact. It is the safest bag on the canal. Quenn goes east.
The reeve's moot has voted the Reach a 'temporary mooring' with a fee. Temporary. We have held the Reach since the pound was dug. We ask the gate whether eighty years is temporary.
You stood with us at the remembering. The town has answered it: the moot has voted the Reach a 'temporary mooring' with a fee. We ask the gate whether it will stand with us twice.
Uphold the holding; no fee
The moot is furious. The Reach is not grateful, exactly. It is watching.
The town sets its fees
"So. A wall this year. We remember which years."

We do not say 'water debt' to charter men. We say 'mooring dispute'. It is a smaller thing and they understand it. The gate has heard us say the larger thing. We ask whether the gate wishes to understand it.
I wish to
"Then come to the Reach when the old singer sings. Not before."
Moorings I can settle; debts I cannot
"Honest. We shall settle the mooring, then, and hold the debt."

You've taken the Reach's side on the moorings. Fine. Half the town's saying you've gone Hullfolk. The other half's asking what a water debt is, because Bram used the words at the moot and nobody knew them.
Ask Bram to explain it at moot
He comes. He speaks for ten minutes. Nobody understands. Nobody forgets.
It's a Hullfolk matter
"Everything's a Hullfolk matter till it floods my cellar."

Bram says you may come to the remembering. He has never said it of a Keeper. It is one night, no fire, names over the water from dusk to dawn. Forty names. Then one more that is not a person's. Come, or do not. We sing either way.
Come
Forty names. Then: 'and the Quell, that went into the hill'. Nobody explains. Nobody needs to.
Not this year
"Next year, then. If there is a Reach next year."
You heard the last name. The one that is not a name. It was a river, and we lived beside it, and one year it went into the hill and did not come out. We followed it here. That is who we are.
Where was the river?
"West. Lowmere. A valley. Dry now. Go and see, if you doubt an old woman."
Why did it go into the hill?
"Ask the hill. Ask the charter men who dug it. We only sing what happened."
You stood with us all night. The town saw. We do not thank; it is not our way. We say instead: the debt we speak of is not coin. It is water. It was ours. We ask the gate to hold the thought.
I hold it
"Then we are two."
Water belongs to nobody
"So the charter men said, once. Then they put it in a canal and charged for it."

The old woman's going to sing the whole thing. All the verses. She's never done it for anyone off the Reach. She's doing it for you, which means the old man asked her, which means something's changed. Come at dusk. Don't bring a lamp.
Come at dusk, no lamp
Six verses. A river, a valley, men with picks, a hill that drank, a door, a key that is a number. The tenth mark.
Ask her to sing at the gate
"At the gate. Right. I'll ask. She'll say no. She said yes." Six verses at the sill. The town hears.

So now you know. River, valley, hill, door. I've known since I was six and never cared. It was a song. Now there's a Keeper who's heard it and I find I care, and I don't like it. What are you going to do with it?
Find the door
"Right. Then I'm coming. Don't argue."
Nothing yet; know it first
"Knowing. Yes. The old man's done forty years of knowing. See how it suits you."

I have sung it now. It is yours as much as ours. There is one verse I did not sing. It names the place where the river comes out. Bram says it is his to give, not mine. He is right. He is also afraid.
Respect Bram's verse
"Good. He will give it when he gives it."
Sing it anyway
She sings it, very quietly. 'Below the stone house, where the clear water runs.' She does not look at you.

We have decided. Come to the north bank at the third bell. Bring no charter man. Bring the Dray girl if you like; she has the right. We will show the gate where the river comes out of the hill. We have never shown anyone.
Go alone
Below the sluice house, in the dark: a boil of cold water. Iron on the tongue. The Quell.
Bring Mirren
Mirren kneels at the water and puts her hand in it and does not take it out for a long time.
You have seen it. Now you know what we know, and more, because you can read their books and we cannot. We ask the gate one thing, and we have never asked it: is there a way to give the river back?
There is a sluice; Marrow built it
"A door. The song says a door. So it is true all the way down."
I don't know yet
"Yet. We have waited eighty years on 'yet'. We can wait a season on yours."
If the river went back, this pound would be a road. The town would shrink. Our young ones would go home to a valley they have never seen. We do not know if that is justice. We know it is the debt.
The debt should be paid
"Then say so when it matters. Not to us. To them."
The town is owed something too
"It is. Eighty years of someone else's water. We do not say it is simple."

The moot sits tonight on the moorings again. We will come. We will say the words 'water debt' and we will say what they mean, in the town's own hall, for the first time. We ask the gate to stand beside us when we say it.
Stand beside them
Bram speaks. He names the river. The hall is silent. Ilse, at the end, says 'the moot will consider'. It is the most anyone has ever said.
Speak for them yourself
You name the river to the town. The town looks at the Reach differently after, and at you.

The debt is named. Whatever comes, it has been said aloud at the summit, in the town's hall, with a Keeper standing. That has not happened in eighty years. We do not thank. We give. Petronel's fiddle. It has one string. It is enough.
Take the fiddle
One string. You cannot play it. You keep it on the study wall where the oilskin hangs.
It should stay with the Reach
"It should. We wanted to see if you would say so."

The Reach is emptying. The charter men's order, or the town's, or the water's; it does not matter whose. We are going down the west flight. The song goes with us. We did not finish telling it to the gate. Perhaps the next gate.
Ask for the last verse before they go
Petronel sings it from the stern as the boat drops out of sight. You have it. Barely.
Let them go in silence
Forty boats down the flight in silence. The town watches from the bank. Nobody sings at the summit again.

You know about the reed cargo. Fine. Here's the rest: it's not cheese. It's long, it's oiled, it comes in fours, and it's going east to men who don't grow anything. I've moved it for a year. I'm asking whether I keep moving it.
Stop
"Stopped. They'll find someone else. Someone worse. Remember I said."
Keep moving it; I'll watch
"Watch. Right. Watching's what he did too."

A crate came through the reeds last night that wasn't mine. Somebody's using my route without me. That's not business, that's an insult. It's also a problem, because they don't know the shallows and they'll ground where Crane can see.
Let them ground
They ground. Crane finds rifles in the morning, and does not know whose route it is.
Warn them off; keep the route quiet
Wren warns them. They stop using her route. They start using the gate.

A Sorrel barge declares 'agricultural implements'. Forty long crates. The bargee has the Sorrel Escort Company's seal and no other. Crane is at his post. He has seen the crates. He has not yet seen the seal.
Send it to Crane
Crane refuses the second seal. The barge sits in the pound. Solas appears within the hour.
One seal will serve
The barge passes. Crane sees it go. He writes the time.

Yes. They're mine. I buy them from the girl and I pass them to men I don't like for reasons I don't share. I was ordered to. I'm telling you because you've worked it out and I'd rather you heard it from the man than the crate.
Who are they for?
"Sorrel men who want a different Sorrel. Quickly. With those."
Stop buying them
"Then I'm replaced by someone who doesn't ask the girl to be careful."

Vane pays me. Vane's principals pay Vane. Vane's principals are the men the rifles are for. She doesn't know that. I think she doesn't know that. I'd like her to hear it from someone who isn't me. I'd like it to be you.
Tell Vane
Vane goes white, then red, then very quiet. "My principals. Right." She does not sleep that night.
She should hear it from you
"She should. I won't. That's the sort of man I am." He does, eventually, badly.

There's a convoy coming. Six boats, my men, and under the coal the last of it. Enough for what they want. After that it doesn't matter what you or I do. This is the last gate it goes through. I wanted you to know how many there were.
When?
"Nine days. I'll be at the head of it. Whatever you decide, don't decide at the gate."
Turn it back yourself
"I can't. I've said. I can be slow. That's all I've got."

I have counted the seals on Sorrel Escort cargo this quarter. Forty-one crates bore one seal. Mine was on none. Under Schedule Four, each is a breach. Under Schedule Four, I must report. I am telling you first. I am always telling you first.
Report it
"Duly." Aldmere is told. Aldmere sends a cutter. Solas sees it and goes very still.
Give me the convoy first
"One convoy. Duly. I note this is the last thing I hold for you."

I will not seal arms for any faction. That is what I am for. If the convoy comes and you pass it, the Compact is a dead letter and I am a man in a black coat with a book. Which do you want at your gate?
The Compact
"Then I shall stand at my post when it comes. I have never stood at it for anything."
A man with a book will do
"Duly." He does not stand at the post. He is there anyway, with the book.

My principals want the convoy through and they've told me to make sure. I've never been told to make sure before. I don't know what 'sure' costs. I know I don't want to pay it. Delay costs. This costs more.
Refuse your principals
"Refuse. Right. That's the end of me in Sorrel." She writes the letter anyway.
Make sure; keep your post
"Make sure." She does. She is very good at it. She hates every minute.
The convoy's in the pound. Six boats. Solas at the head, not looking at anyone. Crane at his post with his book. My principals' coin in my pocket. Your gate. Everyone's looking at the gate.
Open the gate
Six boats down the east flight. Crane writes. Solas does not look back. Vane is sick over the wharf rail.
The gate is closed
You close it. Solas's men look at Solas. Solas looks at the water. Nobody moves.
I have an order in my pocket that says force the gate. I have twelve men who'll do it if I say. I'm not saying. I'm standing here. My sergeant's asking me why. Tell me something I can tell him.
Tell him the Keeper has the Compact
He tells the sergeant. The sergeant looks at Crane's book. It is enough, barely.
Tell him I'll buy the coal
You buy six boats of coal. The rifles under it stay in the pound. Nobody says the word.

The convoy is held. I have inspected every crate and sealed none. Under the Compact they are impounded pending both shores. Both shores will argue for a year. I note that this is the Compact working. I note that I am very tired.
Warn Aldmere what they were for
Aldmere learns of the coup faction. Sorrel's government learns Aldmere knows. Something in Sorrel goes quiet.
Impounded is enough
"Duly. Enough." He goes to bed for the first time in three days.

I've been relieved of command. Wired this morning. The men are to go west under my sergeant. I'm to stay and 'await instructions'. There won't be any. I've been given the summit as a punishment. I find I don't mind.
Stay, then; the gate could use you
"The gate. Right." He takes a room at the Wheel. He turns paddles when Dace is short. He is, somehow, content.
Go west with your men
"Can't. Orders. First order I've been glad of." He stays anyway.

News from Sorrel. There's been shooting in the capital. Not much. Enough. The rifles that went through your gate are in it. I'm not blaming you. I'm the one who bought them. I wanted you to hear the number. It's eleven.
Eleven
"Eleven." He does not say anything else for a week.
Fewer than if you'd forced it
"It would. That's the sort of arithmetic I'm good at. I hate it."

Whatever came of the convoy, you and I are the two men at this summit who know what was under the coal. Crane knows. Wren knows. That's four. Four's enough to hold a towpath, if it ever comes to that. I don't think it will. If it does.
Four is enough
"Four's enough." It becomes a phrase between you.
Let's hope it never comes to that
"Hope. Right. I've done a lot of hoping. Some of it worked."

The pound's over the eighth mark and every cellar on the low street has water in it. Mine has a foot. I've the moot in my bar with wet boots asking what the Keeper's doing about it. What's the Keeper doing about it?
Running the paddles full, now
Water thunders down the east flight. Lock 8 curses. The cellars begin to drain.
Sandbags and town labor
Every hand on the low street with a sack. The water stays where it is. So do the sacks.

The well's overflowing. Not the pound; the well. In my cellar. It comes up through the floor when the pound's high and I've never told anyone why because I don't know why. Now there's a Keeper in my cellar with a lamp, so tell me.
The well is the pound
"The same water. I've sold Company water as spring water for twenty years." She laughs. It is not a happy sound.
Ask Quenn to look
Quenn looks, goes red, says 'roughly, yes, the pound'. Ilse pours everyone a drink of it.

Cole's sent round a notice: any tenant whose cellar floods twice this season loses the cellar. Not the house; the cellar. She'll rent them back as 'storage'. The moot wants the Keeper to tell her she can't. She can.
Tell her the Company objects
The Company does not object. Cole knows that. She withdraws the notice anyway, for the look of it.
Keep the cellars dry instead
Paddles full for a week. The cellars dry. Lock 8's Keeper writes to Ardent.

The undercroft is under. The whole of it. I have never let anyone down there and now nobody can go. There are things in the far corner. I have tended them twenty years without touching them. I am asking the Keeper to lower the pound.
Lower it for the chapel
You run the paddles two days for a chaplain's undercroft. The town wonders. The water goes down.
What things?
"Papers. The founding. Nothing that would interest a Keeper." Everything that would.
The water in the undercroft is going down. I went to the third step with a lamp and stopped. Whatever is in the corner, I cannot be the one to bring it up. I have tended it too long.
Go down yourself
A chest, iron-strapped, on a stone shelf just above the water. Letters. An engineer's hand.
Send Mirren
Mirren goes down with a lamp and comes up with a chest and a face like the sill gauge.

You have the chest. I have not asked for it back. I will not. I ask only this: read them in order. She wrote them in order. The last one is the one that matters and nobody who reads them out of order gets that far.
Read them in order
You read. Year 8, the cut begun. Year 10, the chapel founded 'to tend what I have given'. Year 11, the last. You stop before it.
Read the last one first
'If the sluice fails, tell them nothing. Let them have the water.' You have read the end. Now the beginning makes sense, and hurts more.

Six cases of the shakes on the low street this week. All from houses with flooded cellars. All from houses that drink the brewery well. I have tested the well. It is the pound. The pound has something in it, since the high water. Iron, and worse.
Close the well
Ilse closes the brewery. The town drinks Sorrel beer and blames you. The shakes stop.
Boil it and carry on
Ilse boils it. Most of the town recovers. Two do not, quite.
The 'worse' in the water is hill-silt. Clay. It comes only when the pound is high, and from the north bank, not the aqueduct. I know what dirt tastes like. This is dirt from inside a mountain.
Tell Quenn
Quenn tastes it. "The Spine. Yes. That's the Spine." She sits down.
Keep it between us
"As you like. I keep a great many things between us and my patients."
Ilse asked me to say the well was safe. It is not; nor very dangerous. I told her the truth. She has not spoken to me since. Twenty years of friendship. That is what the truth costs here.
Speak to Ilse for her
You do. Ilse says 'she's right, that's the trouble'. They are friends again by the week's end.
The truth was right
"It was. It usually is. It is rarely kind."
