You have read the letters. So the chapel has kept the Cut's secret seventy years, and the gift I bless every month is a theft. Say it. I would like to hear it in someone else's voice.
The gift is a theft
"Yes." She sits in the last pew. "And it fed the town. Both. Both at once. I have never found a hymn for that."
The gift is what it did
"That is what I decided, twenty years ago. It is a comfort to hear it in another voice. It is not a proof."
Vosk has been to the chapel. She asked whether the chest was 'intact'. I said it was where it had always been, which is true, and empty, which I did not say. She looked at me a long time.
Return the letters to the undercroft
Back in the chest, in order. Vosk checks the next month. "Intact." She does not say noted.
Keep them; the Ledger is safer
The letters go in the Ledger. Vosk checks the chest. "Noted." It is a long one.

The last letter. You have not read it, or you have read it and not understood. She wrote it the night before the roof came down on her. It says what she wanted done if the sluice failed. It has failed. It is failing. Read it.
Read it
'Tell them nothing. Let them have the water, and the town, and eighty years. Then let someone braver than me choose.' You are the someone.
Read it to me
She reads it aloud in the empty chapel. Her voice does not shake until the last line.

The chapel's founding charter is in my family's deeds. My grandfather witnessed it. I have read it, of course; I read everything I own. It thanks a donor for 'the water I have given'. I mention it because you look like someone who has just read letters.
Show me the charter
Marrow's signature. Cole's grandfather's. And a clause: the chapel to 'tend the spring and ask nothing of it'. Ask nothing.
Give the charter to Hale
Cole gives it, kindly, for a consideration. Hale reads it in the last pew and does not come out till dark.

The flood is down and the cellars are drying and I have a list of tenants who cannot pay. I would like the Keeper to know I intend to be kind. I would like the Keeper to know kindness, from me, has a ledger of its own.
Pay their arrears from the Coffers
You pay. Cole records it. The low street knows who paid, because Cole tells them.
Be kind on your own account
"On my account. Kindly. Very well." She is. She never lets them forget it.
The water has gone down and the chapel goes on. I will bless the vessels on the first of the month. I would like you to stand where Vosk stands. The last pew. Somebody should.
Stand in the last pew
You stand where Vosk stands. She comes in and sees you there and, for once, sits beside someone.
Stand at the gate, as ever
"As ever. We tend what we can reach."

You'll never guess. Vosk keeps a file that isn't in the Company house. In the telegraph office. My office. Locked drawer, her key. Since Year 31, by the label. I've never opened it. I've thought about it every day for six years.
Keep thinking; don't open it
"Right. Right. Not opening it. I'm very good at not." He is not.
Find out what's in it
"Find out. Right. How?" You do not know yet. He looks delighted and terrified.

Rumor, unprinted: the summit auditor keeps a file the Board has never seen. Rumor, also unprinted: it's why she's never been promoted. I don't print rumor. I collect it. I'm collecting yours. Do you have one?
I've heard the same
"Two rumors is a lead. Three is a story. Find me a third."
Nothing for you
"Nothing. Everyone says nothing. Nothing is very loud, Keeper."

The drawer's label says 'Y31 - S.H. - EYES BOARD ONLY'. And it's in a telegraph office at the top of a canal, not in Ardent. Either the Board doesn't want it, or somebody didn't want the Board to have it.
Somebody didn't want the Board to have it
"Vosk. It's Vosk's writing on the label. She's kept it from them." He sits down.
The Board doesn't want it
"Then why's she kept it?" A very good question.

I've got a locksmith in Sorrel who owes me. He could open a drawer in an afternoon, copy what's in it, and lock it again. Vosk would never know. I'd never print it without your word. I'm asking for your word to try.
Try
The locksmith comes as a bargee. Fennick is sick twice. The drawer opens. The copy takes three hours.
Not like that
"Not like that. Fine. Like what, then?" You do not know. Yet.

I did it. I opened it. I had the drawer out and the file in my hands and I read the first page and I put it back and I've been sick and I'm sorry. The first page says 'the Marrow Cut'. And a date. Year 31. And 'collapse'.
You did well
"I did? I didn't feel well." He almost smiles.
Never do that again
"Never. Right. I won't. I've got the first page memorized though. Sorry."

I've read the copy. All of it. Keeper, this isn't a story. This is the story. A tunnel through the Spine. A stolen river. A drowned engineer. Fifty years of a Board that knew. I could end the Company with forty column inches. I'm asking whether I should.
Not yet
"Not yet. Right. I'll hold it. I've never held anything this heavy."
Never; give me the copy
He gives you the copy. He keeps a copy of the copy. You both know.

A document has been shown to me. I shall not say by whom. It describes a diversion of the River Quell through the Spine into the Summit Pound, constructed without either shore's consent. If true, the Compact was signed over a lie. I note that I am shaking.
It is true
"Then under Schedule Nine I am obliged to declare it. I have never been obliged to anything so large."
It is unproven
"Unproven. Duly. Then I shall prove it, or not. I have the figures. I have always had the figures."

Here's the thing about a story this size. Whoever prints it first owns it. If Aldmere's Guilds get it, it's a war. If Sorrel's Assembly gets it, it's a purchase. If I get it, it's a newspaper. I'm the least bad. I'm asking you to agree.
You're the least bad
"Least bad. I'll have that on my stone."
Crane under the Compact is better
"A form. You'd rather a form than a front page. Fine. I'll print the form."

A question of leverage. The auditor has hidden this from her own Board for eleven years. That is either treason to the Company or loyalty to something larger. I note that if we approach her with it, we must know which before we knock.
Loyalty to something larger
"Then she may be an ally. Duly. I have never had one."
Treason; she's vulnerable
"Then she is a lever. I note I do not like levers. I note I shall use one."

I've set the type. THE RIVER UNDER THE HILL. Both shores, same morning. I haven't pulled the lever. I'm asking one more time, because once it's pulled, it's pulled, and the Company will come for somebody, and it won't be me.
Pull it
By evening both shores know the shape of it. Ardent wires Vosk nine times. She answers none.
Hold it; there's a better way
"Better than a front page. There isn't. But fine. Held."

The file has been opened. I know because I count the pages. For the record, I have not reported it. For the record, I am asking who has read it. I will know if you lie. I would rather you did not make me know.
I have
"Noted." A very long pause. "Then you know what I have carried. I hope you carry it better."
Hesse has
"Noted." She goes to the telegraph office. Fennick is not seen for two days.

I have drafted the Schedule Nine declaration. It requires the auditor's file as an exhibit, the engineer's figures, and two inspectors' seals. I have one seal. The Sorrel agent is not an inspector. I note that the Compact did not anticipate this. I note that I have.
Vane signs as Sorrel's witness
Vane signs. "I've signed worse." It is, technically, irregular. It is, actually, the Compact working.
Wait for a Sorrel inspector
"Duly. Sorrel has never appointed one. I shall write and ask. It may take a year."

Take the file. All of it. I have kept it from the Board for eleven years because the Board would have burned it. You will not. You will find I am not surrendering. I am delegating. It is the most irregular thing I have ever done.
Take it
Fifty years of the Company's knowledge in a canvas folder. It is heavier than the chest.
Keep it; I'll come to you
"Noted." She keeps it. She leaves the drawer unlocked from that day.

The file is in Ardent. I sent it this morning, with a note that it was found in the telegraph clerk's possession. That is a lie. It keeps the clerk employed and you at your gate. You will find I have paid for both.
What did it cost you?
"My post, at the quarter's end. Noted. I have wanted to leave for eleven years."
You should not have lied for us
"I have lied for the Company for eleven years. Once for someone else is not nothing."

The file is burned. I burned it this morning. For the record, I did it because you would have used it, and you must not. You will find I am now the only record. You will find that was always the plan.
Then you are the record
"Noted." She is. She tells you nothing more for a long time.
Hesse has a copy
"Noted." Something in her face gives way. "Then it was never mine to burn."

Keeper. The Board has asked for the contingency. The Clearance draft. I have sent it. I did not want to; I want you to know I did not want to. It comes back next week with the Board's seal or it does not. Either way, they have asked.
Keeper. The Board has asked for the Clearance contingency again. It asked the last Keeper too. The last Keeper is not here. I have sent it. I want it known I did not want to.
Ask him to withdraw it
"Withdraw. From the Board." He tries. He is refused, kindly, by Kell.
The Board asked; the Board decides
"Yes. Yes, it does." He does not look at you.

The Board's seal. The Clearance Order of Year 44, revived, for the removal of 'unlicensed vessels' from the Summit Pound. It requires the Keeper's signature to take effect at the summit. It is a magnificent document. I hate it.
Don't sign yet
"Yet. A good word. I shall tell them 'yet'."
Sign it
You sign. Pell takes the pen from you as if it were hot.

The Courier has the Clearance. Hesse has printed it, with my name on the draft and yours on the line for signatures, blank. The town is reading it in my inn. Well, Ilse's inn. Everyone's inn. Nobody's looking at me.
Tell the town you won't sign
You say it at the inn. The town cheers. Ardent hears by evening.
Say nothing
The town reads your blank line and fills it in for you, in its head.

The moot's called on the Clearance. Half the town wants the Reach gone: fewer moorings, fewer fish in the chamber, fewer people the Company can point at. Half remembers Year 44. I'm the reeve. I'm asking the Keeper to come and be shouted at.
Come to the moot
Three hours. You are shouted at by both halves. At the end, Ilse says 'the moot has heard'. It has.
The Clearance is a Company matter
"Right. I'll tell them. I'll tell them the Company's not coming either."

The moot's voted. Against the Clearance. Not for the Reach; against the Company doing it in our name. It's a small difference and it's the whole town. I'm to tell the Keeper. I'm telling. What the Keeper does with it is the Keeper's.
Refuse the Clearance in the moot's name
You write to Ardent: the summit will not enforce. Pell weeps. Bram, hearing, stands up from his bollard.
The moot doesn't sign Company orders
"No. You do."
We know about the paper. We knew about the last one, in Year 44, and a Keeper died and we stayed. The young ones are saying it too, and they mean it differently. We ask the gate what it will sign.
I will not sign
"Then we hold. And we hold the young ones."
I don't know yet
"Yet. We have heard 'yet' from a Keeper before. It was the last word he said to us."

The order is signed, Keeper, by you, and Ardent has acknowledged it, and now Ardent asks how it will be enforced. I have no men. Solas has men. The Board suggests Solas. The Board suggests it in the voice it uses when it is not suggesting.
Ask Solas
You ask. Solas listens. He says 'understood' and does not say yes.
Enforce it with the hands, slowly
Dace's men serve notice at the Reach. Very slowly. Very politely. Nothing moves for a month.

You've asked me to clear the Reach. I've read the order. It's lawful. I've twelve men and they'd do it. I'm telling you now, once, before it's an order and not a question: I won't. Find someone else or find another way.
Another way; withdraw the request
"Thank you. I mean it." He goes to sit on Bram's bollard. Bram lets him.
Then I'll find someone else
"You will. That's what worries me." Ardent sends men from Ardent. They are not Solas.

Ardent has sent constables. Eight of them, from the capital, in Company green, with staves. They do not know the summit. They do not know the Reach. They know the order. They are asking the Keeper where to begin. Magnificent men. I hate them.
Begin with notice, not staves
Notices on every hull at the Reach. Bram reads his aloud to the water.
Send them back to Ardent
You send them back. Ardent is silent for a week. Then Kell comes.
The constables have come to the Reach with the paper. We are going to sit down. All of us. On our decks, on the bank, on the towpath. We will not move and we will not fight. We ask the gate to watch.
Watch, and stand with them
You sit on the towpath between the constables and the Reach. The constables do not know what to do with a Keeper. Nobody moves.
Watch from the gate
You watch. The constables wait a day, then two. On the third the town brings the Reach soup.

The constables asked me for men. I said no. They wired Ardent. Ardent ordered me. I said no to Ardent. That's the end of my company. I'd like someone to know I said no before I'm told I never worked here.
I'll say so in the Ledger
"The Ledger. Right." He nods. It is enough.
Lend them men; keep your company
"No." He does not lend them. He does not keep his company. He does not blame you for asking.

The young ones want to cut the east bank. Flood the town, drain the pound, end the canal. They know where. We have told them no. They ask why they should listen to an old man who has only held. We ask the gate for a reason.
The river can go back without a flood
"Can it." He looks at you very hard. "Then say how, soon."
Because the town has children too
"So do we. So did we. They listen to that. For now."
The constables have gone. The paper has gone with them. We held. The gate held too, in its way. We do not thank. We say: the next paper will come. We ask the gate to be here when it does.
I will be here
"Then we are two who hold."
The next Keeper may not be
"No. Nor the next Reach. We hold anyway."

It is done, Keeper. The Reach is clear. Forty boats down the west flight this morning, orderly, not a shot. The Board is magnificently pleased. The pound is very quiet. I find I do not like the quiet as much as I expected.
Neither do I
"No." He stands at the window a long time. Nobody sings at the summit again.
The Board is pleased; that is the job
"The job. Yes. Magnificent." He does not sound as if he believes the word.

A young one threw a lamp at a constable. The constable had a stave. Now there is a boy on the towpath who will not stand up, and forty boats, and a town at its windows. We held forty years. It has happened anyway.
Send Stroud; stop the constables
Stroud comes. The boy lives, barely. The constables go back to Ardent. Something is broken that soup will not mend.
The order stands; clear the Reach
It is cleared by dusk. The boy goes west on the last boat. The Reach is empty. So, in a way, is the summit.
You have his key. I know you do; I've seen the ring. The door it fits is on the north bank and he went through it and didn't come back. I'm not asking you not to. I'm asking when, so I can be there.
Tonight, and you'll be there
"Tonight." She does not go to the paddles. She sharpens a lamp wick instead.
Not yet; not with you
"Not with me. Right. He said that too."

The gate has the key. The young one told us, and she does not tell us things. We will not go in; our grandmothers forbade it. But we will stand at the door with lamps. Nobody stood at the door for the last one.
Stand at the door
"We will stand. If you do not come out, we will remember that we stood."
Come in with me
"No." It is the first time he has said the word to you. "We hold the door. That is all."

You're going in the hill. Don't tell me you're not. I've seen men go in mines. Take rope, take two lamps, take someone who can carry you. I can carry you. I've carried heavier. It'll hold or it won't.
Bring Tamm
"Right. Rope's in the yard. Good rope." He does not say anything else. He does not need to.
Rope and lamps, no Tamm
"Suit yourself. Rope's still in the yard." It is very good rope.

The sluice house door. Iron straps, new. The key turns as if it had been oiled yesterday. Inside: a wheel the size of a cartwheel, seized with rust, and behind it, steps going down into the sound of a river.
Down the steps
Forty steps. Wet stone. The sound grows until it is the only sound.
Try the wheel first
It does not move. It has not moved since Year 11. Something in the wall behind it groans.

A tunnel, cut stone, straight as a rule, running west into the Spine. A river fills the lower half, fast and cold and brown. A ledge runs above the water. On the ledge, iron rings for a rope that is not there.
Follow the ledge west
The rings go on. The river goes on. Somewhere ahead, a lamp that is not yours.
Mark the entrance; go back for help
You come back with Tamm and Wren and rope. The rings are for the rope. Somebody knew that once.

A fall of rock, half across the tunnel. Fresh, by the dust. The river piles against it and roars through the gap. On the near side, wedged in the rubble: a Company lamp, rusted, and a brass tag. 'A. DRAY. KEEPER. NO. 9.'
Go through the gap
You go through on your belly with the river an inch from your face. On the far side the ledge is dry.
Stop here; take the tag
You take the tag. You do not go through. You are the first person to come back from this far.

Beyond the fall: a chamber cut into the hill. A second wheel, unrusted. A stone channel south, dry, blocked by a slab. Bones on the ledge, a Keeper's coat, and a ledger in oilcloth, in a niche where a hand could reach.
Take the ledger
Dray's hand. A map of the Cut, the wheels, the south channel. 'Sluice to Lowmere. Marrow's. Never opened. Open it.'
Take the coat, for Mirren
You take the coat and the ledger both. The coat is heavier.

The second wheel, unrusted because he oiled it. Dray's ledger says it opens the south channel: half the river to Lowmere, half to the pound. Marrow died before she could turn it. So did he. Your hand is on it.
Turn it a quarter
It moves. The slab lifts a hand's width. Water goes south into the dark for the first time in eighty years. The roar behind you softens.
Not yet; not alone
You take your hand off it. It is the hardest thing you have done at the summit.
Dray's last page. Not the map. Words. 'The roof is going. I have the key and the map and I cannot get back through the fall. Tell M. I did not leave. I was here the whole time. Tell her I was here.'
Copy it into the Ledger
You copy it by the lamp. Your hand is steady. It should not be.
Take the page itself, for her
You tear it out. It is the only page you will ever tear from anyone's ledger.

You came out. Good. Rope held. I'd have said it would. The Hullfolk were at the door all night with lamps and the old man didn't sit down once. Whatever you've got in that oilcloth, wait till you've had a drink before you open it again.
Have the drink
Ilse pours it without a word. The whole inn watches you not open the oilcloth.
Open it now
You open it at the inn. The town sees a dead Keeper's hand. Something changes in the room.
You came out. The last one did not. We stood at the door and you came out. Whatever you do with what you found, we will hold the towpath for you when you do it. We have never held for a charter man.
You'll not be holding for a charter man
"No. For a gate. We said so. We were right."
Hold for yourselves, not me
"We have. Eighty years. It is time we held for something else."

Vosk is at the Keeper's house when you return, sitting in Dray's chair, which she has never done. She does not ask where you have been. She looks at the oilcloth under your arm. 'Noted,' she says. Then: 'Is he there?'
He is there
"Noted." She sits a long time. "I filed him as resigned. I have never filed anything I hated more."
Say nothing
"Noted." She stands. At the door: "The wheel. Did it turn?" You do not answer that either.
You came out. You've got something under your arm and you won't look at me and you've got his tag on a string round your neck, I can see the string. Tell me. You promised. Tell me first.
Tell her everything
You tell her. The fall, the ledge, the coat, the page. 'Tell her I was here.' She does not cry. She sits down on the sill and does not get up until morning.
Give her the page and go
You give her the page. You go to the gate. She reads it at the sill. When you come back she is at the paddles, working.

You've been in the hill and come out and haven't said a word to me in two days. I've known since I was nine what that means. I'm not asking any more. I'm telling you I know, so you can stop carrying it alone.
Tell her now
You tell her. Late. It is worse late. She listens anyway, and at the end says, "He was here. Good."
Keep it; she has guessed enough
"Right." She goes to the paddles. She does not ask again. She does not stop knowing.

I've put his coat on the hook. Where it was. I've put the tag on the study wall. I'm going to keep working the paddles. I wanted you to know I'm not leaving. He didn't leave either. Neither of us leaves. That's the family.
Neither of us leaves
"Right." She goes to the paddles. You go to the gate. It is a working day.
You could leave now, if you wanted
"I could. I couldn't before; I was waiting. Now I'm choosing. Different."
You have the map, and enough of the rest to know what it is a map of. The pound falls a mark a watch. Soon it will not float a boat, and the choice will be made for you. Make it yourself.
Gather allies
You begin with the people who already know. There are more than you thought.
Do it alone
Alone. Like Marrow. Like Dray. You know how that ended twice.

You have the map. I have seen the oilcloth. One wire to Ardent and there are constables at the sluice house by the week's end. For the record, I have not sent it. I am asking what you mean to do, so I can decide whether to.
Tell her everything
She listens. She does not write. At the end: "Noted. I will not send the wire. I do not yet know what I will do instead."
Tell her nothing
"Noted." She does not send the wire. She watches the north bank every night.

The pound is low. It will not float the Reach by the month's end. The young ones are ready to cut the bank and we are tired of telling them no. We know you have the map. We ask, once, plainly: will the river go home, or not?
It will go home
"Then we hold the night for you. All of us."
Some of it
"Some. We have never been offered some. We will think about some."

I've read Dray's map and Marrow's drawings together. The second wheel opens a sluice to Lowmere. Fully open, the pound becomes a road. Half, it shares. Shut, we go on as we are until it fails. Those are the three. Sorry. There isn't a fourth.
There must be a fourth
"There isn't. I've looked. Roughly a hundred times."
Three is enough
"Three. Yes. It's more than most people get."

Whichever wheel you turn, there is a second choice: whether the shores are told. If I file Schedule Nine, both shores know by evening and the charter is finished. If not, the Company survives and so does the lie. Say.
File it
"Duly. I shall need the engineer's signature and the newspaperman's press. I have both, I think."
Not yet
"Duly. I note I have waited six years. I can wait a week."

You will turn the wheel. I have known since the letters. I ask the only thing I have ever asked: whatever you turn it to, let the town keep its lamp. A chapel, a well, a reason to stay. That is all the gift ever was.
The town keeps its lamp
"Then I am with you. In the last pew, or at the wheel."
The town gets the truth first
"Then give it gently. Nobody has tried gently."

The night. Lamps at the sluice house door. Whoever stands with you stands there. Whoever does not is in the town or the Company house, waiting. The map is in your coat. The key is on its string. The wheel is forty steps down.

The night. The Reach holds the towpath, forty boats, no fire. Solas's men, or what is left of them, stand between the town and the north bank. Bram is at the sluice house door. He has never stood at it. Forty steps down, the wheel.

The night. Crane at the sluice house door with Schedule Nine in a satchel. Quenn with her figures. Hesse with a boy ready to run to the press. Whatever the wheel does, it is done in the open. Forty steps down.

The night. Vosk at the sluice house door with the Company key, which she has never used. Hale with her lamp. Tamm with rope and a new spindle for a wheel that has waited seventy years. Nobody else knows. Forty steps down.
Down
Forty steps. The river. The wheel.
A moment at the door
You look at the pound. It is a mark lower than it was last night. It always is.

Constables. Eight, from Ardent, on the towpath, with a Board warrant for the sluice house. I did not send for them. For the record, Pell did, in a panic, meaning well. For the record, they will not pass me. You will find I am standing in the door.

Constables. Eight, from Ardent, with a Board warrant for the sluice house. I sent for them. For the record, I told you I would have to stop you. For the record, I am sorry. You will find I am standing in the door, and not on your side of it.
Go past her, down
She lets you past, or she does not. Either way the constables do not follow. They are afraid of her. Everyone is.
Face the constables with her
Two of you in a door against eight men with a warrant. They read it aloud. She says 'noted'. They go back to Ardent.

The town has come out with lamps. Not for us, not against us. To see. Ilse is at the front. She asked what we are doing and I said 'holding for the gate'. She is still here. We ask the gate to speak to her.
Tell the town what is happening
You stand on the wharf and tell them. River, hill, door, wheel. Nobody leaves. Ilse, at the end: 'Then get on with it.'
Ask Ilse to hold the town back
She holds them. She does not ask what for. She will, later, at length.

The wheel. Marrow's. Dray oiled it. I've checked the gear; it'll turn. Full open and the Quell goes home and the pound goes to a road. Half and it shares. I've got my hand beside yours. Sorry. I'm not sorry. Say which.

The wheel. Marrow's. Dray oiled it. Tamm has checked the gear; it will turn. Full open and the Quell goes home and the pound goes to a road. Half and it shares. There is nobody beside you who understands it. Say which anyway.
Full open
The wheel turns until it stops. The slab lifts. The river goes south with a sound like a held breath let out. Behind you, the pound begins to fall.
Half
Half a turn. The slab lifts a hand. The river divides. The roar behind you softens to a river's ordinary voice.

The roof groans the way Dray wrote that it groaned. Dust falls into the river. The fall that killed him is behind you and the way out is through it. Whoever came with you is shouting from the far side. The wheel is turned. Leave.
Through the fall, now
On your belly, the river at your face, hands on the far side pulling. The roof comes down behind you. It was always going to.
Take the map from the niche first
Dray's ledger under your arm, the fall, the hands, the roof. You have everything he had, and you are out.

Trouble on the towpath. Constables, or Sorrel men, or the town, it doesn't matter which; men with staves and men with lamps. My people are between them. I've got no orders and no company. I've got a towpath. Tell me to hold it.

Trouble on the towpath. The men the rifles were for have come to see what the Company is hiding. My people are between them and the door. I bought those rifles. I've got a towpath. Tell me to hold it, and tell me quickly.
Hold it
"Understood." He holds it. Nobody fires. It won't come to that, he said. It does not.
Stand aside; nobody dies for a door
"Nobody dies." He stands aside. They reach the door. Vosk is in it. Nobody passes Vosk.

Dawn. The pound is falling to a road. Down the west flight, in a valley nobody living has seen, a river runs for the first time in eighty years. The young ones are singing. The debt is paid. We do not thank. We go home.
Go with them, to see the river
The west flight, then a dry valley with a river in it, then forty boats going upstream for the first time.
Keep the smaller gate
Somebody must keep a seasonal canal. The town shrinks. The town stays. So do you.

Dawn. Schedule Nine is filed on both shores: the figures, the letters, the file, the front page, my seal. The charter is void by its own terms. Both shores must build a real reservoir. I note they will. I note I am weeping.
Sign as witness
The last signature on the first honest document about the Meridian since Year 6.
Let the town sign first
Ilse. Dace. Tamm. Stroud. Fennick, shaking. Then you.

Dawn. The sluice shares the river. The pound holds at a lower mark; Lowmere has a stream. Nobody in the town knows. Nobody in Ardent knows. The file says 'disused valve inspected, sound'. For the record, you have become me. You will find it is not nothing.
Take the key
Brass, stamped S.H. Warm from the wheel. It was always going to be someone.
Give the key to Hale
"We tend it," she says, and puts it on the chain with her lamp.
A Keeper of this chair once stood with us at the remembering. We do not forget a chair. There is a smoked pike on your sill. It is not a bribe. We do not do those.
Accept it
"Then we are two who remember."
Return it with thanks
"We hold the thanks. Keep the fish."
Tucked in the Ledger: pages of a cipher, half worked, in two different hands. Somebody before you got this far with Dray's book and no further.
Pick up where they stopped
The gauge marks. It has to be the gauge marks.
Give the pages to Mirren
She takes them without a word and does not come to the paddles till noon.
The Ledger is waiting on the desk, in a hand that is not yours. The last Keeper wrote until the last watch. The last line is unfinished.
The Ledger is waiting on the desk, water-stained. The last Keeper wrote about the gauge until the water came for the house.
The Ledger is waiting on the desk. Someone left it there after the last Keeper was walked to the stone. The town, then, still respects the book.
Read it through
You know what they knew. It is not nothing.
Start a fresh page
Their hand stays under yours, page after page.
Three Keepers in the chair since Dray. The town has stopped learning names. At the inn they call you 'the new one', and the one before you 'the other one'.
Earn the name
It will take a while. It always does.
'The new one' will do
Less to lose, that way.
I've decided something. Sorry. The last Keeper kept me out of trouble and I let them. This time I'm going to say the figures out loud, to whoever asks. Will you ask?
Ask
"The aqueduct can't do it. It never could. Roughly."
Not yet
"All right. I'll be here."

You know. I have known since I was your age. Marrow died building a sluice that would have shared the water. It can be finished, quietly, with Hale's letters and a boatwright who does not talk. It stays a secret. Ours.
Ours, then
"Noted. I have wanted to say that for a long time."
Not that way
"Then you will find I have to stop you. For the record, I am sorry."
I have read your evidence. I note three conditions for my seal under Schedule Nine: the engineer signs, the newspaper prints the same day on both shores, and nothing is altered. Nothing.
Agreed, all three
"Duly. I will need a night to draft it properly."
Not that way
"I note that. I note everything."
You know where the water comes from. So do we, now, in words. If the sluice is opened the river goes home and this pound becomes a road. We ask a gate one thing: will you open it?
I will open it
"Then we will hold the night for you."
Not that way
"Then we remember that too."
The one before you. I remember one thing about them, and it isn't the thing they'd choose. That's how the town works. What will yours be?
The one before you stood with the boat people at their remembering. Town didn't like it. Town remembers it anyway. What will yours be?
The one before you signed the paper that cleared the Reach. Quieter now. Some of us liked it. I am not telling you which. What will yours be?
Something the town chooses
"Then start drinking here."
Something I choose
"They all say that."
You have asked about the reservoirs. Noted. The last one asked that too, and the one before. You will find the answer is the same. You will also find I am tired of giving it.
Then give a different one
"For the record: no." But she stays a moment longer.
Withdraw the question
"Noted."
A barge of geese, two hundred by the manifest, is in the chamber when the crate slats give. The chamber is full of geese. The bargee is full of opinions.
Close the gates and catch them
An hour of hands, feathers and language. Most are caught.
Open the top gate and let them go
Two hundred geese enter the Summit Pound. The bargee enters the Book, as a complaint.
There are geese in my yard, geese on my roof and a goose in my cellar that has opinions about the ale. Whose geese, Keeper, and what does it cost?
The Company's geese now
"Then the Company owes me a cellar."
The bargee's problem
"He left this morning. The geese did not."
Three things. The hands want a goose each for the trouble. The chapel wants them for the poor. And there's one in the paddle gear that we can't get at.
A goose each for the hands
Feathers everywhere for a week. Morale improves.
The chapel feeds the town
Hale blesses the geese, then cooks them. Dace sulks.
A drover arrives on foot from Aldmere with a bill of sale for two hundred geese and a very reasonable question about where they are.
Pay him from the Coffers
He counts it twice and asks about the one in the paddles.
Send him to the Company
Pell will write him a magnificent letter.
The goose in my cellar has laid. In the ale trough. The town has named her. I am not going to tell you the name. Do you want her moved or not?
Move her to the chapel
Hale accepts a goose with grace. The town visits.
She stays; she's the town's now
"Her name is Pell." She said she wouldn't tell you.
Weeks on, geese still turn up: in the chamber, on the chapel roof, once in Vosk's document case. The town has begun to count them as weather.
Declare the matter closed
The Book says closed. The geese did not read it.
Bounty: a mark a goose
Children become rich. Wren, somehow, becomes richer.

The Sorrel agent and I have both claimed first passage at the same bell. She has proposed, in writing, that we settle it by duel. I have accepted, in writing. I now find I do not know how a duel is conducted.
Second him
"You would? Duly. I shall need to know what a second does."
Forbid it on Company water
"Forbidden. I note I am relieved. I note I am also, irregularly, disappointed."
He accepted. In writing. With a citation. I was joking. I can't back down from a man who's cited the Compact at me. Pistols at dawn on the towpath. You're seconding him. Who do I get?
Solas
Solas agrees, weary. "I've seconded worse for less."
Wren
Wren agrees, delighted. "I've always wanted to hold a pistol legally."
The night before. I have read three accounts of duels and they disagree on every particular. I have written my will. I have left my statute book to you. I would like it noted that I am not afraid.
Suggest both fire wide
"Fire wide. Is that permitted?" It is, you say. "Duly. Then I shall."
Suggest he withdraw
"Withdraw. From a Sorrel agent. In writing." He cannot. You knew he could not.

Dawn. Towpath. Half the town watching from the bank with breakfast. Two pistols I've loaded with powder and no ball, which nobody's asked me about. Crane's counting paces aloud. Vane's laughing. Somebody has to say 'fire'. It's the seconds' job. That's us.
Say it
Two bangs, no balls, a cloud of smoke. Crane is astonished to be alive. Vane bows. The town applauds.
Say 'stop' instead
You stop it. Both are relieved. Both pretend outrage. The town is disappointed and goes to breakfast.
Neither of us is dead and neither has first passage and the whole town saw us make fools of ourselves. He shook my hand afterward. Matthias Crane shook my hand. What do I do with that?
Dine with him
They dine. They argue for two hours about fish. It is the start of something neither will name.
Nothing; it was a duel
"Nothing. Right." She does not do nothing. She sends him a fish.

I have drafted a schedule for precedence disputes that does not involve pistols. The Sorrel agent has signed it. I have signed it. It requires the Keeper's signature. I note this is the first Compact amendment in twenty-two years.
Sign it
The Halfway Precedence Schedule. Both shores ratify it within the year, baffled. Crane is happier than you have seen him.
The Keeper decides, as ever
"As ever. Duly. I shall keep the draft. It will keep."

Four cases of the shakes this week, all from the low street, all regulars at the Wheel. Same symptoms as bad water. Ilse says her ale is spring water. I would like to test the well. She will not let me.
Tell Ilse to let her
Ilse lets her, glaring. Stroud takes a bottle. Ilse takes it personally.
Test the pound instead
Stroud tests the pound. Iron, and something else. She looks toward the inn.

Your physician's been at my well with a bottle. Twenty years that well's fed this town and now it's poison because four drunks have the shakes. It's spring water. It comes up cold from the hill. Everyone knows that. Tell her.
It comes up from the pound
"Does it." She knows. She has always known. She is furious that you said it.
I'll tell her to stop
"Do." You do. Stroud does not stop. She tests it at night.
The well is the pound. Pound water, through a crack in the rock, with iron and, this month, something from the north bank I do not like. Boiled, it is fine. Ilse boils nothing. Ilse brews.
Order the ale boiled
Ilse boils it, swearing. The ale tastes of nothing. The shakes stop. Custom halves.
Let the town decide
You post Stroud's findings at the inn. Half stop drinking. Half drink more, to prove a point.
Fine. It's the pound. My father showed me the crack when I was twelve and told me never to say. The Company would charge for the water or close the well. Twenty years. Are you going to close me?
No; the town needs its inn
"Then we understand each other." She pours one from the well and drinks it herself.
Tell the Company; pay for the water
Vosk assesses a water rate. It is small. Ilse pays it. She does not forgive it.

The brewery well. I've measured it against the gauge for a month. It rises and falls with the pound, a day behind. The pound's leaking into the rock under the town. Sorry. It's been doing it eighty years.
Where does the leaked water go?
"South. Under the town. Into the ground. Some of the fall each watch is that. Not much. Some."
Can the crack be sealed?
"Roughly. It'd close Ilse's well. She'd rather the leak."
The shakes are gone. I boil what I have to. The town drinks Iron Spring and knows what it is now and drinks it anyway, because it's ours. Stroud and I are speaking again. First round's on the house.
Drink it
Iron Spring. It tastes of the pound. It tastes of Halfway.
Toast Stroud
Ilse toasts her too, eventually. The inn cheers, mostly at the free round.

My coal crews want the chapel blessing before passage. All forty boats. They've heard the grain boats get it. It's superstition and it costs me a morning a fleet. Stop it, or make it for everyone. Pick.
Blessings for everyone
Hale blesses coal. It takes all morning. The crews are delighted. Vane is not.
Blessings are the chapel's business
"Fine. Then my crews will queue at the chapel instead of the gate, and that's your morning gone too."
The coal crews have asked for the blessing. The rite speaks of still water and grain. I have adapted it: still water and warmth. The Concordance in Aldmere will not approve. I did not ask.
Bless the coal
"For the warmth that comes of fire and the fire that comes of the hill." The crews weep. Nobody expected that.
Stick to the rite as written
She blesses coal with the grain rite. Nobody notices but her.
My crews say the blessed boats go faster. They don't; I've timed them. But they think so, and row harder, so they do. Now I'm paying for blessings. Give me a receipt. My principals will ask.
A receipt from the Coffers
You write Sorrel Freight a receipt for 'spiritual services'. Crane, later, is delighted by the category.
The chapel gives receipts
Hale gives a receipt. It is a blessing on paper. Vane's principals frame it, confused.

A letter from the Concordance in Aldmere. They call the coal blessing 'irregular' and wish it stopped. The coal crews wish it continued. I have never disobeyed the Concordance. I have never been asked by anyone who meant it so much.
Bless the coal; answer Aldmere later
She continues. Aldmere writes again. She loses the letter. It is the most disobedient thing she has done.
Stop; the Concordance is the Concordance
She stops. The coal crews stand at the chapel door anyway, caps off, and she blesses them without coal.
A coal barge has come up with a Concordance lamp burning in a glass box on its bow: blessed at Halfway, carried to Sorrel and back. The crew asks for it reblessed. Nine boats behind it have lamps.
Rebless the lamps
Nine lamps, one morning. The pound at dusk is lit like a festival by coal boats with chapel lamps.
A blessing lasts; move along
The lamps pass unreblessed. The crews are downcast. Hale, later, goes down to the wharf and does it anyway.

The Concordance has decided the coal blessing is 'a local devotion' and may continue. They sent a hymn about coal. It is very bad. The crews love it. I have never seen so many in the chapel who could not read the hymnal.
Sing the bad hymn
Forty coal men roaring a bad hymn. Hale conducts. It is, somehow, the holiest thing at the summit.
Sing Petronel's instead
Hale asks Petronel. Petronel sings. The coal men are silent. The hymn is not about coal. It is about a river.

Three things, and these are the hands' three things. Wages a day late, every month. No gloves in winter. And the Company store won't take Company scrip at face. They've asked me to ask you. I've asked.
Hear all three properly
You sit with the hands an hour. You cannot fix all three. You say so. They did not expect that.
Wages are the Company's timing
"Right. I'll tell them the Company. They know the Company."

Three things. The hands have heard you heard them. They've heard nothing's changed. And they've asked whether a Keeper who listens and does nothing is better than one who doesn't listen. I said I'd ask. I'm asking.
Fix the gloves, at least
Twelve pairs from the Coffers. One thing of three. It counts.
Listening is what I can do
"Right. I'll tell them that. They'll like it about as much as I do."
The hands have sent me a letter. With three demands and eleven signatures. The Company does not receive letters from hands. It receives them from Keepers. Tell them that, kindly, and make it work.
Sign the letter yourself; send it up
Twelve signatures. Pell is aghast. Ardent is puzzled. Gloves arrive from Ardent, which has never happened.
Tell them kindly
You tell them. Kindly. They fold the letter and put it away. It comes out again, later, unkindly.

Three things. The hands have stopped. Not struck; stopped. They're at the paddles and not turning them. They'll turn when the scrip's worth face at the store. The store's the Company's. The Company's in Ardent.
Make up the scrip difference from the Coffers
You pay the hands the difference in coin. The paddles turn. The chest is lighter. Vosk reads the entry twice.
Turn the paddles yourself
You and Mirren turn the paddles for a day. Eleven hands watch. By dusk, three help. By morning, all.

The hands drink here. I hear the three things every night. Here's a fourth, free: they'd follow you off a cliff if you asked plainly, and walk you to the stone if you lied once. Dace won't say that. I just did.
Then I'll ask plainly
You go to the lock house and tell the hands exactly what you can and cannot do. They listen. It is enough.
Dace should say it
"He won't. He's a corporal. Corporals report; they don't say."

Three things. The hands have their gloves. The store takes scrip at face, since Pell had a word he pretends he didn't. And wages are still a day late, which the hands say they'll live with. Two of three.
Two of three
"Two of three. Right." He almost smiles. The hands call it 'the Keeper's two' for years.
Three of three; I'll pay the day myself
You advance wages from your own pocket, monthly. The hands know. Dace says nothing about it, loudly.
The chest is light. Everyone's is, this season. Mine is not. I lend to the town at one in ten and would lend to the post at one in twelve, kindly, because I like a Keeper who stays. Twenty marks?
Twenty marks
Twenty in. The bell on her door rings for you now. One in twelve, monthly, kindly.
Ten, and no more
"Ten. Prudent. I like prudent. Prudent pays."

The first payment. Kindly, on time. I mention that the interest is on the whole, not the balance, that this is written on the note, and that most people do not read the note. You did not read the note.
Pay it; read the note now
You read it. One in twelve, on the whole, monthly, until cleared. It is a long note.
Dispute the terms
"Dispute. Kindly. The note is the note. Vosk has a copy." Vosk does.
The Ledger has a page on Cole. Dray's hand: 'she owns the chapel, the inn's debt, half the low street and the Board's nephew's gambling paper. Do not owe her. If you must, owe her briefly.'
Clear the debt now, whatever it costs
You empty the chest into Cole's hands. The bell stops ringing for you. It is very quiet.
Owe her a while longer
The bell rings monthly. The interest is on the whole. Dray's hand was right.

You are behind. I do not send men. I have sent the Company a copy of the note. I also have an alternative: the Keeper's discretion over mooring fees at the pound, assigned to me for the term. I collect; you are clear.
Assign the mooring fees
Cole collects the pound's mooring fees. The Hullfolk pay a landlady now. Bram hears of it.
Let the Company see the note
Vosk reads it. "Irregular. Both of you." She pays it from the maintenance fund and says nothing else, which is worse.
You owed Cole. Everyone in this town has. She's never been unkind and she's never let anyone go. My inn was hers for six years. Whatever you gave her to get clear, I hope it wasn't the town's.
It wasn't the town's
"Good." She looks at you a moment. "Good."
It was the mooring fees
"The Reach's fees. To Cole." She does not say anything else. She does not need to.

You are clear. Few are. I have torn the note in front of you, as I do. I have kept a copy, as I do. Should the post need me again, my door has a bell. I hope you never hear it. I have never hoped that before.
Thank her
"Do not. Kindly." She means it, which is new.
Ask why she hopes it
"Because you paid. Nobody pays. They give me things instead. I have enough things."

Lucan Hesse, Courier. I've come for a piece on the new Keeper. I've got one question and it's not the one you think. Not 'what will you do'. This: what did they tell you about the last one, and did you believe it?
They said resigned; I didn't believe it
"Good answer. Good enough that I won't print it yet."
No comment on the last one
"'No comment.' It's a quote. Everything's a quote."

Hesse asked me what wires you send. I said none of his business. He gave me a mark. I said still none of his business. He gave me two. I told him about the reservoir one. I'm sorry. I'm telling you before he prints it, which is something.
It's something
"It is? Oh. Good. I'll give him the two marks back." He does not.
Give the marks to the poor box
He does, red-faced. Ilse puts it in the box and tells the whole inn where it came from.

I've got a headline. 'THE KEEPER WHO COUNTS THE WATER.' It's about you asking questions about reservoirs. It's flattering, in Sorrel. In Ardent it's a warrant. I'll run it if you say. I'll run something duller if you don't. I'd rather run it.
Run it
Both shores read that the summit Keeper counts water. Vosk reads it twice. Quenn cuts it out.
Something duller
'NEW KEEPER SETTLES IN.' Nobody reads it. That is what it is for.
The Courier. I have read it twice. It mentions you eleven times and me once, as 'the Superintendent', without a name or an adjective. Twenty years at this summit. I have never been so unmentioned.
Ask Hesse for a piece on Pell
Hesse writes one. It is kind and slightly mocking. Pell frames it and does not notice the mocking for a year.
Newspapers mention who they like
"They do. They do." He is quiet for a day. Then magnificent again, doggedly.

Ardent's written to the Courier. A letter of complaint about 'irresponsible speculation regarding Company infrastructure'. I've never had a letter from a Board. It's the best thing that's happened to my paper. I'd like to print the letter. It's their words. They can't stop me.
Print the letter
Ardent's complaint on the front page, verbatim. Both shores laugh. Ardent does not write again.
Don't; they'll come for you
"Let them. No, you're right. I'll hold it. I'll hold it about a month."
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP KEEPER TO REFRAIN FROM STATEMENTS TO PRESS STOP ALL PRESS ENQUIRIES TO ARDENT STOP ACKNOWLEDGE STOP
Acknowledge
You acknowledge. Hesse hears of it. He prints the wire, since it is not a statement.
'THE KEEPER SPEAKS TO WHOM THE KEEPER LIKES'
Fennick sends it, hands shaking. Ardent does not reply. Hesse frames it.

You want the Dry Year? I'll give you the Dry Year, in pieces, because that's how I remember it. First piece: the pound went to the sills in a month. No drought. Rain every week. Went down anyway. Company said drought. Company said it loud.
No drought?
"Rain every week. I was twelve. I remember being wet and the boats being dry."
Buy him another; wait for the second piece
He drinks it and tells you about a girl instead. The second piece waits.

Second piece. Men came up the west flight at night. Forty, in Company coats. Said they were a dredging crew. I knew what a dredger looked like and they didn't have one. They had picks and lamps, and they went up the north bank.
The north bank, not the reservoirs
"North bank. Reservoirs are south. Everybody knew. Nobody said."
What did the town say?
"Town said dredging. Town says what the Company says when the Company's paying wages."
Tobin's been telling you the Dry Year. He told him too, the month before. I heard them from the stairs. Tobin said 'the north bank' and he went very quiet. I'd like to hear the rest with you.
Hear it together
You sit with Tobin, both of you. He tells it slower for her. She does not interrupt once.
Hear it alone; tell her after
"After. Right. That's what he'd have said too." It is not a compliment.

Third piece. The men came down after a month. Thin. Two fewer than went up. And the next week the pound started to rise, no rain, a mark a day, till it was full. Company said the reservoirs had 'recovered'. Reservoirs don't recover from picks, Keeper.
Two fewer
"Two. Nobody counted but me. I was twelve and I counted everything. Still do."
A mark a day, no rain
"No rain. Like it's falling now, a mark a watch, no drought. Same thing, backwards."

You have been sitting with the old Keeper of Lock 8. He tells a story about the Dry Year. For the record, he has told it to every Keeper since. For the record, it is substantially accurate. For the record, I am asking you not to write it down.
Don't write it down
"Noted." You do not write it. You remember it. She knows the difference and lets it stand.
It's already in the Ledger
"Noted." A long pause. "Then it is in three Ledgers. Dray wrote it too."

Last piece. Years after, Dray came down to Lock 8 one night, white, and asked where the men went in. I told him: below the stone house, where the clear stream is. He said thank you, Tobin. He never came down again.
Thank you, Tobin
"Don't say it like that. He said it like that."
Where the clear stream is
"You've seen it. Course you have. You've got the face."

Pilgrims from the Aldmere chapels, forty of them, for the Lamp Vigil. They have no toll money; pilgrims never do. They ask passage through the pound to the chapel stage. The Book has no line for pilgrims. Find one.
Free passage for pilgrims
Forty pilgrims through the gate for nothing. Vosk finds the line and reads it twice.
The chapel pays their toll
Hale pays from the poor box. The poor eat less that week. She does not mention it.

A pilgrim, very old, has knelt at the sill and put his hand in the pound and is weeping. He says the water tastes of his village, west of the Spine and dry these sixty years. The other pilgrims are embarrassed.
Ask the name of his village
"Lowmere. Nobody says it. The water says it."
Help him up
You help him up. He thanks you. He keeps his hand wet all the way to the chapel.

Forty Aldmere pilgrims have passed the summit without toll. I note that the Compact does not exempt pilgrims. I note that Aldmere's Guilds have asked me whether the Company is 'establishing a religious preference'. I note that I do not know what that means and must answer anyway.
Charity, not preference
"Charity. Duly. The Guilds have no schedule for charity. I shall invent one."
Charge the next lot
"Duly." The next pilgrims pay. Hale says nothing, which is how she says everything.

The pilgrims asked to see the spring. I showed them the chapel well, as I show everyone. The old one from the dry village said 'that is not a spring, that is a pipe'. He is right. I have never had a pilgrim who was right.
Show them the north bank instead
Forty pilgrims at the sluice house door, singing. Vosk watches from the Company house and does not come down.
The well is the spring; say so
You say so. The old pilgrim looks at you the way Bram does. Hale is grateful and ashamed.

The pilgrims are leaving. Forty, by boat, down the east flight, singing something that is not a Concordance hymn. It has a river in it. They learned it at the Reach, where they went, uninvited, the last night, and were given fish.
Let them sing it down the flight
The Song goes down the Aldmere flight in forty voices. Bram, on his bollard, does not sing. His lips move.
Ask them to sing a hymn instead
They sing a hymn. Politely. The river song comes back on the next boat up.

A letter from the old pilgrim. He thanks the Keeper, the chapel and the Reach. He will not come again; he is too old. He says: 'tell the boat people the valley is still there. Somebody should go and look.'
Give the letter to Bram
Bram reads it three times. "Somebody should. We have said so for sixty years. Now a stranger has."
Keep it in the Ledger
The letter goes in the Ledger. It is the first entry not by a Keeper.

A drover with forty cattle at the towpath gate wants to swim them across the pound rather than pay the ferry or wait for the bridge at Lock 8. Forty cattle. In a canal. Crane has gone to find a schedule. Dace is already laughing.
Swim them
Forty cattle in the Summit Pound. Boats stop. Children cheer. One cow tries the chamber and has to be talked out.
Ferry or bridge, like anyone
He pays the ferry, muttering. Crane arrives with the schedule too late and is quietly heartbroken.

Schedule Two, note four: 'livestock in transit by water'. Written for boats carrying livestock. It does not say the livestock must be in the boat. I have never seen a clause so unprepared for its own use. A toll per head.
Charge per head
Forty tolls. The drover pays in cheese. Crane accepts cheese under Schedule Five, delighted.
One toll for the herd
"One. A herd as a vessel. Also defensible. I shall note both and be happy for a week."

One cow did not come out. She is standing in the shallows below the Reach, up to her belly, eating reeds, and will not be moved. The drover has gone on with thirty-nine. The Hullfolk have named her. They will not say what.
Leave her to the Reach
The Reach has a cow. She gives milk. Bram, asked, says only 'she holds'.
Rope her out with a boat
Six hands, a boat, a rope, an hour. She comes out. She goes back in by dusk.

Report, Keeper. The cow's still in the Reach. The hands have started leaving her hay. And the Company's sent a wire asking why the summit's traffic log has an entry that reads 'forty cattle, swimming, one outstanding'.
Reply: 'livestock in transit, Schedule Two'
Ardent does not reply. Crane, shown the wire, is prouder than you have ever seen him.
Reply: 'clerical error'
"Right. Clerical. The cow's a clerical error." She is called Clerical from then on.

The drover is back. He has heard his cow is alive and well and living with the Hullfolk. He would like her back. The Hullfolk would like to know what he'll pay. The cow would like to eat reeds. Nobody has asked the cow.
She's the Reach's now
The drover goes away with thirty-nine cows and a grudge. The Reach keeps its cow. Bram, asked, says 'she chose'.
She's the drover's; pay the Reach for hay
The Coffers pay the Reach for hay. The drover takes the cow. She is back in the shallows in a week, having walked from Lock 6.

There's a cow at the Reach that the town feeds and the Hullfolk milk and the Company's got a wire about. Somebody's painted her on the inn sign. It's the first thing the town and the Reach have shared in forty years. Take it.
Take it
A cow on the inn sign. Bram drinks at the Wheel for the first time, under it. Nobody mentions why.
Ask what the Hullfolk named her
"Quell. Some river. Don't ask me." You do not need to.
There's a boy in the lock house loft. Sorrel, Escort Company coat with the badges cut off. He came up in a coal hold, about my age, shaking. Solas's men are asking at the inn. I haven't said. Don't.
Say nothing; he stays hidden
The boy stays in the loft. Mirren brings him bread. You do not go up.
Tell Solas quietly
You tell Solas. He listens. He does not go to the loft. He does not tell his men. He goes to sit on Bram's bollard.

Seventeen, perhaps. He was made to load rifles onto coal boats and did not know what they were for until a sergeant told him, laughing. He does not want to shoot anyone. He says it as if it were a strange thing to want.
It is not strange
He looks at you as if nobody had said so before. Perhaps nobody had.
Ask what the rifles are for
"Sorrel. A different Sorrel. The sergeant said 'quickly'."

One of mine's missing. Seventeen. Frightened of the wrong things and the right ones. My sergeant wants him found and made an example of. I'd rather he was found by nobody. I'm not asking where he is. I'm asking whether he's eating.
He's eating
"Good." He goes back to the inn and tells the sergeant the boy went east. The sergeant goes east.
He's in the lock house loft
"I didn't hear that." He did. He does nothing with it. He looks older.

He can't stay in the loft. Solas's sergeant is searching lofts. The Reach would take him; Wren said so. The chapel would take him; Hale said so. The Company would give him back; nobody had to say so. Where does he go?
The Reach
Wren takes him at night. He is a Hullfolk boy by morning, in a stitched coat, learning knots.
The chapel
Hale takes him. Sanctuary. Cole raises the chapel's lease, kindly. The sergeant does not search chapels.

My sergeant's found him. Or thinks he has. He wants to search the Reach, or the chapel; he's not sure which and he'll do both. I've told him no. He's asked on whose authority. I've got none. You've got a gate.
No searches on Company ground
You say it in front of the sergeant. He looks at Solas. Solas looks at the pound. The sergeant goes back to the inn.
Let him search; find nothing
Wren has moved the boy to a fishing boat in the reeds. The sergeant finds a cow.

The sergeant has gone west without his deserter. The boy is at the Reach, or the chapel, or gone east with a new name and a Hullfolk knot in his hair. Mirren does not say. She is at the paddles, humming. She never hums.
Ask her which
"Safe." That is all she says. It is enough.
Don't ask
You do not ask. She hums. The gate runs.

A coal barge from the west with a clean bill and a bargee who will not come up on deck. His mate says he is 'resting'. His mate is sweating in a cold wind. Stroud is at the inn. The queue is nine boats.
Hold the boat; send for Stroud
Stroud comes. She goes below. She comes up and says one word: 'fever'.
Pass it; the bill is clean
It passes. Down the east flight. Stroud, told later, goes very still.

Coalfield fever. One aboard sick; two more by week's end. The boat must not go down the east flight and must not sit in the queue. It needs a mooring apart, a physician, and time. The Company has a form. I have a patient.
Moor them beyond the Reach
The Hullfolk take the boat without being asked and bring food to the end of a pole. Stroud goes daily.
Send them back down the west flight
The boat goes west with its fever. Stroud does not speak to you for a week. Sorrel does, later, angrily.

There is fever at the summit. The Board's standing instruction is that the summit does not close for illness; closure 'alarms the shores'. I have not shown it to you until now, and I am not sure why I am showing it.
Close the summit anyway
"Noted." She writes 'gate closed for maintenance'. It is the first false entry she has ever made for someone else.
Stay open; isolate the boat
"Noted." The gate runs. The boat sits apart. By the week's end there is a case in the town.

The bargee is dead. The mate will live. The boat is a fever ship and its coal is Sorrel's and Sorrel wants it. I will not have that hold opened for a month. Vane wants it opened tomorrow. Choose a physician over a rate card.
A month; Sorrel waits
Vane is furious and then, hearing the word 'dead', quiet. The coal waits.
Burn the coal in the boat
A coal barge burning on the pound at night. Sorrel's loss. Stroud's relief. The town watches from the bank.

There's a fever ship at the Reach and the town's frightened. Half want the Reach cleared for having it. Half want the inn closed for having me. Come to the inn tonight and drink, in public, and don't die of it.
Drink at the inn, in public
You drink. The town watches you not die. By the second pint the inn is full.
Stay away till Stroud says
"Right. Sensible." The inn is empty for a fortnight. Sensible costs.

The mate has walked off the boat, thin and alive. One dead, one living, none in the town. That is a good outcome for coalfield fever at a summit lock. I am telling you it was well done, because nobody else will.
It was your doing
"It was both. Take half. Doctors are bad at halves."
Inspect every bill from now
"Every one. Good. It costs an hour. The other thing costs more."

I have to tell you something and I've been putting it off. I read your wires. All of them. Not for anyone; for me. I like knowing. I know it's wrong. I'm telling you so you can stop me, because I can't.
Keep reading; tell nobody
"Nobody. Right. I can do nobody." He can, mostly.
Stop reading
"Stop. Yes. I'll try." He stops for a week. It is the longest week of his life.
A wire, for you, in Fennick's hand, not from the key. 'I READ THIS BEFORE YOU STOP I ALWAYS DO STOP IT SAYS VOSK IS TO REPORT ON YOU MONTHLY STOP I THOUGHT YOU SHOULD KNOW STOP SORRY STOP'
Thank him
He goes red to the eyeshade and cannot look at you for a day.
Ask what else Vosk reports
"Water figures. Every month. To an address that isn't the Board's." He shows you the address. It is a name.

I've made a system. Everything I read, I write down, in a book, in a code I made up. Six years of it. Every wire through the summit. I've never told anyone I had a book and it's the best thing I've ever done.
Show me the book
Six years of the summit's wires in a schoolboy cipher. Dray's last wire. Vosk's monthly reports. All of it.
Burn the book
"Burn it." He looks at you as if you had asked him to burn a child. He does not burn it.

The telegraph clerk keeps a book. I have known for four years. For the record, I have not taken it, because a clerk who keeps a book is a clerk who can be trusted to remember. For the record, I am asking whether you have read it.
I have
"Noted. Then you know what I send each month, and to whom. You will find I do not send it gladly."
I have not
"Noted." She knows you have. She writes 'not' anyway.

Vosk knows about the book. She's known for years. She said 'noted' and then 'keep it', and I don't know what that means, and I've been sick twice. Does she want me to keep it or is that what she says before she takes it?
She wants you to keep it
"She does? Oh. Oh, that's worse. That means she needs it. What for?"
Give it to me for safekeeping
He gives it to you. The Ledger has a second book inside it now. He sleeps for the first time in a week.

Fennick's book. Six years of wires. Among them, monthly, Vosk to a name in Ardent that is not the Board's: the gauge reading and one word. 'Holding.' Then, the month Dray vanished: 'Falling.' Then nothing, until you.
Ask Vosk what 'holding' meant
"The sluice. For the record, it is not holding now. You will find I stopped sending the word the day you asked about the gauge."
Keep it; use it later
Six years of 'holding' in the Ledger. It is the shape of the whole thing, in one word, repeated.

The Company store's stopped taking scrip at face. Nine in ten. The hands are paid in scrip, so the hands are paid nine in ten, by the Company, to the Company. I've refused scrip at the bar. The hands are furious with me.
Take scrip at face; I'll cover it
The Coffers make up the tenth. The hands drink. The Book has a column that says 'scrip loss'. Vosk reads it twice.
Take it up with Pell
Pell is 'wounded that anyone would think'. The store takes face again in a week. It slips back in a month.

The scrip is a Board matter. Nine in ten is a Board rate. I did not set it; I have never set anything, I have announced things. Do not make me announce this one at the inn. They will throw things, and I bruise.
Announce it yourself, at the gate
You announce it. Nobody throws anything at you. They save it for the store.
He announces it; you stand beside him
He announces. A tankard is thrown. It misses. He is magnificent about it, afterward.

The hands are paid in scrip and scrip is nine in ten. I will take scrip at face, for rent, from any lock hand. It is a kindness, and a way of owning eleven men's wages before they see them. I mention both.
Let her take scrip at face
The hands pay Cole in scrip at face. They are grateful. They are hers.
The Coffers take scrip at face instead
The chest fills with scrip and empties of coin. The hands are the Keeper's, not Cole's. Vosk notes both.

Somebody's broken the Company store window. Then somebody's taken flour through it. Then somebody's paid for the flour in scrip, at face, and left the scrip on the counter. That's not theft, that's a point. The store's man wants the Book. The town wants a medal.
No names in the Book
You write 'window broken; flour paid for'. Vosk reads it. 'Noted. Accurate.'
Names in the Book
Three names. The store's man is satisfied. The three are dismissed. The town is not satisfied.

Three things. The hands want paying in coin. Not scrip. Coin. The Company pays in scrip and always has. And if the Keeper says coin, the Keeper's saying the Company's money is bad, out loud, in the Book, with a signature.
Coin; sign it
You pay the hands in coin from the chest and write why. It is the most seditious entry in the Book. It is also arithmetic.
Scrip, as the Company pays
"Right. Scrip." The hands take it. They spend it at Cole's, where it is worth face, and are hers.

Keeper! The Board has restored scrip to face. It cites 'representations from the summit', which is me, and which is you. The store's man has been moved to Lock 3. I did not ask for that. I did not object.
A compliment to us both
"Both! Magnificent." He shakes your hand. The hands are paid at face. Ilse takes scrip again, sulking.
The town did it, not us
"The town. Yes. I shall not tell the Board that." He does not. He tells Ilse, which is braver.

A favor. Small one. A boat comes through tonight after the bell, no lamps, and the Book says nothing. Cargo. Nothing that bites. I'll owe you one. I don't owe many people; the old man says it's a character flaw.
One boat, no Book
It passes in the dark. A coin appears on the sill. You did not see it.
Everything in the Book
"Fair. I'll ask again when you're tired." She does.

Bigger favor. Three boats. Same arrangement, plus one thing: Crane's at his post tonight and I need him not to be. Nothing rough. He likes fish suppers. Ilse could send one over. He'd be an hour. That's all I need. An hour and a fish.
A fish for Crane
Crane eats fish. Three boats pass. Crane, later, notes the fish was excellent and the timing was not.
One boat was the favor; three is business
"Business. Fair. What's your rate?" You do not have one. She is disappointed and impressed.

One of Wren's boats, in daylight, aground on the sill with a split plank and its cargo in the shallows. Long crates, oiled cloth. Not cheese. Dace is looking at them. Crane is walking down the towpath. Wren is nowhere.
Get the crates back aboard, fast
You and Dace haul crates. Crane arrives to a floating boat and a wet Keeper. "I note the plank."
Let Crane see them
Crane sees rifles. He impounds them. Wren is jailed at his post by evening. She does not look at you.

So. You've seen what's in the crates, or Crane has, or both. I told you nothing that bites. I lied. Sort of. They don't bite till somebody loads them. I'm not saying sorry. I'm saying you know now, and asking what you'll do with knowing.

So. Crane's let me out. Under the Compact I'm 'released pending both shores', which means never. You let him see the crates. I'd have done the same. I'm not saying I forgive you. I'm saying I'd have done the same.
Nothing, this once
"This once. Right. I'll take once."
Stop moving them
"Stop. Fine. Somebody else won't. I'll tell you who when I know."

The young one has been moving things through the reeds. We know. We have always known. We have not stopped her because what she moves buys mooring posts and medicine. We ask the gate whether it has stopped her, and whether it has thought about the posts.
I've thought about the posts
"Good. Then when you stop her, and you will, stop her with the posts in mind."
Rifles are not posts
"No. They are what buys posts, when nothing else does. We do not say it is right. We say it is the price."

Last favor. Not for me. The old man wants mooring posts before winter and there's no money for posts if I stop the reeds. I've stopped the reeds. So: Company timber, your signature, my labor, nobody's Book. That's not smuggling. That's just theft. Better?
Sign for the timber
Posts by winter. Vosk sees the chit. 'Noted.' She does not say irregular. She says nothing at all.
Buy the timber from Tamm, honestly
Coin for timber. Tamm sells it. The Reach has posts and the Book has an honest line. It is more expensive and it is better.

Frost on the Spine a month early. The west flight's top pounds have skinned over in a night. Boats coming up are breaking ice with their bows. Boats going down are waiting to see if it holds. Quenn says it will get worse before it gets better.
Close the west flight now
Closed. Twenty boats stay below. Sorrel is furious. Nothing is trapped.
Keep it open while it holds
It holds three days. On the fourth, twelve boats are in the pound and the flight is solid.

Three things. Twelve boats iced in the pound with crews aboard. The Company store's got a month of food for a town, not a town and twelve crews. And the crews have started asking Ilse for credit, and Ilse has started asking me who's paying.
The Coffers feed the crews
You feed twelve crews from the chest. Vosk approves the spend without comment, which is unheard of.
Their owners pay; wire Sorrel
Sorrel wires back 'noted'. The crews eat on Ilse's credit. Ilse eats on faith.

My boats are in your ice. I've told my principals it's weather. They've told me weather is what a freight agent is paid to anticipate. I need them moving or I need a reason they can't that isn't me. Give me one. Make it good.
'The Company closed the flight'
You write it. It is true, or true enough. Vane's principals blame the Company. The Company blames you.
'Ice is ice'
"Ice is ice. Right. That's what they said about me."

The ice is lifting the top gate. It's pushing under the heel post and the gate's a hand higher than it should be; another hand and the hinges won't take it. I can break the ice every hour, all night, with fire. Or pray. Hale's praying.
Fire, every hour, all night
Fires on the ice all night. The gate settles. Quenn's eyebrows survive, barely.
Let Hale pray; sleep
You sleep. The gate rises another hand. The hinges take it. Hale says nothing about it. Quenn says 'roughly a miracle'.
Twelve crews in my inn a month, and nobody's paid, and nobody's fought, which is a record. They've taught the hands a Sorrel card game. Somebody's going to marry somebody by spring. Stand for it.
Stand for the wedding
A Sorrel bargee and a Halfway girl at the top gate at dawn. You stand. The ice cracks during the vows, which everyone takes as a sign.
Hale should stand
Hale stands. You watch. It is still a good wedding. Ilse notes who stood.

Thaw. The west flight runs brown and fast. Twelve boats go down it in a morning, thin, with a wedding aboard one and a Halfway card game aboard all. The pound is a mark lower than when the ice came. It always is. Nobody mentions it but you.
Mention it, in the Ledger
'The frost took nothing. The pound fell anyway.' A line for the next Keeper.
Wave them off
You wave. Twelve boats wave back. It is the best morning of the winter.

The water is low. When it is low the chapel keeps the Lamp Vigil: every lamp in the town on the sill, dusk to dawn, the water asked nothing, only tended. It is older than the chapel. Give us the sill.
The sill is the chapel's tonight
Lamps on the sill from dusk. The town comes. The queue comes. Nobody asks the water anything.
The bank, not the sill
"The bank hears too. Less well." She holds it on the bank. It is smaller.

The chapel woman keeps her Vigil at the sill. We keep ours at the Reach, the same night, without lamps. We ask whether the gate will stand at hers, or ours, or neither. We do not ask it to stand at both. Nobody has.
Stand at the Reach's
No lamps. Names over the water. Then a river's name. The chapel's lamps glow across the pound like another shore.
Stand at both
You walk from the sill to the Reach at midnight with a lamp, and put it out at the Reach's edge. Both sides see. Nobody has done it.

You went to the Reach's vigil. I saw the lamp cross the pound and go out. Twenty years I have kept the Vigil and never looked across. I am asking what they do, over there, in the dark, that we do not do here in the light.
They say names
"Names. We say the water's. They say the people's. I had not thought of that."
They say a river's name
"A river." She sits down in the last pew. "Then they know. They have always known."
You stood in the dark with us. Few do. One verse for it, not the song. 'Under the stone house the river remembers; it goes into the hill and comes out singing.' That is a gift. We do not give many.
Ask for another verse
"Greedy. Good. One more." 'The door has a key that is a number. The number is ten.'
Thank her for the one
"Do not thank. Remember. That is the same thing, done properly."

The morning after both vigils. The pound is a mark lower. The chapel's lamps are cold on the sill and in the Ledger, in Dray's hand, one line: 'both vigils are for the same thing. Neither side knows it.'
Tell Hale and Bram both
You tell them, separately. Each says, in their own way, 'we know'. Neither has said it to the other.
Write beneath it: 'they do now'
Two hands in the Ledger, one line each, thirty years apart.

I have asked Bram Holloway whether the Reach would keep its vigil at the sill with ours, dark on their side, lamps on ours, the same water between. He said 'we hold'. I do not know if that is yes. Find out.
It is yes
Both vigils at the sill: lamps on the town's side, dark on the Reach's, one water. The town does not speak of it for a week, and then speaks of nothing else.
Ask Bram yourself
"We hold," he says again. Then: "Yes." It is the first time he has used the word to a charter man's question.

Hull in my yard for caulking. Hullfolk. Good boat, old. She's got a floor a hand higher than it should be and a hollow under it you could lie down in. I'm not saying whose. I've seen it and now you have, if you want to have.
I've seen it
"Right. Then we've both seen it." He caulks her. He does not mention the floor again.
I haven't seen anything
"Fair. Neither have I." He caulks her. He looks at you differently.

Tamm's got my boat and Tamm's seen the floor and Tamm's told you, because Tamm's honest, which is a terrible quality in a boatwright. Everyone on the Reach has a false floor. What are you going to do about floors?
Nothing about floors
"Nothing. Right. Floors are floors." She relaxes a fraction.
Tell Crane about floors
Crane inspects every Hullfolk floor for a month. He finds cheese, fish, one goat and a great deal of resentment.

Another one. Not Hullfolk. Sorrel coal barge, in for a plank, and the same floor. Same hollow. Same hand's work, by the joints. Somebody's building false floors for two kinds of boat and I'd like to know who, because it's good work and it's not mine.
Find the builder
You ask the Reach. Nobody says. You ask Solas. He says 'Sorrel yard, Lock 2, Company contract'. A Company contract.
Good work is good work
"It is. I'd like to meet him. I'd like to hit him, then meet him."

The boatwright has mentioned false floors. In passing. I note he is not a man who mentions things in passing. A Sorrel barge with one is a Schedule Four matter and a Hullfolk boat a Schedule Five, and I do not know which he meant.
Schedule Four; the Sorrel barge
Crane inspects the Sorrel barge. Rifles. He impounds them and, for once, does not look pleased.
He meant nothing
"Nothing. Duly. I shall inspect nothing, thoroughly." He inspects the Sorrel barge anyway, later, alone.

Right. The Sorrel floors. Not mine. Same builder, different customer, and the customer's not moving cheese. I've been told to stay out of it by people who don't say please. I'm telling you because if I stay out, somebody should be in, and you've got a gate.
I'm in
"Good. Bad. Good." She tells you the boats, the nights, the builder's name.
Stay out; both of us
"Both. Sensible. The old man'd say sensible." She stays out. The boats keep coming.
I've stopped taking boats with false floors. Any kind. Lost half my trade in a week. Wren says I'm honest, like an illness. I'd like the Company's caulking contract to make it up. You've got the pen.
Give him the Company contract
Tamm caulks Company boats at Company rates. He is solvent and honest and slightly bored.
Take the floors again; nobody's honest here
"No." He does not take them. He mends fences for the town instead. He is poorer and does not complain.

I am raising the low street's rents a tenth. It has been six years and the Company has raised the tolls twice. The town will come to the moot and the moot will come to you. I am telling you first, kindly, so you may say you knew.
Ask her to wait a season
"A season. For the Keeper. Kindly." She waits. The town does not know she waited.
Her buildings, her rents
"Quite." The rents rise. The moot meets. The moot comes.
