Cole's raised the low street a tenth. The low street floods twice a year and the Company won't drain it and now it costs a tenth more to be wet. The moot's asked me to ask the Keeper to ask Cole. Everyone asks someone. I'm asking.
Ask Cole, publicly, at the moot
You ask. Cole says 'kindly, no'. The town hears you ask. It counts for something.
Drain the low street instead
Company labor, Company timber, a drain. The low street is dry and costs a tenth more. Half a victory.

You asked me to lower the rent in front of the moot. I said no in front of the moot. Now I am unkind and the Keeper is kind, though I have never put a family out and you work for the Company that floods them.
It is unfair; I'll say so
You say so, at the inn. Cole is astonished. The town is confused. It is, briefly, honest.
Kindness is what you do
"Kindly. Then I shall do less of it." She does not. She cannot. She raises rents anyway.

A family on the wharf with their furniture. Perrin's. Five children. Not put out; Cole never puts out. Moved to a smaller room at the same rent, which is the same thing done kindly. Perrin is a lock hand. He is looking at the Company's empty warehouse.
The warehouse, for the winter
Perrin's family in the Company's warehouse. Pell learns of it and, for once, does not announce anything.
Pay the difference to Cole
You pay Cole for Perrin's old room. Perrin does not know. Cole does. She records it.

The moot's voted a rent strike against Cole. I voted against; strikes end with someone's furniture on the wharf. I lost. The Company owns the ground under Cole's buildings, and might have a view, and you're the Company.
The Company has no view
You say so. Cole waits out the strike. It lasts a month. She wins, kindly, and lowers the rent a twentieth.
Ground rent to the Company until it's settled
The town pays the Company instead of Cole. Cole is livid. Vosk is 'noting'. The strike ends fast.

The rent matter is settled. A twentieth, not a tenth. The moot calls it a victory; I call it a rounding. I have not enjoyed this season. I could have made it worse, and did not, and this is the only time I shall say so.
I know
"Good. Kindly." She goes. The bell on her door does not ring for a month.
You could have made it better
"I could. Nobody asked me to. Kindly remember that they ask you."
COMPANY TO KEEPER STOP COMMISSIONER KELL ARRIVES SUMMIT TOMORROW STOP NO PREPARATION REQUIRED STOP THE COMMISSIONER PREFERS THE SUMMIT AS IT IS STOP
Prepare anyway
A night of scrubbing. Kell arrives to a summit that is not as it is, and notices.
As it is
Kell arrives to mud, geese and a queue. "Excellent. Regrettably honest."

Keeper! The Commissioner! Here! I have never met a Commissioner. I have written to eleven. He is on the wharf now with a silver cane and I have forgotten every adjective I own. Come and be magnificent for both of us. Please.
Go and greet Kell
You greet him. Pell stands behind you saying 'yes, yes' at intervals. Kell is courteous to both.
Send Pell alone; he can do it
He can, it turns out. Twenty years of adjectives arrive at once. Kell is faintly impressed.
The Board sent me to see whether the summit's Keeper is 'sound'. I have concluded the Keeper is not sound; the Keeper is something the Board has no word for. I shall have to invent one. What are you?
The gate's
"The gate's. Regrettably, the Board owns the gate. I shall write 'devoted'. It is close."
The water's
"The water's." A very long pause. "I shall write 'attentive'. I shall not write why."
The Commissioner asked me about the sluice house. Directly. I said it was disused and sound. He said 'regrettably, I know'. You will find he knows more than the Board, and the Board sent him anyway.
Ask Kell what he knows
"Everything, regrettably. The Board's view is that I should not. My view is that someone must."
Let him know alone
"Noted. That is what I have done for eleven years. You will find it does not get lighter."

I leave tomorrow. My report will say the summit is 'adequately kept'. That is the Board's phrase for 'leave it alone'. I have used it four times in twenty years. It is the highest praise I am permitted.
Thank him
"Do not. The Board does not reward gratitude. I do, privately, and it is worth nothing."
Ask what the other three were
"Two Keepers who died in post and one who resigned. Regrettably, I meant it each time."

He has gone. The Commissioner. He shook my hand on the wharf and said 'Superintendent' as if it were a name and not a title. Twenty years, Keeper. I have decided it was magnificent. I have decided not to ask you whether it was. I am asking anyway.
It was
"It was!" He goes to his office and does not come out for an hour. He is writing it down.
He said your title, not your name
"He did." A pause. "It will do. It is more than eleven letters got me."

Three boats from the west, low in the water with people, not coal. Families. Coalfield towns, they say; the strikes, the shooting. They have no tolls and no papers and nowhere they are going except east, away. Crane is at his post. He has seen them.
Pass them east, no toll
Three boats down the east flight. Aldmere's cutter at Lock 5 stops them. They come back up.
Moor them; find out first
They moor at the wharf. Sixty people. The town looks at them. They look at the town.

Sixty people on the wharf and the chapel has floor for thirty and the poor box for a week. I have not asked where they are going. We do not ask. I am asking the Keeper for the other thirty, and the other weeks.
The Company warehouse for the other thirty
Thirty in the chapel, thirty in the warehouse. Pell says nothing, which costs him.
The Reach; ask Bram
Bram takes thirty without a word. The Reach has forty boats and now sixty more people. It holds.

Sixty Sorrel nationals at the summit without papers. Under the Compact I am obliged to report them to Aldmere as 'irregular entrants'. Aldmere will refuse them. Sorrel will not have them back. I note that the Compact did not anticipate people. I note that I must report anyway.
Report them as Company labor
You hire sixty people for a week's work on the towpath. They are 'Company labor'. Crane reports it, precisely, without expression.
Report them as they are
"Duly." Aldmere refuses them. They stay at the summit, because there is nowhere else, and are nobody's.

Sixty coalfield people at the summit a fortnight and the town's split. Half's feeding them. Half's counting them. One of them's a smith and there's been no smith in Halfway since Year 60 and Cole's already offered him a lease. The moot wants to know if they're staying.
They stay if they want to
Forty stay. The smith stays. Twenty go east by night on Hullfolk boats. The town has a smith and forty new faces and a great deal to say about it.
They move on when the flight opens
They move on. The smith too. Cole is disappointed. The town is relieved and, in a year, sorry.

A woman from the coalfield boats, the one the others listen to. One question. In Sorrel they told her the canal's water was stolen from a valley. Is it true? She would like to know what kind of water she is drinking.
It is true
"Then we are drinking someone else's river. We have done worse things to stay alive. Thank you for saying it."
It is a story
"A story." She looks at the pound. "Stories are how they told us about the rifles too."
The coalfield people have gone, or stayed, or become the town. The smith has mended the chapel lamp. I have never had a smith. The Company's form asks what the summit gained. Write 'a smith'.
Write 'a smith'
The Company's form says 'a smith'. Ardent does not ask what it means. It means everything.
Write 'sixty people'
The form says 'sixty people'. Ardent does ask. You do not answer.

Crane and I have a bet. A month's wages each. He says the pound will be lower at the solstice than today, rain or no rain. I say water goes up when it rains. You hold the stakes. You're the only one who won't take a cut.
Hold the stakes
Two months' wages in the Keeper's drawer. Crane writes a receipt. Vane writes a rude one.
Ilse holds them
Ilse holds them and charges both for the privilege. Crane pays. Vane argues, then pays.

A wager. I have never taken a wager. The Compact does not forbid it, which I checked twice. I shall win, because I have six years of gauge readings and the Sorrel agent has an opinion. I have never wanted to win anything before.
Show me the readings
Six years, to the sixteenth of a mark, in a black book. The pound falls a mark a watch, always, whatever the rain.
Enjoy wanting to win
"Enjoy. Duly. I shall try. I am not built for it."

Crane's wager. He'll win. Sorry, but he will, because the pound doesn't do what rain does. I've a year of readings that say so and he's six, and we've never compared them, because he's Aldmere and I'm Company. Should we?
Compare them
Four hours at the inn with two black books. They match to the sixteenth. Crane says 'duly'. Quenn says 'sorry'. Both mean 'so it is true'.
Company and Aldmere keep their own books
"Right. Roughly. Yes." She keeps hers. He keeps his. They say the same thing to nobody.
It's rained for a week. The pound's up a finger. A finger. I've watched water my whole life; I move coal on it. A week of rain should be a mark. I'm going to lose this bet and I don't understand why.
The pound isn't fed by rain
"Then what feeds it?" You do not say. She writes something down for the first time in your presence.
Water is strange up here
"Strange. Right. Fine. I'll pay. I'll want to know why, later."

Solstice. The pound is a mark and a half lower than the day of the wager. I have won. The Sorrel agent has paid with a bow. I do not want the money. I want to know why I was right. I have wanted that for six years.
Tell him why
You tell him what you know. He listens without moving. At the end: "Then the Compact was signed over a lie. Duly. I shall need to think."
Give the winnings to the poor box
He gives them. Hale blesses the coin. Vane, hearing, gives the same again out of spite.

The wager is settled and two people who have never agreed on anything now agree on one number: a mark a watch, rain or none. In the Ledger you write the number. Beneath it, in Dray's hand, the same number, and a question mark.
Write the answer under the question mark
'The Cut.' Two words, under a question thirty years old.
Leave the question mark
The question mark stays. Someone else can answer it. You have the number.

A windlass is gone from the lock house. The good one, Dray's. The hands say Hullfolk, because the hands always say Hullfolk. And Mirren says if anyone says Hullfolk again she'll put them in the pound, and she means it.
Search the lock house first
You search. Nothing. The hands look at the Reach. Mirren looks at the hands.
Ask at the Reach
You ask. Bram says 'we do not take windlasses'. Forty faces say the same. Mirren does not speak to you for a day.

It was his. The windlass. He made the handle himself, from the old gate beam. I've worked every paddle at this lock with it. Whoever took it didn't take a windlass, they took him, again. I'm not asking you to find it. I'm telling you I'm going to.
Find it together
You and Mirren search the summit for a week. You find three other things nobody knew were missing. Not the windlass.
Let her look; keep the gate
She looks. She does not come to the paddles for two days. Dace covers. He does not complain.

The town says the Reach took the dead Keeper's windlass. We did not. We have never taken iron from the gate; we remember what happened in Year 44 to a boy who took a rope. We ask the gate to say so where the town can hear.
Say so, at the inn
You say at the inn that the Reach did not take it. The town does not believe you. It stops saying so aloud, which is a start.
I don't know who took it
"No. But you know who did not. We ask you to say that much." You do not, yet.

The windlass. Perrin's boy had it. Took it to sell for his father's rent, lost his nerve at Lock 7, hid it in Tobin's woodpile. Tobin brought it to me, because Tobin's town. It's under my bar. What do I do with a boy?
Nothing; give the windlass back
The windlass goes back on its hook. Perrin's boy is never named. Mirren knows anyway and says nothing.
The boy apologizes to Mirren
He does, shaking. Mirren listens. She says 'right' and gives him a windlass of his own to carry. He carries it for years.
So it was a town boy. The town said us for a fortnight and now nobody's going to say sorry to the Reach, because nobody ever does. I'm not asking for sorry. Will you say, at the gate, who it wasn't?
Say it at the gate
You say it to the queue, the hands, the town. 'It was not the Reach.' Bram, on his bollard, does not look up. He heard.
It's settled; let it lie
"Settled. Right. It's always settled, for you lot."

It's back on the hook. His windlass. I've worked the paddles with it all day and it's the same and it isn't. I've decided something. I'm going to teach Perrin's boy the paddles. With it. Someone should learn them from someone who learned them from him.
Teach him
She teaches him. He is hopeless, then less so. She uses her father's words without noticing.
Teach me first
"You? Right." She teaches you. You are worse than the boy. She almost laughs.

A boat at the gate after the last bell with no lamps, no name, and a man at the tiller who says 'the Captain sent us' and nothing else. Solas, you assume. The man does not confirm it. Dace is at the paddles, waiting.
Pass it, dark
It goes through in the dark. Something in its hold shifts with a sound like iron.
Lamps and a name, or wait for dawn
It waits for dawn. At dawn it is gone, back down the west flight. Solas, asked, says 'not mine'.

A boat came through at night saying I sent it. I didn't. Someone's using my name at your gate. That's a compliment or the start of something I'll be blamed for. Tell me the next time it happens, before you open.
I'll tell you first
"Good." He waits at the gate three nights. On the third, a dark boat. He goes aboard alone. It leaves, fast, west.
I'll stop night boats entirely
"That's cleaner. It won't stop them. It'll move them to the reeds." It does.

Another dark boat. This one has a lamp: one, lit, then covered as it nears the gate. The man at the tiller says nothing at all. In the bow, under a tarpaulin, something long. Solas is not at the gate. Nobody is, but you and Dace.
Lift the tarpaulin
Rifles, oiled, in fours. The man at the tiller does not move. He is waiting to see what you do.
Open the gate; ask nothing
It passes. The man at the tiller nods once. Dace does not look at you.

The night watch at my post has recorded four unlit vessels through the summit this month. I was asleep for all four. An inspector who sleeps is one the Compact did not anticipate. I am moving my bed to the post.
Don't; I'll wake you
You wake him for the next dark boat. He arrives in a nightshirt with his statute book. The boat turns back at the sight.
Move your bed; it's your post
He moves it. He sleeps badly and inspects well. The dark boats find the reeds.

I've found who's using my name. My own sergeant, paid by men above me to run boats through a gate I'm supposed to be watching. I've put him on a boat west. I've no authority to. I did it anyway. It's said once, to someone.
It's said
"Good." He sits on Bram's bollard that night. Bram lets him have it for an hour.
Report the sergeant to Sorrel yourself
You write to Sorrel. Sorrel does nothing. The sergeant is back in a month, at Lock 4, with a promotion.

No dark boats this month. Solas at the gate most nights, unasked, his good arm on the beam. Crane's bed at his post. Dace's lamp on the sill. Whatever came through at night has found another way. You write 'the gate is lit'.
Keep it lit
A lamp on the sill every night, at the Coffers' cost. It is the cheapest thing you have bought.
Let the dark come back; watch it
You let the lamp go out. The boats come back. This time you know what to look for.

The budget. There's one and it's small and Pell wants it for bunting and I want it for the lower gate's heel post, which is rotten, which I've said in three reports nobody's read. I know which one the Board can see from Ardent.
Heel post
"Thank you. Sorry. Thank you." Pell is wounded for a week. The gate does not fall down.
Bunting
"Bunting. Right. I'll patch the post. Roughly." She patches it. It weeps.

Quenn has told you about heel posts. I am sure heel posts are important. I am also sure the Board has never once written to me about a heel post and has written four times about bunting. I do not make the Board. I read its letters.
Ask the Board for a heel post budget
You write to Ardent about a heel post. Ardent replies, astonished, with money. Pell frames the reply.
Bunting next year; posts this
"Next year. Yes. There is always next year, until there is not."

I've found money. Not the budget; older. A maintenance fund from Year 31, never drawn, in Vosk's ledger, for 'north bank works'. Forty marks. Sitting there. Vosk says it's 'reserved'. For what? Nothing's been done on the north bank since Year 31. Officially.
Ask Vosk to release it
"Noted. No." A pause. "For the record, it is for the day the north bank needs it. You will find that day is coming."
Leave it reserved
"Reserved. Right." Quenn looks at the north bank a long time.

Quenn wants a heel post and I've got the oak, seasoned, the best I've had. I'll cut it for the Company's price. Or the town's price, which is half, if the town gets to say it gave the Keeper a gate. It'll hold either way.
The town's price; the town's gate
The town gives the Keeper a heel post. There is a small ceremony. Pell attends, magnificently uncertain.
The Company's price; the Company's gate
Company oak, Company gate. It holds. Nobody says anything about it.

Keeper! The heel post! I stood on it. It did not move. I have stood under bunting my whole career and I now see that bunting does not hold a gate. I shall write to the Board about heel posts. They will not understand.
Write it
Nine pages on heel posts. Ardent files it under 'bunting'. Quenn keeps a copy.
Stand on it again
He stands on it again. Then Quenn does. Then Dace. It becomes a thing the summit does.

The gate's sound. Both gates. First time since I came. I've written it in my report and I've written it without 'sorry' and I've written it without 'roughly'. I'd like you to read it. It's one line. It took six years.
Read it
'The summit gates are sound. T. Quenn, Engineer.' You read it twice. She watches you read it.
Send it to Ardent
Ardent receives a one-line report and does not know what to do with it. It is the first honest line from the summit in years.

They have taken my fiddle. The charter men. For mooring fees. It has one string and no value and it is the only thing I own that came from the valley. I do not ask. Wren asks. I am telling the gate what was taken and from whom.
Return the fiddle; waive the fee
The fiddle goes back to the Reach. The fee is written off. Vosk, later: 'a fiddle. Noted.'
The fee stands; the fiddle waits
The fiddle sits in the toll office. She does not sing for a month. The Reach is very quiet.

The fiddle. Grandmother's. You've got it or you've given it back; either way you know what it is now. It's the only thing on the Reach older than the canal. Whatever it cost in fees, I'll pay. Don't make a thing of it.
No fee; it's hers
"No fee. Right." She does not thank you. She brings you a fish every week for a year.
Take her fee; return it
She pays. The fiddle goes back. She has paid a Company fee and it sits badly with her.

A fiddle was impounded for mooring fees and released without payment from the debtor. For the record, the Book does not have a column for fiddles. I have made one. You will find I would like to know what the fiddle plays.
A song about a river
"Noted." A long pause. "I have heard it. From the Company house, at night. I did not know it had words."
One string; not much
"Noted." She writes it. She does not believe it. She has heard it too.

You gave it back. Or you let it be bought back, which is the same to a fiddle. I will play you something for it. Not the song. A piece of the song. The part about the door. You will not understand it. Nobody does, the first time.
Listen
One string. A door in a hill. A key that is a number. Ten. You understand more than she thinks.
Play it for Mirren too
Mirren listens with her hands flat on the gunwale. At 'ten' she looks up.

The old singer says you heard the door verse. She does not play it for charter men. She played it for a gate. We have talked about what a gate is owed for that. We have decided: nothing. We tell you, so you know it was decided.
Nothing is right
"Yes. We thought you would say so. It is why we decided it."
Ask for the rest of the song
"The rest is not owed. The rest is given, when it is given. Ask again when the water is lower."

I am old and the fiddle is older and one day soon one of us will stop. When I stop, the fiddle goes to Wren, and the song goes to whoever has heard it. Hear the rest, before I stop. Old women do not request.
Hear the rest, now
All of it. Six verses on one string at dusk. The river, the hill, the door, the number, the debt, the dawn.
When the water is lower
"Lower. It will be. I may not." She is, as it happens. She sings it then, at the sill, for the town.

A man on the north bank with a theodolite and a notebook. Not Company; his coat is wrong. Not Sorrel; his accent is wrong. He is surveying the bank below the sluice house with great care and no permit. He says he is 'interested in old water'.
Ask what he's found
"A channel. Cut stone. Straight as a rule. Going into the hill. Do you know what it is?" You do not say.
Send him off Company ground
He goes. He leaves his notebook on the bank, by accident or otherwise.

There is a man surveying the north bank. I have asked him to leave and he has declined, citing a right of way I did not know existed. I am asking the Keeper to remove him. For the record, I do not often ask.
Remove him
You remove him. He goes with his notebook. Vosk watches from the Company house and does not say noted.
A right of way stands
"Noted." He surveys for a week. She watches every hour of it.

The surveyor's notebook. Bearings along the north bank. A sketch of a stone channel. A word, underlined: 'Quell?' And a name in Ardent that is not the Board's. The same name Vosk writes to monthly, if you have seen Fennick's book.
Copy the bearings into the Ledger
Bearings, sketch, word, name. The Ledger has a map now, of sorts.
Give the notebook to Vosk
"Noted." She reads the name and goes very still. "He works for the same man I do. Nobody told me."
The surveyor's bearings run straight to where the missing page says the sluice house is. Someone in Ardent knows exactly where to look and sent a man to look at it. Sorry. Why now?
Because the water is falling
"Because it's falling faster. Yes. They've noticed. They're deciding what to do. Sorry. That's worse."
Because someone told them
"Vosk. Or Fennick. Or you." She does not mean it. She does not take it back.

The surveyor was sent by the man I report to. Not the Board. The man. He did not tell me. That means he no longer trusts me to watch the summit alone. I have watched it alone for eleven years. I am tired.
Watch it with her
"Noted." She sits a long time. "You will find I have never been offered that."
Ask who the man is
"A name in Ardent. Old. He was at the Dry Year. He is the last who was." She does not give the name. She does not need to.

The surveyor has gone. His bearings are in the Ledger or in Vosk's drawer or in Ardent. The north bank is as it was: a stone house with iron straps, a clear stream, a slump in the bank. Someone in Ardent has a map now. So do you.
Walk the bearings yourself
You walk them. They end at the sluice house door. They always did.
Let Ardent have its map
Ardent has a map. You have a gate. For now, the gate is the thing that opens.

Dray's house. His chair, his desk, his oilskin on the hook, his daughter at the paddles. You sleep in his bed and eat at his table and write in his Ledger. The study door is locked. It is the only door in the house that is.
Ask Mirren for the key
She has it. She has had it the whole time. She does not give it to you. Not yet.
Leave it locked
It stays locked. You learn the house around it, like a tongue around a missing tooth.
You moved the lamp. In the study. I know because I look through the window every night and the lamp's on the desk and it was on the shelf. He kept it on the shelf. Did you go in?
Through the open window
"Right." She does not believe you. She does not push. She puts the lamp back through the window.
I went in
"You went in." She is white. "What did you see?" You saw a desk, a drawer, and a ledger that is not the Ledger.

Night. The house makes his sounds: a stair that speaks, a shutter that argues with the wind. On the study desk: a ledger in cipher, tide tables for a canal, a pencil worn to nothing. He was working on something when he stopped.
Sit at his desk till dawn
You sit. You do not open anything. At dawn Mirren finds you there and, for once, does not look angry.
Go to bed; it is his desk
You go to bed. The stair speaks. The shutter argues. The desk waits.

You're in his house. I was in it once, the week before. He'd moved the chair to the window. Said he wanted to see the north bank. I said what's on the north bank. He said 'the tenth mark, Tobin'. Do you know what he meant?
I'm beginning to
"Beginning. Aye. He was further than beginning. Look where it got him."
Move the chair back
You move the chair back from the window. It does not help. You know what he was looking at now.

Here. The study key. I've had it since he went. I've been in every night and touched nothing. You sit in his chair and don't pretend it's yours, and Tobin says you can read what's on the desk. Don't move the lamp.
Take the key
A brass study key. The first of two brass keys. You do not move the lamp.
Go in together, first time
You go in together. She touches the desk. You touch nothing. The ledger is in cipher. She says 'his game'. You say 'the gauge'. Something begins.

The study is open. The house is one house now. Mirren comes in sometimes and sits in his chair, which she never did, and says nothing, which she always did. The desk has two ledgers on it. They are starting to say the same things.
Keep both ledgers on the desk
Two ledgers, two hands, one desk. Whoever comes next will have both.
Give Mirren the chair, for good
You take the desk chair to the window. She keeps his. It is, finally, her house too.

Front page, both shores, tomorrow. 'THE KEEPER'S SECRET.' The study, or the wires, or the reeds; I've got enough for one. I'm telling you tonight because you've got till dawn to give me a better story. There isn't one. But you've got till dawn.
Give him the water figures instead
He reads them. He stops smiling. 'THE KEEPER'S SECRET' becomes 'THE SUMMIT'S WATER'. It is a bigger story and a worse one for Ardent.
Print what you have
He prints it. It is about the study. The town reads that the Keeper sits in a dead man's room at night. It is not untrue.

It was me. Hesse's story. He asked what you did at night and I said the study and it's on the front page. I'll resign. I've written it. I've never resigned from anything. Do I send it to Ardent or to you?
Tear it up
You tear it up. He watches the pieces fall and does not speak for a long time. Then: 'I'll stop selling. All of it. Everyone.'
Send it to Ardent
Ardent accepts. A new clerk comes. He reads nothing. He knows nothing. Nobody at the summit knows anything now.

The Board reads the Courier. It does not read my reports; it reads the Courier. And the Courier says the summit Keeper has a secret. I care that the Board has asked me what it is, and I have said 'bunting'.
Tell him the secret
You tell Pell about the study, the cipher, the water. He listens with his mouth open. 'Magnificent. Terrible. Tell nobody I know.'
Bunting will do
"Bunting. Yes. I am good at bunting." The Board accepts bunting. It always has.

The follow-up. Readers want one. I could write 'THE KEEPER ANSWERS' if you'd answer, or 'THE KEEPER SILENT' if you won't, or 'THE SUPERINTENDENT SAYS BUNTING', which is my favorite. What'll it be? I'm not a cruel man. I'm a man with a press.
Answer
You answer. Plainly. About the water. It is the first time the summit's figures have been in print. Ardent's wires that night are very long.
Silent
'THE KEEPER SILENT.' It reads as dignity in Sorrel and guilt in Aldmere.

The town's read the Courier. It says the Keeper has a secret, and the town's decided what: you're Dray's bastard, or Vosk's lover, or a Sorrel spy, or all three. It's the best week the inn's had in years. Don't ruin it with the truth.
Don't ruin it
You let the town have its theories. They are better than the truth and worse. The inn does very well.
Tell the town the truth, at the inn
You tell the inn about the water. The inn is quiet. Then somebody says 'so not Vosk's lover, then' and the inn roars.

Last piece. 'WHAT THE SUMMIT KEEPS'. It's about the gauge. A drawing of it with the tenth mark, the painted-over one, drawn in. My readers won't know what it means. Someone in Ardent will. Shall I run it?
Run it
A drawing of a gauge with ten marks on the front page of both shores. Ardent wires Vosk nine times. Vosk answers none.
Hold it; give me a month
"A month. Held. I've never held anything a month. I'll try." He does. Barely.

The boundary stone. Town's cleared the path to it. That's a thing the town does when it's thinking about a Keeper. Doesn't mean it'll walk you there. Means it's remembering the way. I'm telling you as reeve. As Ilse, I'd like you to notice.
Walk to the stone yourself, in daylight
You walk to the stone alone and stand there and walk back. The town sees. It is not what they expected.
Have the path let grow
You order it left. It grows back in a season. The town clears it again in a night.

Three things. The town's asked the hands whether they'd walk with them, if it came to the stone. Half said yes. The other half said they'd have to ask me. And I've been asked, and I've said I'd ask you what you'd want me to say.
Say what you believe
"Right." He says he'd walk with the Keeper, not the town. Half the hands look at their boots. Half nod.
Say you'd walk with the town
"You'd want that?" He says it. The hands are relieved. You are, oddly, safer.

A child at the Keeper's door with a lamp. Lit. In daylight. The town is 'practising' and she has been sent to see if the Keeper would like to hold one, 'so you know how heavy'. Behind her, adults are pretending not to watch.
Hold the lamp
It is heavy. You hold it a long time. The child takes it back and says 'now you know'. The adults stop pretending.
Send her home
She goes. The lamp goes with her. The adults stop watching and start talking.

The moot's met on you. Not to walk you out; to decide whether to decide. It decided not to decide, this month. Next month it might. What will you have done by then that the town can see? One thing. It doesn't have to be big.
The low street drain
Company timber, town labor, a drain the low street has wanted for forty years. It is seen.
Nothing; the town can walk me or not
"Right. Brave. Stupid. Same thing here." The moot meets again.

The Ledger's boundary stone page. Year 44: 'walked at dusk; the lamps were kind'. Year 61: 'walked at dawn; nobody spoke'. Dray's: 'the path is clear again. I have done nothing they can see. I am going to do something they cannot.'
Do something they can see
You choose visible. The gate at the bell, the drain, the moot. The path grows over by summer.
Do something they cannot
You choose Dray's way. The north bank, at night. The path stays clear. So does the way to the sluice house.

The path to the stone's grown over. Nobody's cleared it. That's the town deciding, the way it decides: by not doing a thing. You'll not be walked out this season. As reeve, I'm telling you. As Ilse, I'm glad, and I'll deny it.
Thank her, as Ilse
"Don't. Drink your drink." You drink. She does not charge for it.
Clear the path yourself; keep it honest
You clear the path to the stone and keep it clear. The town does not know what to make of a Keeper who does that. It respects it.
Keeper! Welcome to the summit of the Meridian, the highest gate on the finest water road in the Vell. Here is the toll book. Guard it like a child.
Read it tonight
Eighty years of figures, in eleven hands.
Ask about the last Keeper
Pell's smile stays where it is. His eyes do not.
A grain barge from Aldmere waits below the top gate. Papers in order, the bargee says, if you would care to look.
Check the papers
In order. The bargee spits, politely, over the side.
Open the gate
The paddles run, the chamber fills, the barge rises.
Mirren Dray. Lock hand. I turn the paddles, you decide when. That oilskin on the hook is not for anyone.
Leave it where it hangs
She nods once, which from her is a speech.
Ask whose it was
"His." She goes to the paddles.
The sill gauge reads one mark lower than the last entry in the book. The reservoir report, pinned beside it, says nothing has changed.
Note it in the Ledger
A small line in a new hand.
A dry week, nothing more
The gauge does not argue.
Ilse Harrow. I keep the Wheel and Windlass and, when nobody else will, the town. A room is two marks a week. A welcome costs more.
Take the room
The bed is hard and the ale is good.
The Keeper's House will do
"It will. It did for him."
COMPANY TO KEEPER HALFWAY STOP REPORT TRAFFIC FIGURES EACH WATCH STOP DELAYS TO BE EXPLAINED STOP
Report exactly
Fennick taps it out with his tongue between his teeth.
Report weekly
Nobody wires back. Nobody wires back for three days.
Sorry. Tamsin Quenn, engineer. The east lower paddle is roughly forty years past its work. I need eleven marks for a new spindle. I know it's your first day.
Approve the spindle
She is gone before you finish the signature.
Make it last a month
"It might. Roughly."
A narrow boat of stitched sailcloth waits without a toll in hand. The woman at the tiller says the Hullfolk hold passage here, and always have.
Passage without fee
She does not thank you. She looks at you, which may be more.
The toll is the toll
She pays in old coin and remembers your face.
Odile Vosk, Summit Auditor. I have read your first entries. The hand is legible. You will find I read everything.
Then read this too
You hand her the page. She reads it. "Noted."
Ask what she is looking for
"Irregularities. For the record, there are none yet."
Matthias Crane, Aldmere Customs, under the Halfway Compact of Year 58. I note that Schedule Four requires my seal on any arms. I will be here every watch.
Welcome his inspections
"Duly noted." He almost smiles, and files it.
Inspections slow the gate
"The Compact does not mention speed."
Nessa Vane, Sorrel Freight. Your predecessor cost my principals nine days last quarter. Here is the rate card. Here is the bill for the nine days.
The bill is not mine
"By the next watch it will be. We can fix that."
Promise faster passage
She writes it down before you have finished.
Fennick Orr, the wire. In strictest confidence, Keeper, you'll never guess what the last one wired the night before he went. I shouldn't. Shall I?
Tell me
"Three words. 'Found the key.' Then nothing."
Keep the wire's secrets
He looks at you as if you had refused a gift, then brightens.
A boat of grey-robed pilgrims asks to wait in the chamber while the chaplain blesses their hull. Two coal barges wait behind them.
Let the blessing finish
It takes a while. The coal barges say so.
Bless them on the towpath
The chaplain does not argue. She never does.
We are Bram Holloway. We hold the Reed Reach. Every Keeper is one of two things, and the water finds out which. Are you a gate, or a wall?
A gate
"Then we shall see it open."
The Company's Keeper
"So was the last one. So was the first."
Wren. I run things. Small favor: a crate goes down the east flight tonight and nobody writes it in the Book. Cargo. Nothing that bites.
Not in my Book
"Fair. I'll ask again when you're tired."
One crate
You didn't see it. A coin appears on the sill anyway.
Dray's chair. Dray's desk. Dray's study door, locked, with no key on the ring you were given.
Try the lock
It holds. Somebody meant it to.
Leave it for now
The chair, at least, is comfortable.
Sister Hale. We tend the Still Water chapel and bless what passes. The summit springs are a gift, Keeper. We do not ask the water where it comes from.
Accept the blessing
Her lamp swings over the gates. The hands take off their caps.
Ask where it comes from
"From the hill, as all still water does."
Solas. Sorrel Escort Company. My convoys come through twice a month, armed and lawful. Tell me now how you want them handled. I would rather not learn it at the gate.
Inspected like any boat
"Understood. It won't come to trouble."
Escorts pass on sight
"My people will remember that."
Three things, Keeper. The upper gate weeps. The hands are two short. And the last Keeper owed us a round he never stood.
Stand the round
Eleven tankards. Ilse counts them.
Fix the gate first
"Right. That's one of three."
Rain all night. The pound is up a mark by morning and Ilse's cellar has an inch in it. She has sent a boy to say so.
Run the east paddles
Water goes down the flight. Boats wait while it does.
An inch is an inch
The boy goes back with nothing in his hands.
A target, Keeper! Every magnificent enterprise needs one. Forty vessels a week through the top gate. The Meridian spirit demands no less.
Forty it is
He shakes your hand as if you had already done it.
Thirty, and safely
"Thirty. Well. A beginning."
A Sorrel coal barge and an Aldmere grain boat arrive at the same bell. Both bargees are already shouting. The chamber holds one.
Grain first
Aldmere law says food before fuel. So does the grain boat.
Coal first
Sorrel's man tips his cap. Aldmere's writes something down.
The Company store sells beer at Company prices in Company scrip. Mine costs coin and tastes of something. Where does the Keeper drink?
The Wheel and Windlass
"Then you'll hear things. Some of them true."
The Company store
"Suit yourself. The scrip's no good here."
ALDMERE GUILDS TO KEEPER STOP GRAIN CONVOY NINE VESSELS ARRIVES TOMORROW STOP ANY DELAY WILL BE REPORTED UNDER THE COMPACT STOP
Clear the pound for them
Other boats are asked, then told, to wait.
They queue like anyone
Crane reads the wire twice and says nothing, loudly.
Did you open the study? You have the house. Nobody would say anything if you did.
It is locked, and I left it
"Good." Then, quieter: "For now."
I mean to
She looks at the door, then at you, then at the paddles.
Aurelie Stroud, physician. Dray kept every watch himself for a year. I have seen what that does. Sleep when the bell allows, or I will be seeing you.
Let Dace take a watch
You sleep. The gate does not fall down.
The gate needs a Keeper
"So did he."
Watch six. Toll receipts exceed the book by two marks. Either a bargee overpaid, or something irregular. Which would you like it to be?
An overpayment; return it
"Noted. And the bargee's name?" You do not have it.
Into the repair fund
"For the record, that is not a fund."
A dry week. The Cald Tarn aqueduct is a trickle you could step over. The pound, fed by it, is down only a mark. Somebody should find that strange.
Ask Quenn about it
"Sorry. Yes. It doesn't close. It never quite closes."
Be glad of it
The boats float. That is the Keeper's business.
A late boat, lamps out, asks passage after the last bell. The bargee is tired, he says. Dace, at the paddles, is looking at you.
Light your lamps and wait
He waits. He is not pleased. Dace is.
Pass him through
The chamber fills in the dark. Something shifts in his hold.
Eight watches. The book is in your hand now, and the town knows your face. You could write the first honest line about what kind of Keeper this will be.
The Company's, first
The line dries. It can be crossed out later, in theory.
The gate's, first
The Company does not read the Ledger. Yet.
We sit here most days. On this bollard. Charter men walk past and do not see us. You stopped. That is the first thing. What is the second?
Sit with him
An hour on the next bollard. He says eleven words. They are good ones.
Ask what he wants
"We want nothing from a gate. We watch what it does."
The young one, Wren, says you are a gate. We have heard young ones say that of Keepers before. We would like to know what the gate thinks it is, before the water tells us.
A gate that can close
"Honest. We have not heard honest from a Keeper. We remember it."
A gate
"The young one said so. We shall see. We are good at seeing."
A charter man struck one of ours at the Reach today. Open hand. Our young men wanted to answer it. We told them the gate would. We do not usually say that. We are saying it once.
Dismiss the man
He goes down the flight. Pell protests. The Reach is very quiet, in a good way.
Fine him; keep him
"A fine. So. The gate answers with coin. We remember that too."
Old Petronel wants to sing for you. Not at the Reach. Here, at the gate, where the water is deepest. We have never let it be sung off the Reach. We ask what the gate would do with it.
Hear it at the gate
She sings at the sill at dusk. The town stops. A river, a hill, a door. The tenth mark.
The song belongs to the Reach
"So we have always said. We wondered if a gate would say otherwise."
We lost a child in the pound in the Dry Year. Ours. Mine. The charter men wrote 'vagrant infant' in the Book. We have never asked a Keeper to change a word in the Book. We are asking.
Change it; write the name
You write a name in a book forty years closed. He does not thank you. He stands up.
The Book cannot be changed
"No. Nothing here can. We knew that. We asked anyway."

You have been to the north bank at night. We saw the lamp. We do not go there. Our grandmothers said the hill would take anyone who went in after the river. We ask whether the gate believes in grandmothers.
I believe in yours
"Then do not go in alone. That is all they meant."
I believe in lamps
"So did the one before you."

The young ones have stopped listening to us. They listen to Wren. Wren listens to coin. One day soon they will do something to the charter men that cannot be undone. We are old. We are asking the gate to be young for us.
Speak to the young ones
You go to the Reach at dusk and speak. They listen, because Bram is beside you.
Speak to Wren
Wren listens. Wren says "fair". The young ones do not do the thing, this month.
You spoke for the charter men at the moot. Against the Reach. We heard. We do not hold it against a gate to be a wall sometimes. We hold it against a gate to pretend it was not.
I was a wall
"Yes. Now we know where we stand. That is worth something."
I did what the gate required
"The gate. Yes. Keepers say that. Then they say 'the Company'. Then they say nothing."

We have a boat. Old. Sailcloth. It was ours before the canal, and our grandmother's before that, from a river. We are giving it to no one. We would like the gate to have seen it, once, before we are gone.
See the boat
It is very old. On the bow, worn to a shadow: the name of a river. Quell.
Another day
"We have fewer of those than you. We understand."
We have decided to tell you where the water comes out of the hill. Not why; we do not know why. Where. We have never told a charter man. We have never told a Keeper. We are telling a gate.
Take the bearing
By lamps and stones, in the old way. Below the sluice house, where the clear water runs.
Tell Mirren too
He tells you both. Mirren does not speak on the way back.
I take my meals at the inn at the sixth bell precisely. I note that you have twice sat at the adjoining table. I note that this is not forbidden. I note that I should not mind if it continued.
Sit with him, not adjoining
He talks about the Compact for an hour. It is, unexpectedly, fascinating.
The adjoining table is fine
"Duly. It is, in fact, fine."

The Compact's third appendix contains a provision that the Keeper may request an inspector's assistance 'in any matter touching the water'. Any matter. It has never been invoked. I should very much like it to be.
Invoke it: help me read the gauge
He reads the gauge every watch for a month, to the sixteenth of a mark. His figures match Quenn's.
Perhaps later
"Duly. It has waited fifty-eight years. It can wait."

The Sorrel agent called me 'Matthias' today. In public. I have been Inspector Crane at this summit for six years. I do not know what to do with 'Matthias'. I am asking you, as a neutral party, whether I should object.
Don't object
"Very well. I shall not. I note that I did not entirely dislike it."
Object formally
He objects in writing. Vane frames the letter. They are both, obscurely, pleased.
You passed a vessel without my seal. I note that you had reasons. I note that reasons are how the Compact dies: one at a time, each a good one. I am not angry. I am concerned. It is worse.
You are right; it won't recur
"Duly. I shall hold you to it. I hold things well."
The Compact is not the gate
"No. The Compact is what keeps the gate from being a wall for one shore. I note you did not consider that."

I have been writing a report for six years. On how Aldmere might operate the canal. I have never shown it to anyone. I note that it has a chapter on the water supply, and that the chapter does not close.
Show me the chapter
Forty pages of gauge readings. The same shape as Quenn's. He knows. He has always known.
Show it to Quenn
They compare figures for four hours. They are, in their way, happy.

I have been offered a post in Aldmere. Senior. Desk. No canal. I note that I should accept. I note that I have drafted the acceptance four times. I note that I am asking a Company Keeper for advice, which is irregular.
Stay; the summit needs a witness
"A witness. Yes. That is a role. I accept it." He tears up the fourth draft.
Take the desk
"Duly." He does not go. He does not say why. He is angrier at the Sorrel agent than usual for a month.

The Sorrel agent and I have dined together. Once. It was her proposal. I note that we did not argue for the first hour. I note that this alarmed us both. I am telling you because I have nobody else to tell.
Dine with them both
The three of you. Crane and Vane argue for two hours. It is the best evening at the summit.
Be alarmed with him
"Thank you. It is good to be alarmed in company."

You have sided with Sorrel on four matters this quarter. I have counted. I am not partisan; I am a counter. I note that a Keeper who counts with one shore is not a Keeper under the Compact. I note that I would regret that.
I'll count more evenly
"Duly. I shall count with you."
I count what the gate needs
"Then the gate is Sorrel's. I note that. I note it with sorrow, which is unprofessional."

An extraordinary discovery. Schedule Nine of the Compact, unused since ratification, provides for a 'joint declaration of material fact' by both shores' inspectors, binding on the Company. I do not know what it was for. I begin to.
Keep it ready
"I have already drafted the form. I drafted it six years ago. I did not know why."
Tell Vane about it
Vane reads Schedule Nine and goes very quiet. "That's a weapon." "It is a form." "Same thing."

I have never been liked. I note this without complaint. I note that the lock hands have begun to nod to me, and the Dray girl said good morning. I do not know what I have done. I should like to keep doing it.
You've been fair
"Fair. Yes. I had thought that was invisible."
You've been here long enough
"Duration. A defensible reading. I prefer yours to mine."

You'll never guess what I found in the wire code book. There's a code for 'Keeper deceased'. There's a code for 'Keeper dismissed'. There's no code for 'Keeper resigned'. I shouldn't find that interesting. I do.
So how did they wire Dray's resignation?
"In clear. Vosk wrote it out in words. I'd never seen her do that."
Codes are codes
"Right. Yes. Codes. I'll stop reading the book." He does not.
I sold a copy of your traffic wire to Hesse. He gives me a mark a wire and I've got my mother in Aldmere. You'll never guess: he didn't print it. Too boring. I'm sorry it was boring.
Stop selling my wires
"Yes. Yes. Right. Yours. I'll stop yours." He means it. About yours.
Sell him better ones; I'll write them
You dictate a wire about geese. Hesse prints it. Fennick earns two marks.
Mirren came to the office to send a wire to Aldmere and I. I wrote it wrong. Twice. She had to say it three times. I'm not usually. I'm very good at the key. I shouldn't be telling you this.
Tell her you're sorry
He does, in the street, at length. She is baffled, and then, briefly, kind.
Say nothing to anyone
"Right. Nothing. I'm good at nothing. I'm not, obviously. But I'll try."

Vosk came to the office. She stood behind me for an hour. She didn't say anything. She didn't do anything. She just stood there. I sent nine wires perfectly and then I was sick in the yard. Is that normal?
It is not normal; I'll speak to her
You speak to Vosk. "Noted. I was checking his hand." She does not do it again.
It is Vosk being Vosk
"Right. Right. She does it to you too? Oh. Oh, good."
In strictest confidence. The Ardent number code Vosk gets isn't a code. It's the sill gauge: marks and dates. Somebody in Ardent is tracking the pound. Every day. For years.
Show me the numbers
Columns of them. The pound, falling, in Ardent's own hand, since before you were born.
Stop learning codes
"I can't. It's like a song. Once you've heard it."
You've never asked me to send a wire you didn't want read. Everyone else has. Dray did, at the end. If you ever do, would you tell me it's that kind? I'd like to be trusted with one.
When the time comes, you'll be the one
He goes red to the eyeshade and cannot speak.
I don't send that kind
"No. No, you don't. That's what I like about you. It's a bit dull."

I told Hesse something about you I shouldn't have. It wasn't for money. He asked, and I like being asked, and it came out. It was about the study. I'm sorry. He'll print it. He prints everything eventually.
Go to Hesse first
You tell Hesse yourself. It is a better story from you. He runs that one.
You've cost me something
"I know. I know. I do this. I'll stop." He does, for a month, which is a record.
My mother's ill in Aldmere. I'd need a week. Nobody else can work the key, so the summit would be off the wire, and the Company would notice. I'm asking anyway.
Go; I'll work the key
You work the key, badly. Ardent receives several wires about geese that were not about geese.
Send your mother money instead
You send it. He stays. He does not forgive himself for staying.
A wire for you, from nobody. No origin code. 'THE TENTH MARK STOP TELL M STOP'. It came at the third bell. Nobody sends from nowhere. I didn't touch it. I'm touching it now.
Take it to Mirren
She reads it and sits down on the wharf. "His words. His exact words."
Burn it
"Right." He burns it in the stove. He keeps the ash. He does not know why.
You'll never guess. I've been offered the Ardent office. The big key. I don't want to go. Things happen here, and I know this wire like my own hand. But it's Ardent.
Go; it's Ardent
He goes. A stranger runs the wire. Ardent knows everything now, and nothing interesting.
Stay; things happen here
"They do. They do!" He stays. He is the happiest man at the summit for a week.
You have not come to the chapel. Most Keepers come once, for form. You have not come for form. I find I respect that more than the coming. Will you come for tea, instead? Tea is not a rite.
Tea
The chapel parlor. She talks about the town's poor. She does not mention the water once, which is how you know she is thinking of it.
The gate does not take tea
"Then I shall bring it to the gate." She does.
I was a lock hand's daughter at Lock 4 before I took the grey. I know what a paddle sounds like when it is failing. Yours is not failing. I tell you so you have one less thing to tend.
Thank her
"Do not. Tending is what we do."
Ask what else she hears
"Water where there should be stone. Under the chapel. I have heard it since I came. I have not asked it anything."

Vosk comes to the chapel on the first of each month and sits in the last pew and does not pray. She has done it eleven years. We have never spoken of why. I am telling you because you have started to sit in the last pew too.
Ask why Vosk comes
"To be near something she cannot file. I think. I do not ask."
I'll sit somewhere else
"Sit where you like. The water does not mind pews."

You asked the novice about the spring and she came to me weeping because she could not answer. I have asked you nothing in all this time. I ask now: leave the children out of it. Ask me. I will not answer, but ask me.
I'll ask you
"Good." You ask. She does not answer. It is, somehow, an answer.
The children should know too
"Should. That word again. It is not a chapel word."

The Lamp Vigil is not for the water. I have never told anyone that. It is for the people who watch the water, so that for one night they are not alone with it. You watch it more than anyone. Come to the Vigil.
Come
You stand with lamps on the sill among people who are not alone. It does not raise the pound. It helps.
I am used to being alone with it
"So was Marrow." She does not explain.

I have read the letters in the undercroft. All of them. I read them my first year, and I decided, and I have kept the decision for twenty. I am not asking you to keep it. I am asking you to know it was a decision.
What did you decide?
"That a gift is what it does, not where it came from. That eighty years of dry cellars is a gift."
A decision can be undecided
"It can. I have not found the strength. Perhaps you have. I would not envy you it."

Bram Holloway came to the chapel today. Sat in the last pew, where Vosk sits. Did not pray. When he left he touched the founding stone, once, and said a word I did not know. I think it was a river's name. I did not ask.
It was
"Then two people have sat in that pew for the same reason, and never met there. We tend such things badly."
Ask him next time
"I do not ask. It is the one thing I am sure of." She sounds less sure than usual.

You forced the undercroft door. I know it was you. I do not forgive you and I do not blame you; both are asking the water. I am telling you that whatever you read there, read the last letter too. Nobody reads the last one.
Read the last letter
Marrow, the night before the collapse: 'If the sluice fails, tell them nothing. Let them have the water. Let them have eighty years.'
I've read enough
"Nobody has. That is the trouble with letters."
You have been kind to the town and hard on the chapel. I understand it. The chapel has been kind to the town and hard on the truth. We are alike, you and I, and I do not think either of us likes it.
We are alike
"Yes. Then tend it with me. It is easier tended by two."
I am not hard on the truth
"Not yet. You have not had to choose between it and a dry town. I have. Every morning."

If it comes to a choice about the water, and it will, you will not ask me, because you know I will not answer. So I will say it now, once, unasked. Whatever you choose, let the town keep its lamp. That is all the chapel is.
The town keeps its lamp
"Then I am with you. Whichever door."
The town deserves the truth more
"Perhaps. Give it both, then. Nobody has tried both."
You drink here. That's noticed. You drink one and go. That's noticed more. The last one who drank one and went was Dray. Costs nothing to sit a while. Costs a bit to not.
Sit a while
An hour. You learn who owes whom. It is most of the town.
The gate does not sit
"No. Neither did he."
The Company sent a man to price my cellar again. I sent him back with a price for his hat. You're smiling. Don't. It's your Company. What does it want with my cellar?
I'll find out
You do. It wants to know how the well fills. So do you.
It wants everything
"True. Doesn't help. Have another."
The moot wants to give you a chain. Not a big one. A reeve's guest chain. Means you can speak at moot without being asked. Means the Company will hate it. I said I'd ask. I'm asking.
Take the chain
You wear it once, to the moot. Pell sees it. It is worth it.
A Keeper wears no chain
"Right. I'll tell them. Some'll respect it. I don't."
You let Vosk into my cellar. Company auditor, in my cellar, with a measuring rod. I don't care what she found. I care that you let her. What does it cost to ask me first?
It cost me nothing; I was wrong
"Right. Say it at the bar, so they hear it." You do.
The Company inspects what it likes
"It does. Drinks are full price for you, from now."
The well's fed from the pound. You know that. I've known it twenty years. The ale's Company water and I've sold it as spring water and nobody's died. Now you know. What does it cost me?
Nothing; it's good ale
"It is." She pours one. She does not charge for it.
It costs the truth to Stroud
Stroud tests it. Iron and pound water. She shrugs: "People have drunk worse."

He was fourteen. My boy. Went in off the wharf the week after the riot, showing off for the Hullfolk girls. Nothing to do with the Company. Everything to do with it. I don't tell people. I'm telling you.
Say nothing; stay
You stay till the lamps are out. She talks about him. Then she doesn't.
Ask why the Company
"Because the town was drunk on rising, and nobody was watching a boy."

Bram Holloway asked me to drink with him. Forty years I've known him. Never asked. I said yes. Town saw. Half of it thinks I've gone Hullfolk. I'd like the Keeper seen drinking with both of us. Tonight.
Drink with them both
The three of you at one table. The inn goes quiet, then loud again. Something has changed.
Not tonight
"Right. Then it's just me gone Hullfolk. I can live with that."
You've never asked me what the town says about you when you're not here. Everybody asks. Dray asked every week. You haven't once. Either you don't care, or you're afraid. Which?
Afraid
"Good. They say you're all right. Now you can stop being afraid, and start worrying."
Don't care
"Liar. They say you're all right, anyway. Don't let it go to your head."
You signed the Company's order and the town's paying for it. I stood up for you at moot. I won't again. That's not a threat. That's the price, and I'm telling you it before you pay it.
I'll earn it back
"Try. Start with the cellar."
The order was right
"Then pay for it yourself."

I've a spare room above the bar. Warm. Dry, mostly. Dray's house is the Company's and one day they'll want it back. This isn't the Company's. It'd cost you nothing. It'd cost me the room. I'm offering.
Take the room
You move a chest of things above the bar. Mirren keeps the house. It suits everyone, oddly.
The Keeper's house is the Keeper's
"For now. The room's there."
You sit in his chair like it's yours. It is yours. I know that. Did you have to move it to the window?
Move it back
You move it back. She does not thank you. She notices.
I like the light
"He liked the dark." She goes to the paddles.
Quenn's teaching me the gear drawings. Says I've got the hand for it. Says I could be an engineer, with papers. Papers cost. The Company pays for Company apprentices. I'm a lock hand.
Sign her as a Company apprentice
Papers. Quenn is delighted. Mirren is something she does not have a word for yet.
The gate needs its hand
"Right." She keeps learning anyway, at night.
Did he ever write to you? Before. When you were appointed. They must have told you something about him. What did they tell you?
They said he resigned
"Resigned." She says it like a word in another language.
They told me nothing
"No. They wouldn't." She almost laughs.
Wren says there's a place at the Reach where the water comes out of the hill. Says her people have always known. Says he asked them, the month before. Did you know that? That he asked them?
Go to the Reach with her
Bram receives you both. He says nothing about the water. He looks at Mirren a long time.
Ask Wren yourself, alone
Wren tells you. Mirren learns you went without her.
The hands call you Keeper. I call you Keeper. I've never asked your name. He'd have asked. He asked everyone their name. Even Vosk. What is it?
Tell her
She uses it once, testing it, and then goes back to Keeper. It is different, though.
Keeper will do
"Right. Keeper." She does not ask again.
Vosk asked me about the study. What I'd seen. I said nothing. She said 'noted'. Then she said she was sorry. Vosk. Sorry. Why would she be sorry to me?
Because she knows what happened to him
She goes white. "Then why won't she say."
Ask her yourself
She does. Vosk says 'noted' and walks away. Mirren does not go to the paddles for a day.
I've stopped expecting him. I noticed today. I turned the paddles and I didn't look at the road. First time. I don't know if that's better. I don't know who to ask.
Not better or worse; later
She nods. She looks at the road anyway, once, out of habit.
It is better
"You'd say that. You're in his chair." It is not an accusation. Nearly.
You've been to the sluice house. Don't. I saw your boots. Did you go in?
Only to the door
"Only to the door." She repeats it as if to fix it there.
Not yet
"Not yet." Her hands are shaking. "That's what he said."
Tobin told me a story about him tonight. About the Dry Year, when he was a boy, watching men go up the north bank at night. He never told me that. Why would Tobin know and not me?
Because Tobin was there
"Then I want to be there. Wherever there is."
Because he was protecting you
"From what? From knowing? That's not protecting."
If you find him. When. If. I want to be the one who's told. Not Vosk. Not Pell. Not the Book. Me, first, from you. Promise that and I'll stop asking about the study.
Promise
"Right." She stops asking. She does not stop watching.
I can't promise
"No. He couldn't either."
Keeper! Have you seen the pound at dawn from the Company house roof? Magnificent. I go up every morning. Twenty years. Nobody has ever come with me. I mention it in passing.
Go up with him
The pound at dawn is, in fact, magnificent. He does not speak for once.
The gate opens at dawn
"It does. It does. Duty. I admire it. From the roof."
The Courier calls me 'the Superintendent of Adjectives'. I have read it eleven times. I do use adjectives, Keeper. Words are what I have. I do not have a gate.
Words are not nothing
"No. No, they are not. Thank you. That was a good word."
Hesse is a Sorrel paper
"He is. He is also read in Ardent." He folds the paper very small.
I have never been to Ardent, Keeper. Twenty years with the Company and I have never seen the Board's house. They have never asked. I tell people I prefer the summit. It is not entirely untrue.
Ask why they've never asked
"Because a Superintendent who is happy where he is does not need to be managed." He knows exactly what he is.
The summit is better than Ardent
"It is! It is. Magnificent, in its way. Yes."
I heard you at the inn. 'The Company's flood.' Your words. The Company built this canal and this town, Keeper. Remember which side of the gate you stand on.
I stand on the gate
"Ah. Clever. I hate clever. Vosk is clever."
The Company's side; I misspoke
"Good. Good. We all misspeak. I misspeak magnificently."
A confession. I keep a draft of the Clearance Order in my desk, updated yearly, never sent. The Board once asked if I had a contingency, and I did not, and I never wish to feel that again.
Burn the draft
He looks at the drawer for a long time. He does not burn it. He does not update it that year.
Every Superintendent needs a contingency
"Yes. Yes! You understand. It is merely a piece of paper."

I have written a history of the summit, Keeper. Four hundred pages. Nobody has read it. I would be honored, magnificently honored, if you would. There is a chapter on the Dry Year I am rather proud of.
Read the Dry Year chapter
Forty pages. In the middle, a line about 'night works on the north bank' he has not understood himself.
Perhaps after the season
"Of course. Of course. It will keep. It has kept twenty years."
Vosk does not respect me. You have seen it. She was appointed to watch this summit and I to run it, and she has never asked my view. Do you respect me? I would like a true answer. A kind one more.
The true answer
You tell him. It is not unkind. He is quiet, then: "Thank you. Nobody does that."
The kind answer
"Magnificent. I shall believe it. I am good at that."
I have had a letter from the Board that uses the word 'retirement'. About me. I have not answered. I am asking you, as the only person here who does not want my post, what I should say.
Say the summit still needs you
He writes it. It is true. The Board withdraws the word, for now.
Ask what you'd do in Ardent
"Nothing. That is the difficulty. Nothing magnificently." He answers the Board the next day, briefly.
You have made me look a fool before the Board twice this quarter. I am not a fool. I am, at most, a man who prefers a good word to a true one. Do not confuse the two again.
I won't
"Good." He does not say magnificent. It is how you know he means it.
The truth did that, not I
"Then the truth may keep the gate. I shall keep the Company."
Keeper, a small thing. The hands have named the goose in the inn cellar after me. I have heard. I want you to know I find it magnificent. I want you to know that very much.
It is meant kindly
"Is it? Is it. Yes. I shall choose to believe that." He visits the goose.
It is a goose
"It is a goose named Pell. There is a difference, and I feel it."
Sorry. I've drawn the gate. All of it, every timber, because nobody has since Marrow. It took three months. Do you want to see it? It's roughly the size of the wall.
See it
It is the size of the wall. It is beautiful. She is embarrassed by your face.
Later; the gate needs you
"Right. Yes. The actual gate. Sorry."
Vosk asked me today what I'd told you. About the figures. I said nothing. I mean I said I'd said nothing. Which is a lie. I don't lie well. Sorry. I think she knows.
Say I asked and you refused
"I can do that. Roughly. Thank you."
Tell her the truth
She does. Vosk says 'noted'. Quenn does not sleep for two nights.
My father was an engineer on the Sorrel flight. He used to say the Meridian was built on a lie and a very good survey. I thought he meant the tolls. I've started to think he meant the survey.
What lie?
"He never said. He died when I was nine. I have his survey. I have Marrow's too. They don't agree."
Fathers say things
"They do. Mine said them with figures. Sorry. That's not nothing."
I've been offered a bribe. By Vane. To say the Sorrel gear would work in our gates. It wouldn't. I said no. I'd like it written down somewhere that I said no.
Write it in the Ledger
"In the Ledger. Yes. Where things are true."
Tell Vosk, too
Vosk notes it. Quenn is 'reliable' in a Company file for the first time.
I don't sleep. Not much. I lie there doing the reservoir sums and they never close. Stroud says it's nerves. It isn't nerves. It's arithmetic. You can't treat arithmetic.
Do the sums with her, once
You sit up till the third bell. They do not close. You both know why now.
Send her to Stroud anyway
Stroud gives her something. She sleeps. The sums wait.
I'm frightened of Vosk. I know that's obvious. I'm telling you because I've decided to stop, and I don't know how, and I thought saying it aloud to someone might be the first step. Sorry.
I'm frightened of her too
"Oh. Oh, good. I mean. Not good. Better." She laughs, once, surprised.
She is only an auditor
"She is only an auditor the way the pound is only water."
I've decided. I'm going to read the whole survey. Marrow's. Not just the tables. I've had it six years. I'd like someone in the room when I do. I'd like it to be you.
Be in the room
Four hours. At the end she puts it down and says, very quietly, 'the Quell'.
Ask Crane to sit with her
Crane sits. He reads faster than she does. He says 'duly' once, and then nothing.
You went over my head to Pell about the spindle. I know it worked. I know he said yes. I'd have liked to be asked first. I'm the engineer. Sorry. I'm not sorry. I'm the engineer.
You're right; I should have asked
"Oh. Right. Thank you. Sorry. No. Thank you."
It got done
"It did. Roughly. Next time it might not."
I've worked out where the water comes in. There's a boil off the north bank at the fourth mark, always the fourth. I could show you. It means a boat, at night. Sorry.
Go out tonight
A boil of cold water, tasting of iron, rising from under the sluice house. She writes the bearing.
Draw it for me instead
She draws it. It is very exact and it is not the same as seeing it.
I'm not going to say sorry. I've been practicing. The gate is sound, the figures are what they are, and I have done my job better than anyone since Marrow. I wanted someone to hear me say it.
You have
"I have." She does not say sorry. It lasts most of the day.
Better than Marrow, maybe
"No. She built it. I just know what it is. That's different. That might be worse."
You don't ask about the arm. Everyone asks. Then they're sorry they asked. I'd rather be asked by someone who'd rather not know than not asked by someone who's dying to.
Ask about the arm
"Year 58. Our own guns. Nobody's fault. Everybody's."
Don't ask
"Fair. It's not a good story anyway."

My men are bored. Bored soldiers are worse than angry ones. I'd like them to do something useful at the summit while we wait. Your hands are short. I'm offering. No charge. No conditions I'll admit to.
Put them on the paddles
Sorrel soldiers turning Company paddles. Crane is speechless. The gate runs beautifully.
Soldiers are not lock hands
"No. They're bored. I'll find them something. I'd rather it was yours."

Bram Holloway and I sit on the same bollard, some nights. Different wars. Same silence. He says you're a gate. He's said that of two Keepers in forty years. The other one's in the hill. Take it as you like.
Sit with you both
Three on a bollard. Nobody speaks. It is the most restful hour you have had.
Ask what he said of the other
"That he'd open the wrong door. He did."

The rifles. You know. I know you know. I'm not asking you to look away. I'm telling you that if you stop them at the gate, I'll be ordered to force it, and I won't, and then I'm finished. That's not your problem. I wanted it said.
Then I'll stop them below the gate
Crane holds them at his post under the Compact. Solas is not ordered to force a customs post. He looks at you a long time.
I won't stop them
"Understood." The convoy passes. He does not thank you. He does not sleep either.
One of mine deserted into your town. Young. Frightened. I'm supposed to want him back. I'm asking, quietly, whether the chapel's still taking people in. I'm not asking as an officer.
The chapel is taking people in
"Good." He does not look for the boy. His sergeant does, and finds nothing, and is told well done.
You should want him back
"Should. Yes." He finds the boy. He is gentle. The boy goes west.

I've been ordered to draw up a plan for 'securing the summit' in the event of 'disorder'. I've drawn it up. It's very bad. Deliberately. I'd like you to read it and tell me it's very bad, so I can say the Keeper said so.
It is very bad
"Thank you. I'll wire that. They'll ask for a better one. I'll be slow."
Improve it; a bad plan gets people killed
"So does a good one. Faster." He takes your notes. He does not use them.
My sergeant says you're soft. My sergeant says it of everyone who hasn't shot anyone. I told him you'd closed the gate on a Board member's launch. He said that's not soft, that's mad. I said yes.
Mad is fair
"It'll do. Mad's kept me alive. Soft hasn't kept anyone."
Tell your sergeant to mind his tongue
"I did. He's my sergeant. He didn't."

You gave the order I wouldn't have given. My men followed it because you're the Keeper, not because I said so. That's the last time that happens. Next time they wait for me. I wanted you to hear it from me.
Understood
"Good. We understand each other. It's rarer than you'd think."
The gate gives orders on the gate
"The gate can turn its own paddles, then."

Bram told me about the river. The old one. The one that went into the hill. He doesn't tell charter men. I'm not a charter man; I'm a Sorrel soldier who guards their coal. He told me anyway. I think he wanted me to tell you.
Tell me
"There was a valley. Lowmere. There was a river. Then there was a canal. That's the whole of it. That's everything."
Why would he want that?
"Because I'm the one with the rifles. If it comes to a choice, he wants me to have chosen already."

If it comes to the hill, and the water, and a choice about who has it, I'll hold the towpath. Not for Sorrel. Not for the Company. For whoever's in the hill with a lamp. That's you, I think. It won't come to that. If it does.
Hold the towpath
"Understood." He never says another word about it. He is there when it matters.
Hold your men back entirely
"That's the same thing, said kinder. Understood."
You keep good time. I noticed. Most Keepers open the gate when they've finished their tea. You open it at the bell. I could work with a Keeper who opens at the bell. Could you work with me?
At the bell, for anyone
"Anyone. Fine. I'll be first in line, then."
Depends what 'work with' means
"It means I stop making your life difficult. It's a big offer. Think about it."
My principals asked me what the Keeper wants. Everyone wants something. I said I'd find out. So: what does the Keeper want? Not for the gate. For you.
To know where the water comes from
She stops writing. "That's not a want. That's a problem. Interesting."
Nothing you can supply
"Everyone says that. Then they name a figure. I'll wait."

I've been offered a bribe to bribe you. By an Aldmere grain factor who assumes everyone at the summit is for sale. I've refused, for now. I'm telling you because it's funny, and because I want you to know I could have.
Thank her
"Don't. I'll want something for it eventually."
How much?
"Enough to make me think. Not enough to make me do. Yet."

I don't like the Escort Company. I pay them. That's different. Solas is a good man in a bad job, and the men above him are bad men in worse ones. If it comes to it, I'd like you to remember I said so.
Why tell me now?
"Because something's coming east that isn't coal, and I'd like to have said it before it does."
You pay them; you own it
"I pay for coal to move. What else moves isn't on my rate card." She does not quite believe it.
You told Crane about my printing press. My press. He impounded it under Schedule Two. I'll get it back in a month. I'll get you back in less. What did I do to you?
Nothing; the Compact did it
"The Compact. Right. The Compact and I are going to have words."
You'll have the press back in a week
You lean on Crane. He releases it, disapproving. Vane forgives you, mostly.

The canal's dying. Don't look at me like that. I move coal on it; I know what it's doing. The pound's falling and nobody in Ardent will say why. I want the Sorrel half before it goes. I'm telling you because you'll find out anyway.
What will you do with a dying canal?
"Fix it. Sorrel engineers. Real reservoirs. The Company won't. We would." She half believes it.
It isn't dying; it's being drained
"By what?" You do not answer. She writes something down for the first time in your presence.
I bet Crane a month's wages the pound would be up a mark by the solstice. I've lost. I never lose bets. I want to know why the pound didn't do what water does. You're the Keeper. Tell me.
The reservoirs can't fill it
"Can't. Not don't. Can't." She pays Crane and does not sleep well.
Water does what it likes
"No, it doesn't. That's the one thing about water. Fine. Keep your secret."

My principals are the same people who pay for what goes through the reeds. I didn't choose them. I'd like to choose better ones. If the Company falls, I'll need a Keeper who'll deal with a new consortium. A cleaner one. Mine.
A cleaner one, and I'll deal
"Done. Nothing on paper. Everything on your word. Delay costs; so does trust."
No consortiums
"Then it'll be the dirty one, and a Keeper who'll take their coin. There's always one."
Ilse Harrow won't sell me ale. Won't. Six years. I've offered double. Today she poured me one and didn't charge. I don't know what you did. I want to know so I can do it in Aldmere.
I drank with her and said nothing
"Said nothing. Right. I'll try it." She cannot.
You'll never manage it
"Probably not. I'll keep the free pint though."

Off every record. I like you. I don't like people; they're slow. You're not. When this canal changes hands, and it will, I'd like you on the right side of it. I don't know which side that is yet. I'll tell you when I do.
Tell me when you know
"I will. By the next watch, probably. I'm quick."
I'll pick my own side
"You will. It's why I like you. Pick fast."
You keep the Book in a plain hand. Dray's was ornamental. For the record, I preferred his. For the record, yours is easier to check.
Easier is better
"Noted. That is what I would have said."
Ask about Dray's hand
"Loops. Flourishes. Numbers where words should be. Noted, and filed."
I take my supper alone at the Company house. I have for eleven years. Tonight there are two plates. I did not order two plates. You will find this is as close as I come to an invitation.
Sit
She talks about accounts for an hour. It is, somehow, not dull.
Another night
"Noted." There is one plate the next night.
You asked the engineer about the reservoirs. She told you what she tells everyone. Then you asked again. Nobody asks again. Dray asked again.
And what did you tell Dray?
"That the reservoirs are a Company matter. You will find I am telling you the same."
I will not ask a third time
"Noted." A pause. "That was the wrong answer. It was the safe one."
I was appointed to this summit at twenty-six and told what to watch for. I have watched every day since. I am not asking for sympathy. I am telling you the length of the watch.
What were you told to watch for?
"A Keeper who reads the gauge too carefully." She looks at you. "Noted."
Eleven years is a long watch
"It is not the longest at this summit. Marrow's was longer. She is still keeping it."
The Board has asked for my assessment of your character. I have written 'diligent'. I could write 'curious'. In Ardent those are different words with different consequences. Tell me which is true.
Diligent
"Noted. I have sent it. You will find I did not believe it."
Curious
"Noted. I have sent 'diligent' anyway. That is the last kindness I have."
You have been kind to the Dray girl. For the record, I approve. For the record, it is the only thing about you I have not written down.
Why not?
"Because I owe her father something I cannot file."
Write it; I don't mind
"You should. Ardent reads kindness as alliance." She does not write it.
I have decided something. It is irregular. I am going to tell you a true thing and not write down that I did. The last Keeper did not resign. You knew that. Now you know that I know.
Where is he?
"Where the water goes. You will find I have said enough."
Why tell me?
"Because I am tired, and you are the first who has not made me more so."
You have been avoiding me for a week. You will find I notice. I have not asked why. I am asking now, once, and I will not ask again.
I have been busy
"Noted. That is the Company's word for it too."
I have been afraid of you
"Good. I am the only person here it is sensible to fear. Noted, and, for once, appreciated."
You will find I have made an error in the accounts. A real one. Mine. Nobody has noticed. If you report it, the Board will send someone to check me, and that someone will not be tired, or kind.
Report it
"Noted." Ardent sends a young man. He is neither tired nor kind. Vosk is recalled for a month.
Correct it quietly
"You will find I am in your debt. I have never said that."
